en: Preface to the Concise Commentary on the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Questions of Brahmā Viśeṣacintin):
Now, the true mind is fundamentally pure and the dharma-nature is originally void. Because it does not maintain its own nature, it manifests in accordance with conditions;

thus, beings become deluded and pursue these conditions, remaining ignorant of how to return to the source. For this reason, the World-Honored One of Great Enlightenment lamented the stagnation of sentient beings.
Compassionate toward the cyclic passage through the six realms of existence, he gave rise to the sorrow of identifying with all beings. He established a transformation of non-action;
though this state is profound and beyond words, his perfect resonance is vast and pervasive. Though empty and void of substance, wondrous forms multiply in layers.

Like the moon reflected in the cold sky as the hundred rivers flow toward it together, or like the return of spring to the great earth where all transformations share the same source—this essence is fundamentally without coming.

That the former and latter teachings of Master Ningyue differ fundamentally is due to the fact that the capacities of sentient beings are unequal, which necessitates skillful explanations in manifold ways.

Whether it be the complete manifestation of the principle of the Dharma-realm, the gradual opening of the tracks of phenomena and principle, the refutation of existence to discuss emptiness, or the censure of emptiness to praise the wondrous—none of these are not expedient means;
at no time was there a fixed doctrine. As for the elimination of the conscious mind, the severing of speech and thought, and the merging [into the ultimate],...

Is it not the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* alone that transcends the ranks of the holy and the ordinary, directly pointing to the human mind so that one suddenly becomes identical with the Buddha-body?

This four-fascicle scripture, comprising twenty-four chapters, takes the simultaneous elevation of person and dharma as its title, the light of fundamental wisdom as its essence, the true nature of all phenomena as its central doctrine, and the dispelling of doubts and the eradication of attachments as its function; it is the "fresh butter" (*mṛdv-ājya*) of the Mahāyāna.
In the mutual exchange of questions and answers between the teachers, from beginning to end, the general meaning is as follows:

to take non-explanation as explanation, non-hearing as hearing, the absence of generating the bodhicitta as generating the bodhicitta, and the absence of realizing the fruit as realizing the fruit—this is called realization.

Far removed from false delusion and transcending both existence and non-existence, it is like a clap of thunder and a flash of lightning that sweeps away all traces without leaving even a vestige; the phenomena reach their ultimate limit and the principle is profound, yet the True Mind remains.
If Du Langran is indeed so, why is the *Laṅkāvatāra* also called a "Sudden Teaching," yet this scripture alone is praised so highly?

This is because while that school belongs to the Category of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-yāna*), this one originates from the principle of Nature (*dharmatā*). Although it is said that by means of characteristics one clarifies the mind, how can this compare to fully realizing the mind and seeing the Way?
Furthermore, while that [tradition] was entrusted by Dharma and upheld by the entire world, this has long been hidden within the treasury, with no one at all recognizing it. Therefore...

One may merely know that the *Laṅkāvatāra* is worthy of esteem, yet how could one recognize that this Dharma is most supreme? Since its arrival in China, the Dharma-vehicle has flourished during these final ages;

the roots of beings have matured at this time, and those who understand it have finally met. There was a great layman, Master Huang Shunxuan, who maintained a heart for protecting the Dharma, never forgetting the entrustment.
Moved by compassionate thoughts, he carved this [text] to circulate it. I, a guest in the capital, the Grand Historian... [end of fragment].
Master Tao has opened wide his precious treasury and bestowed upon me this "Jeweled Robe. Having read it over and over again, I have gained a rough understanding of its great purport;

thus, I have composed these brief annotations, not shying away from imitating the master’s style. Drawing from the writings of Master Zhaoming and relying on the intent of the Elder [Vasubandhu], I pray for supreme goodness.

This work serves as a general introduction, grasping the lead and lifting the framework, awaiting the discernment of future scholars. Should one personally realize the Buddha-mind, they need not rely on words and letters.

To thoroughly clarify one's own fundamental matter, how could it depend on verbal explanation? Should one seek water apart from the waves, the wise would know such a person as mad, and the deluded would mock one for mistaking the reflection for the head.
Do not reject words, yet do not cling to words; whatever is brought forth is entirely this very thing. Whether it be "this thing" or "not this thing," when its function is employed, cease all doubt.
When the mind is harmonized and the intellect is liberated, what more need I say? Recognize the proper measure and know the right time—this you must do yourself.
Selected by himself at Xiansheng Temple in Yuezhong,
during the late spring of the year Wumao (the 31st year of the Great Ming Wanli era).

Table of Contents for the *Brief Commentary on the Sūtra of the Questions of Brahmā Viśeṣacintin* (End).
*The Brief Commentary on the Sūtra of the Questions of Brahmā Viśeṣacintin*, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
Annotated by the junior monk Yuan Cheng of Later Learning from Xian-sheng Temple in Kuaiji.
Revised and collated by Huang Hui, Right Attendant of the Right Spring Palace in Nanchong;
and Tao Wangling, Left Instructor of the Left Spring Palace in Kuaiji.
Revised by Fu Xinde, Left Zhongyun of the Left Spring Palace, Taoyuan.
[Note] Regarding the titles of sutras—whether concerning persons, dharmas, or a combination thereof—this sutra is of the class that mentions both person and dharma.
As for the title "Questioner: *Samsaya-vardhana* (Increasing Thought) Brahmā," *samsaya* (thought) is one gate among the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*), and *brahma*...
"Purity" (*śuddhi*) refers to the subject (*pramātṛ*). Taking purity as the subject and contemplation (*cintā*) as its auxiliary, one cultivates and realizes that which is called "learning.

For those who cannot enter into realization without the application of contemplation, Brahmā is the master capable of posing the questions, and the non-dual, absolute One Mind is the dharma to be explained.
Because the subject and object are spoken of in conjunction, it is titled the *Sūtra on the Questions of Brahmā*.
This is the Way; its systematic organization provides a thorough path so that practitioners have something upon which to progress and cultivate themselves.
Chapter One: The Radiance of the Tathāgata.
[Note] The title of the opening chapter, "The Radiance of the Tathāgata," is appropriately self-evident without further explanation, for radiance is beyond words.
In speech, everything is clear at a glance; as the ancients said, "Before the mouth has even opened, there is already a slight distinction.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove. [Note] "Thus" (*evam*) is a term used to point to the Dharma;
"I heard" (*śrutam*) clarifies that the Dharma has been received from another. Thus, the Dharma is divided into five teachings, and it is said that there are...

Regarding the essential point of the five periods, at what time and within which teaching was this sutra revealed? According to the judgment of Master Xianshou, it is subsumed under the fourth category, the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao) of the Mahayana;
it belongs to the period of the Vaipulya (Fang-deng) teachings.
At the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, I heard such a profound sutra from the Buddha.
He was accompanied by a great community of sixty-four thousand bhikṣus. [Note: Bhikṣu is here translated as "without equivalent" (wúfán).
Because both its causes and effects possess three distinct names, it is difficult to translate fully; hence it is called "without equivalent."
There were seventy-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were well known to the masses. [Note] Their fame was widespread and far-reaching, such that they were known by all.
They had attained dhāraṇī. [Note] This is translated here as "total retention" (zongchi).
Unimpeded eloquence. [Note] This refers to the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).

And various *samādhis*. [Note] This is translated here as "right view" (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*); the old translation was "right reception" (*samyak-samāpatti*). The *Awakening of Perfect Enlightenment* calls them *samādhi* and "right reception.

It clarifies that they are not "right reception" in the sense of being non-perception; it is called "darkness" (*maiti*) because one does not see, yet at the place of non-seeing, one accords with the correct principle (*samyaktva*).
This is called right view.
It is unimpeded regarding all supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). [Note: There are six supernormal powers; "all" refers to their collective enumeration.
One thoroughly understands the true nature (*tattva*) of all phenomena (*dharma*). [Note: This refers to the phenomena that are understood.]
All have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). [Note: This is the fruit to which they have arrived.

It is because through reflection one attains understanding, through understanding one practices, and through practice one realizes. Having realized it, they obtain what are called the *dhāraṇīs*, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), samādhis, and eloquence (*pratibhāna*), and are thus known by all beings.
The preceding section was a general praise of their manifold virtues; what follows is an illustration thereof.
Their names were: the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince Ratnapāṇi, the Dharma Prince Ratnakūṭa,
the Dharma Prince Ratnamudrāhasta, the Dharma Prince Ratnaguṇa, the Dharma Prince Gaganagañja, and the Dharma Prince Cittotpādavikurvaṇa.
Dharmacakra Dharmarāja, Jālinīprabha Dharmarāja, Sarvakleśavaraṇaviśodhana Dharmarāja,
Sarvadharmanirapekṣa Dharmarāja, Guṇakośa Dharmarāja, Avataṃsaka Dharmarāja, Siṃha Dharmarāja,
Candraprabha Dharmarāja, Gaurīyasa Dharmarāja, and Susaṃskṛta Dharmarāja. [Note] These are the sixteen herein.

The Dharma Prince opens the one mind into eight consciousnesses: when they are within the bonds of *saṃsāra*, they are called "consciousnesses" (*vijñāna*); when they have emerged from the bonds, they are called "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
Through the movement between cause and effect across these sixteen minds, this mind is capable of succeeding to the rank of a Buddha;

thus it is called a "Dharma Prince. In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the sixteen princes of Tathāgata Jñānavijaya who left home to cultivate the Way also took the eight consciousnesses as their symbolic representation.
Because he proceeds from the conventional toward the ultimate, he is called a "Prince" (*kumārabhūta*); because this very ultimate is itself the conventional, he is called a "Dharma Prince.
Since cause and effect are simultaneous and perfectly integrated within the single mind, this constitutes the Sudden Teaching (*tongjiao*).
If one were to establish a name based on specific virtues, there would indeed be distinctions; yet by inferring through its meaning, it can be understood.
And there were the sixteen virtuous men, such as Bhadrapāla and others. [Note:
While the previous sixteen Dharma-Princes manifest the simultaneity of cause and effect, these sixteen virtuous men represent the shared station of the sages and worthies.
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa, the Bodhisattva Jyotīrasa, the Bodhisattva Indradeva, the Bodhisattva Varuṇadeva,
the Bodhisattva Balasena, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Viśeṣamati, the Bodhisattva Vardhamānamati, the Bodhisattva Susaṃprasthitamati,
the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, the Bodhisattva Anikṣiptadhura, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, and the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa.
The Master [was accompanied by] seventy-two thousand Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, such as the Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha and the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara. [Note:
The previous passage specifically names those who are the primary audience (the *adhikārika*), whereas this passage names the assembly of listeners who accompany them.
"and the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra-devānām-indra, and so forth. [Note: This is a general enumeration, whereas what follows is a specific listing;
otherwise, there would be the fault of redundancy in the subsequent mention of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and others.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. [Note] Because this heaven governs the entirety of the Thirty-three Heavens, both the general and the specific are mentioned together.
The Yāma Heaven, Tuṣita Heaven, Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven. [Note] These comprise all the heavens of the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).
And [there were] Brahmā kings and other Brahmā devas. [Note: These are the eighteen Brahmā heavens of the Form Realm;
those of the Formless Realm are not mentioned because the faculties of those devas are dull, and they are not included within the sudden teaching gate.
Furthermore, immeasurable other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans all gathered together.
[Note] The sūtra is divided into three parts; the section ending with the introduction is the *nidāna*, and from here below is the *samyak-śāsana* (the main body of the teaching).
At that time, the World-Honored One sat surrounded by a great assembly who paid him reverent homage as he preached the Dharma. Therein was the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha.

[Note: This Bodhisattva named Jālinīprabha directly reveals that the true mind is inherently possessed by both Buddhas and sentient beings, and that ordinary persons and sages mutually contain one another, just like the luminosity of Indra’s net where large and small reflect one another;
this has been thus from the beginning and is not something achieved through artificial effort.
The meaning of this will be fully elucidated in the following "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Radiance.
Thereupon, [the Bodhisattva] rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet in salutation,
joined his palms toward the Buddha, and, shaking this trichiliocosm to guide and inspire the entire assembly, addressed the Buddha.
He said, "World-Honored One, I wish to ask the Buddha about a few matters. If the Buddha would grant me leave, I would venture to request his instruction.
The Buddha told Jālinīprabha, "Ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it for you so as to gladden your heart.

Thereupon, having received this permission, Jālinīprabha was filled with great joy and addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body surpass those of a hundred thousand [others]."
Regarding the radiance of ten thousand suns and moons, I reflect to myself that it would be most rare indeed for any sentient being to be able to see the Buddha’s body.
[Note: The physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body surpass the radiance of hundreds of thousands of millions of suns and moons;

its clarity and manifestation are such that it is fitting that everyone should see it. Yet, to say that those who see it are rare, one should understand that this refers to the *dharmakāya* of self-nature.
It is not a form or color that can be seen; it is the numinous clarity inherently possessed by me, free from all differentiation.

The sun and moon are insufficient to serve as metaphors for its brilliance. It is simply because sentient beings are obstructed by the delusions of ignorance that they are unable to see it themselves.
Those who are able to see it have thinned out their ignorance and are exceedingly rare. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "How marvelous! All sentient beings..."
It is precisely because of the attachment to deluded thoughts that one is unable to realize the wisdom, virtue, and marks of a Tathāgata;
this is what is meant by that.
Furthermore, I reflect that if there are sentient beings who are able to see the Buddha’s body, it is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
[Note]: For example, the essential substance of empty space is formless, yet it can wondrously contain all phenomena.
Were it not for the majestic radiance of the sun and moon manifesting them, all sentient beings would be unable to perceive the virtuous characteristics of empty space.
Those who are able to see them do so entirely through the power of the majesty and divinity of the sun and moon. This [Dharma] is also like this.
The Buddha told Jālinīprabha: "So it is, so it is, just as you have said.

If the Buddha did not bestow his majestic spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), sentient beings would be unable to see the Buddha’s body, nor would they be able to question him. [Note: The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "I shall turn the wheel of Dharma to enable them to attain awakening.
Within this context, there are three kinds of empowerment bestowed: first, empowerment of the body, such as emitting light to manifest and illuminate.]
The first two are called "oral empowerment," such as the opening, showing, awakening, and entering;

the third is called "mental empowerment," which involves the manifestation of spiritual consciousness within the aggregates and the skillful resolution of difficult questions. Although this is so, one must not attribute these to another Buddha;
rather, they are the movements and activities of one's own mind, all of which rely upon its power. To interpret them otherwise is called "erroneous contemplation."
Jālinīprabha, you should know that the Tathāgata has a light named *Śāntavyūha*.

If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, they are able to see the Buddha’s body without their visual faculty being impaired. [Note] The Buddha’s body must be seen with the Buddha-eye; it cannot be seen by the fleshly eye.
The light named *Śāntavyūha* is the true nature of the eye. If one can penetrate the true nature of the eye, then...
It is appropriate that one sees the Buddha’s body without destroying the faculty of the fleshly eye; previously, it was through the Tathāgata’s empowerment that one was able to see the Buddha’s body.
Hereafter, this explains how, through the Tathāgata’s empowerment, one skillfully understands questions and difficulties.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Fearless Eloquence. If any sentient beings encounter this light, they are able to question the Tathāgata with inexhaustible eloquence.

[Note: Because they have realized the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they attain fearlessness; by virtue of this fearlessness, they are able to give rise to various illusory inquiries and debates that are inexhaustible.
This is a general indication of the intent behind being able to question; what follows is a specific elaboration.
Excellent is the inquiry as to its origin.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Gathering All Roots of Goodness. If any sentient beings encounter this light, they will be able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the causes and conditions for the conduct of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
[Note: A Wheel-Turning King takes the ten wholesome paths as his cause and the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) as his practice.
The "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*) is volitional action (*saṃskāra*); "condition" (*pratyaya*) is karma. Therefore, the light is named "Accumulation of Roots of Virtue.

Subsequent passages follow this pattern. Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Pure Adornment"; if any sentient beings encounter this light, they are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the karmic causes and conditions of Śakra, Lord of Devas.
[Note: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "If a person performs a hundred great *pañcavārṣika* assemblies..."
Thus, the light named Pure Adornment of the Practice of Śakra, Lord of Devas, is trustworthy.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named Attainment of Sovereignty; if any sentient beings encounter this light, they are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the causes and conditions of the practices of Brahmā, King of Devas.
[Note: All sentient beings are bound by the five desires and cannot [attain liberation].

The karmic conduct of this deity here consists in practicing meditation while detached from desire; thus, upon encountering the sovereign radiance of the Tathāgata, one is able to initiate [the path].
Previously, when speaking of the karmic conduct of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), it included all human beings;

next, when speaking of the karmic conduct of Śakra, it included the deities of the six heavens; and herein, when speaking of the karmic conduct of the Brahmā King, it includes those of the four dhyānas.
Those who belong to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are not the intended audience for this sutra.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Detachment from Defilements" (*kleśaviraja*); if any sentient beings encounter this light, they will be able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the path practiced by the Śrāvaka vehicle.
[Note: Because the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths effectively detaches one from defilements, when sentient beings encounter it...
This is the initiation of the path of the śrāvaka.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Skillful Distancing"; if any sentient beings encounter this light, they are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the path practiced by pratyekabuddhas.
[Note: The dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination is skillfully able to distance one from birth and death.
The bustling and clamorous world is indeed the Pratyekabuddha’s cultivation of the reversal of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

If one were to follow the flow of the twelve links of dependent origination, that would be the mark of the birth and death of sentient beings through shared karma; it cannot be called "skillfully departing.

Furthermore, there are two types of Pratyekabuddhas: the first is called the *Pratyaya-buddha* (Condition-awakened), also known as the *Vargacārin* (Group-dweller), because they have teachers, disciples, and fellow practitioners.

The "Transmission" refers to those who practice cultivation; the second is called the Pratyekabuddha, also known as the "Rhinoceros-like One," who attains self-awakening in a world without Buddhas and without teachers.
Furthermore, there is the light of the Tathāgata named "Benefiting All Wisdom"; if any sentient beings encounter this light, they will be able to inquire of the Tathāgata.

Coming to the Mahāyāna Buddhist enterprise. [Note] In the preceding realm of ordinary beings, it was merely called "causes and conditions" and not "the Way," for it is not the essential means for transcending birth and death.
Although the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas speak of "the Way," they do not speak of the "Mahāyāna Buddhist enterprise," because they seek only their own benefit and are unable to benefit others.
Bodhisattvas, however, benefit both themselves and others and are capable of initiating [this enterprise].
Because it pertains to the Buddha-vehicle, the light is named "Benefiting All Wisdom. Thus, he inquires about the Mahāyāna deeds of the Buddha.

Herein, it is generally clarified that the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power can empower one to resolve difficult questions. Within these questions, there are three categories of ordinary beings and three categories of sages;
among the ten realms of existence, why are the four evil destinies not addressed? It is because those four evil destinies are not places where practitioners cultivate.

Since this is the path of advancement, it is not questioned here. If this is considered the gateway to self-benefit, as for the gateway to benefiting others, the details shall be fully provided below.
Among the six sense organs, why does the Tathāgata specifically add only the eyes and the tongue, while the other four are not added?
It is because he mentions them collectively: with the eyes one sees the body of the Tathāgata and gives rise to reverence; with the mouth one asks about the meaning of the Dharma.
Listening to these profound sounds, one discerns right from wrong; this is what is meant by "if one corner is raised, the other three do not fail to be reflected.
Within the gateway of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), all six sense faculties are empowered by the power of the Tathāgata.
One should know that when the eyes see thus, the ears hear thus, the mouth speaks thus, and even the mind thinks thus, there is nothing that is not [the work of the Buddha].
Relying on this power, Master Fu Daoshi said: "If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply these very words.
Therefore, we know that what is bestowed by the Tathāgata’s empowerment is the Dharma that accords with the nature of reality.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Benefiting Those Who Go. When the Buddha comes and goes, sentient beings who encounter the radiance from beneath his feet will, at the end of their lives, be reborn in the heavens.
[Note: Previously, the gate of self-benefit was manifested, wherein the Tathāgata’s majestic power enables the posing of questions;

thus, the "light of fearless eloquence" served as the general heading, while the subsequent six questions were the specific instances. Here, because the gate of benefiting others is manifested, the light is named "Going."
Furthermore, consider this as the general [principle], while what follows is the specific [application]. According to the time and according to the capacity, the light has various names;
yet when these are brought together and unified, they are all given the same name, "Ever-Beneficial.
For example, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "All-Adorned"; if the Buddha enters a city and emits this radiance, sentient beings who encounter it...
He attains the joy of rapture, and all manner of ornamental implements adorn his city;
within the city, treasuries of jewels surge forth from the earth. [Note: The radiance of merit and virtue.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Vibration"; by means of this light, he is able to shake immeasurable and boundless worlds.
[Note] Regarding the two types of majestic spiritual light, these belong to the *loka-prasiddha-tantra* (the perspective of worldly convention).
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Producing Joy. By means of this light, he is able to extinguish the suffering and affliction of sentient beings in the hells.
[Note] This is the light of compassion (*karuṇā*). Compassion can uproot the suffering of suffering; once it is uprooted, joy arises.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Supreme Compassion. By means of this light, he is able to cause animals not to afflict or harm one another.
[Note: This is the light of impartial compassion. Because it is impartial, one regards enemies and kin with equal vision, such that they do not afflict or harm one another.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Cool Bliss. By means of this light, he is able to extinguish the heat-affliction of hunger and thirst experienced by hungry ghosts.
[Note: Hungry ghosts, due to their stinginess and greed, receive the retribution of being miserly; they suffer the heat-affliction of craving for food and drink.

Now, encountering the Tathāgata’s light of non-self, they repent and awaken to the fact that stinginess and greed were their transgressions; they immediately experience cool bliss, which eliminates their heat-affliction.

It is said that "coolness" removes hunger and thirst, and "joy" refers to this [state]. Among these, the three evil realms, combined with the six previously mentioned questions, constitute the nine dharma-realms;
it is only the asuras that are missing, as the text is abbreviated.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Luminous Purity"; by means of this light, the Buddha enables the blind to see. [Note]: If there are...
When there is seeing, there is non-seeing; when existence and non-existence mutually oppose one another, they become turbid.
Only the blind have no seeing, and thus for them there is no non-seeing. When subject and object are both transcended, this is called clarity and purity.
Therefore, those who are not illumined by the light of the Tathāgata’s Dharma cannot know for themselves that non-seeing is true seeing; hence they are called "blind."
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Hearing Clearly. By means of this light, the Buddha can cause sentient beings who are deaf to regain their hearing.
[Note] Whereas the former [light] takes the absence of seeing as clarity and purity, this one takes the absence of hearing as "hearing clearly"; the underlying principle may be inferred accordingly.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Shame and Remorse. By means of this light, he can cause sentient beings who are deranged to regain their composure.

[Note: Sentient beings become deranged, confused, and inverted due to a lack of shame and remorse; if they can, for even a single thought-moment, recognize shame and know remorse, then their derangement will be eliminated and right view will manifest before them.
Among the six sense faculties, this passage mentions only the eye, the ear, and the mind.
Regarding the three [faculties] that do not raise [their objects]: why are the nose, tongue, and body the three?

It is because the three faculties beginning with the eye grasp their objects with sharpness, whereas the three faculties beginning with the nose grasp their objects with dullness. Those that grasp objects with sharpness are constantly associated with the discerning mind;
therefore, even if one were blind, deaf, or insane, if they did not receive the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s power of correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), they would not [attain liberation].
Because it can see but cannot hear and cannot correct itself, it is singled out for mention. That which is dull in apprehending objects is constantly in accord with the *dharmatā*;
its entire substance remains as it is, so there is no need to add anything further. The above has set forth the *puruṣapudgala-maṇḍala*.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Cessation. By means of this light, the Buddha is able to cause sentient beings to abandon the ten unwholesome paths and abide securely in the ten wholesome paths.
[Note] The bodily actions of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; the vocal actions of harsh speech, divisive speech, lying, and frivolous chatter;
and the mental actions of greed, hatred, and delusion—these together are named the ten evils. Upon encountering the light of the Tathāgata, they abandon these unwholesome deeds.
This is the practice of goodness.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Departing from Evil" (*Dūraṅgama*); by means of this light, he is able to cause sentient beings with wrong views to all attain right view.
[Note: In the former case, encountering the light one cultivates *śamatha*; in this case, encountering the light one cultivates *vipaśyanā*. *Śamatha* is the entry into goodness.
The initial gate of contemplation serves as a courageous adversary to destroy heterodoxy;

thus, coarse activity relies on cessation (*śamatha*), while subtle activity relies on contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and both require one another in succession. Now, to abandon what is unwholesome and practice what is wholesome seems to fall into dualistic views, establishing two opposing forces;
this is called "evil view" and also "heterodox view. Yet, if one observes it subtly, if evil were real...
If one cannot transform evil into good because good were real, nor can one be deluded by good to fall into evil;
yet because evil has no inherent nature, one may shift from evil to follow good, and because good has no inherent nature, one may turn away from good to follow evil.
If one can understand this lack of inherent nature, then the two views of grasping and rejecting will be abandoned; this is called right view. Question: As for...
"Those sentient beings who come and encounter this emitted light will suddenly obtain benefit; it is not like something achieved in a momentary flash. My son said:
'Cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* seems to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and I fear this is not the Buddha’s intent. He replied:

'The preceding text states that if the Tathāgata does not bestow his empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) upon sentient beings, they are unable to see the Buddha nor able to question him. Since it says the Tathāgata bestows his empowerment...'"
That sentient beings are able to see and inquire, and that they are able to cultivate and practice without contradicting the principle, is said to be due to the Tathāgata’s empowerment.

This is because the Tathāgata’s radiance illuminates the mental ground of sentient beings, causing their own understanding and livelihood to manifest before them, so that they obtain benefit according to their capacities. It is like when the sun rises and the common people [are illuminated].
Each performs its own function; it is not that the sunlight has anything bestowed upon them. Again, he asked: "The Tathāgata’s radiance is one;
why is it that sentient beings who encounter it receive different benefits? He replied:

"In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Tathāgata emits light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, illuminating eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, reaching downward as far as the Avīci hell and upward..."

Reaching up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), within which the six classes of sentient beings cycle through birth and death, receiving retributions of both good and foul, and even the appearances of Bodhisattvas practicing, attaining enlightenment, and entering *nirvāṇa*—Maitreya clearly beheld all these within the light.

While that [text] speaks of "clearly seeing the distinctions," this [text] speaks of "obtaining benefit according to one's capacity"; when these two passages are read together, the doubt may be resolved.
To summarize the essential point: all the teachings he expounds are collectively termed the "Light of the Dharma.
Furthermore, because Maitreya is a bodhisattva in his final birth, he is able to perfectly perceive all distinctions within a single ray of light;
the power of those of the three vehicles cannot reach this, as they can only see according to their respective capacities.
Furthermore, there is a Tathāgata light named Able to Renounce; by means of this light, he can destroy the stinginess and greed of sentient beings and cause them to practice giving.

Furthermore, there is a Tathāgata light named Free from Affliction and Heat; by means of this light, he can cause sentient beings who have violated the precepts to all attain the observance of the precepts.
Furthermore, there is a Tathāgata light named Beneficial and Peaceful; by means of this light, he can... [cause them... to attain peace and benefit.

Sentient beings who harbor anger and resentment all practice patience; furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Diligent Cultivation," by which light he can cause sentient beings who are indolent to all practice diligence.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Single-Mindedness," by which light he can cause sentient beings with distracted thoughts to all attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Able to Understand."
By means of this light, the Buddha is able to cause all deluded sentient beings to attain wisdom. [Note:

Because the six sense faculties are empowered by the Tathāgata’s radiance, they are able to see, hear, and perceive correctly. By virtue of correct perception, they are able to cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Through the cultivation of correct contemplation, they advance toward the six *pāramitās*, becoming distinct from the previous śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Pure. By means of this light, he is able to cause all sentient beings who lack faith to attain pure faith.
[Note: Sentient beings are bound by ignorance and attached to the notions of self and person;
thus, they are unable to give rise to pure faith toward this Mahāyāna because they are defiled by afflictions. What constitutes pure faith? What constitutes impure faith?
Ordinary people believe in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); non-Buddhists believe in the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; those of the Two Vehicles believe in partial emptiness;
and those of the provisional vehicles believe in the degrees of practice—these all cling to the conditioned and are collectively termed "impure faith.
If one believes that one’s own mind is originally perfect and pure, neither empty nor existent, beyond attainment and realization, and that its nature is suchness (*tathatā*), [this is pure faith].
That which does not belong to cultivation is called pure faith.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Capable of Sustaining"; by means of this light, the Buddha can cause sentient beings who have heard little to all attain great learning.

[Note: Sentient beings do not realize the single mind; they merely follow the traces of their practice and count the characters of the texts, so that while their studies increase day by day, their natures become increasingly callous.
Therefore it is said: if one with little learning can thoroughly awaken to one's own mind, then one will know that the myriad dharmas are entirely complete within oneself;
this is what is called "much learning," as when the World-Honored One referred to himself as the "Treasury of Much Learning" (*bahuśrutya-kośa*).

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named Dignified Conduct (*īryāpatha*). By means of this light, he enables sentient beings who lack a sense of shame to attain both shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*).

[Note: Because sentient beings lack shame and remorse, they become deranged and heedless. To have shame is to feel shame before others; to have remorse is to feel shame before oneself. To have shame is to recognize that one has not attained the virtues possessed by others; to have remorse is to recognize that one has committed faults which one does not reform. Thus it is said: *Hrīḥ* is shame regarding what is blameworthy; *apatrāpya* is fear of public reproach. *Hrī* restrains one from evil; *apatrāpya* causes one to abandon it. Shame is the root of all virtues; it is the ornament of the mind. It is the protector of the world and the foundation for attaining nirvāṇa.

Just as a great river flows toward the ocean, So do shame and remorse flow toward the state of Buddhahood. If one possesses these two qualities, one is called a true person; Without them, one is no different from a beast. One who lacks shame and remorse is like a madman; Such a person will surely fall into the three evil realms. Therefore, one should always cultivate shame and remorse, And never abandon them even for the sake of life. If one is endowed with these two qualities, One will quickly realize supreme enlightenment. Thus, the Tathāgata emits this light of Dignified Conduct, Causing those without shame to attain a sense of shame.
By reforming oneself, one becomes fully endowed with dignified deportment and attains a sense of shame and remorse.

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Peaceful Security" (*anavadya*); by means of this light, he is able to cause sentient beings with excessive desire to sever their lustful cravings.
[Note: Sentient beings, being led astray by greed and desire, frequently encounter peril and harm, falling into the evil realms; therefore, in antiquity...
People use the metaphor of honey atop a blade and a serpent beneath it to illustrate that the harm [of desire] is no small matter;
if one can distance oneself from desire and eliminate greed, the mind and body will naturally become peaceful and secure.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Joy"; by means of this light, he is able to cause sentient beings with much anger to sever it.

Anger and Hatred. [Note: Sentient beings are deluded regarding their own minds; unaware that the mind manifests as if it were external objects, they falsely establish the concepts of "self" and "others," falsely give rise to right and wrong, and falsely initiate strife and litigation.
Consequently, anger and rage arise. If one awakens to one's own mind, then within the sensory fields there will be no "self" or "others.
Since these are empty, right and wrong are unreal. When the nature of both internal and external is thusness, opposition cannot be established.
When the mind accords with equanimity, anger is transformed into joy.
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "Illumination"; by means of this light, he is able to cause sentient beings who are greatly deluded to sever their ignorance.
[Note: Sentient beings are bewildered by ignorance, as if dwelling in a long night where nothing is discernible; they are thus termed "deluded."
If delusion (*moha*) can be illuminated for even a single thought-moment, it can transform ignorance into wisdom.

Thus, the six realms of existence possess ignorance in its entirety, while the four noble stages possess it partially. Śrāvakas destroy only the afflictions of views within the realm of desire (*dhātu*), yet they remain entirely ignorant of the afflictions of thought (*vitarka*) beyond that realm.
Pratyekabuddhas partially destroy one portion [of these], and Bodhisattvas cultivate one portion of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
To shatter a portion of ignorance until reaching the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (Miaojue) constitutes the complete realization of clarity;

yet now, encountering this light and forming wisdom should pertain to the initial mind (*ādikarmika-citta*), for according to this sutra, the sudden teaching (*tunjiao*) is identical to Sublime Enlightenment. As it is said:
"The initial mind and the ultimate mind are ultimately no different. Between these two minds, the initial mind is the more difficult; those who realize its essential principle know this.
Exquisite!

Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata named "Pervasive Practice" (*sarvatraga*). By means of this light, the Tathāgata enables those sentient beings who possess equal proportions [of afflictions] to sever those equal proportions.

[Note: Among the eighty thousand gateways of the Tathāgata’s practices, there is not one that does not function in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; yet sentient beings do not realize this, remaining biased.

If one clings to one's own views and judges each other as right or wrong, yet if the provisional and the ultimate were to merge, then biased conceptualization would be forgotten and the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) would be perfectly cultivated;
thus, the "equal parts" are severed. This above is the *pratipakṣa-samudāya* (the comprehensive application of antidotes).
Furthermore, there is a light of the Tathāgata called "All Colors. By means of this light, the Buddha is able to cause all sentient beings to see the Buddha-body in its infinite varieties of colors.
[Note] This is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (ultimate tenet). While the preceding [section] concerned the counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*), this section concerns the fruit (*phala*).
Because the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*) was practiced universally within the cause, the form-body (*rūpakāya*) manifests perfectly upon the fruit, enabling sentient beings [to perceive it].
According to the occasion and according to the capacity, one perceives immeasurable kinds of phenomena as they naturally are.

To discuss this collectively, the section on "Light" is initially divided into two gates. First, within the gate of self-benefit, there are two parts: first, a general enumeration of the seer and the questioner;
second, a specific opening of six questions regarding the questioner to manifest the benefits for the practitioner’s progress and cultivation. Second, [the gate] of benefiting others.

Within the section on the gates, there are two parts: first, a general summary of the benefits conferred upon those who have gone [to hear the teaching]; second, the detailed exposition according to the four *siddhāntas*. Regarding the first, there are four sub-sections:

first, the adornment of the city and the shaking of the earth, which constitutes the *loka-siddhānta*; second, the uprooting of the sufferings of the three miserable realms so that the blind may see, the deaf may hear, and the insane may attain correctness, which constitutes the *pudgala-siddhānta*;
third, because they have both seen and heard, they then practice... (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the third *siddhānta*, specifically the *dharma-siddhānta*.)
As for the remedies: for those who are distracted, one cultivates *śamatha*; for those who are dull, one cultivates *vipaśyanā*. For the stingy, one practices generosity;

for those who transgress, one maintains ethical discipline; for the angry, one cultivates patience; for the lazy, one cultivates diligence; for the distracted, one cultivates concentration; and for the ignorant, one cultivates wisdom.
Once these six perfections are complete, one then gives rise to pure faith in the Mahāyāna. Having gained such faith, one abandons the Hīnayāna and its limited attainments.
To firmly aspire to the Mahāyāna treasury of extensive learning, and having attained such broad knowledge and erudition, to feel shame for past failings;

to look up to the Buddha’s majestic deportment, and by looking up to the Buddha’s majestic deportment, to sever the greed for acquisition, abandon grasping and rejecting, cast off anger and hatred, distance oneself from the ignorance of the knowable, and cut off all attachments to the "equal-parts" (sabhāga); thus to perfectly cultivate the holy life—this is called "confrontation."
Regarding the *Cittavistara*: herein, the manifestation of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) in its entirety is the ultimate *cittavistara*. Question:
The Buddha’s light shines universally, enabling the blind to see and the deaf to hear, even bringing those without faith to believe;

yet within the assembly of the Tathāgata, there are those who receive different teachings, some who have faith and some who lack it, and some who attain realization while others do not. Why is this so?
"Is it that the Tathāgata’s light has preferences of intimacy or distance, or is it that the sutra is not to be trusted? He replied:
"The great light of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma is like a great round mirror; all who approach behold it.

It straightens those whose robes are disheveled, rights those whose crowns are askew, and wipes away the ink from those whose faces are stained. Yet, there are those who see it and yet do not reach its intended purpose."
This is to say that when one sees a reflection in a mirror and thinks, "This is not my body," and fails to wipe it clean, whose fault is it?
When practitioners hear of the Gate of the Radiance of the Buddha-Dharma, they think, "The affairs of the sages and worthies are beyond my reach," and thus do not immediately practice cultivation;
this is likewise due to such a mindset. As the ancients said: "In general, when studying the teachings, one must skillfully turn them back and resolve them within oneself."
Do not recognize external conditions; therefore, the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.
Jālinīprabha, you should know that whether the Tathāgata were to spend one kalpa or less than a kalpa explaining the power, function, and names of this radiance, they could never be exhausted.
[Note: A *kalpa* is a period of time. There are great kalpas (*mahākalpa*), intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*), and small kalpas (*kṣudrakalpa*).
When the human lifespan is ten years, it increases by one year every hundred years for a period of one hundred years until it reaches eighty-four thousand years;
then, it decreases by one year every hundred years for a period of one hundred years until it returns to ten years. One such increase and one such decrease is called a minor kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
Twenty such minor kalpas are called a middle kalpa (*madhyakalpa*). Four such middle kalpas [constitute a great kalpa].
That which is called a *mahākalpa* (great eon) is discussed here in terms of its increase and decrease, which constitutes a *antarakalpa* (intermediate eon).
The statement that one could not exhaust [the praise] by extolling it for an eon serves only to further demonstrate its excellence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is unprecedented, World-Honored One!
The body of the Tathāgata is indeed a treasury of immeasurable radiance, and the skillful means of his preaching the Dharma are likewise inconceivable. [Note:
This concludes the eulogy of the inconceivable; what follows describes the return to one's own mind.]
“World-Honored One, from the past until now, I have never heard the name of this radiance. [Note: ‘The past’ here refers to the period of the Āgamas.
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if there is a bodhisattva who hears the name of this radiance and their mind of faith becomes pure...”
All those who are pure shall likewise attain a body of such radiance. [Note] This may be described as "turning back and returning to one's own self.

World-Honored One, we pray that today you will emit the light of the Invited Bodhisattvas, so that Bodhisattvas from other directions who are skilled in posing difficult questions, upon seeing this light, will resolve to come to this Sahā world. [Note] Previously, it was the Tathāgata himself who spoke.
Regarding the power and function of the names of the luminous manifestations: they reveal the light that is inherently possessed by all, for every person is endowed with it;
thus, Jālinīprabha was the one suited to this occasion. Now, the request addressed to the Tathāgata to emit the light of the Bodhisattvas refers to the light of skillful means (*upāya*);
therefore, the Bodhisattvas have come from other directions. Since within the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) there is neither question nor answer, [the preceding section concludes].
That you are able to see and ask these questions is entirely due to the Tathāgata’s empowerment; this is because they rely upon skillful means (upāya) based on the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi).

As for what is called "skillful means," according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra* (or *Brahmaviśeṣacinti-paripṛcchā*), it corresponds to the capacity of the individual; for hearing, reflection, and cultivation are all themselves skillful means.

At that time, having accepted the request of Jālinīprabha Bodhisattva, the World-Honored One immediately emitted a radiance that illuminated this trichiliocosm and extended throughout the immeasurable Buddha-lands of the ten directions.

Thereupon, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas from those various directions, having seen this light, all came to this Sahā world. At that time, to the east, beyond seven...
In Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of twelve Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Pure and Clean. [Note] First the ten directions are mentioned, and then specifically the eastern direction.
"East" is the head of all movement; it is where the myriad things arise. To pass through Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is to reach the limit of all movement.
Reaching the limit of all movement, one perceives the true mark (*dharmatā*). One perceives...
Because the true nature (*dharmatā*) is free from the defilements of the two extremes, the land is named "Pure.
The Buddha’s title is Sūryacandraprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there. [Note:

Because he uses the wisdom of illusion to simultaneously illuminate both extremes—just as the light of the sun and moon shines everywhere—this Buddha likewise possesses the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
It is said that because the present, by means of skillful means, lacks intrinsic nature and does not belong to the past or the future.
In that buddha-field there are bodhisattvas who are also called Brahmā-devas. [Note: That bodhisattvas are also called Brahmā-devas signifies the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Those who come from the buddha-field of Sūryaprabhāsa are those who emerge from the conventional truth through the wisdom of skillful means.
His name is *Cintāviśeṣa*. [Note: This deity is named *Cintāviśeṣa* because he is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). "Reflection" (*cintā*) takes the Brahma-heaven as its name;
"Brahma" (*brahman*) means purity (*viśuddhi*). When reflection is associated with purity, one proceeds toward the Noble Path;
when reflection is associated with impurity, one proceeds toward the realm of ordinary beings.
Abiding in non-retrogression. [Note] Because one contemplates only that which brings benefit, one does not retrogress.

Having seen this light, one arrives at the presence of the Buddha Candrasūryaprabha. [Note] Expedient practice is the skillful means by which one is summoned through the light of expedient means to the wisdom of expedient means.
Bowing his head to the ground in salutation, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I wish to go to the Sahā world to the abode of Śākyamuni Buddha to pay my respects, make offerings, and attend upon him; I also desire to receive his instructions. That Buddha likewise wishes to see us.
[Note: Both parties here are engaged in a responsive exchange within the second category of meaning.]
That Buddha said, "Go now to the Brahma Heaven; this is precisely the right time. In that Sahā world, several hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas have gathered;
you should travel through that land by means of ten dharmas. What are these ten? They are:

having no increase or decrease in mind whether faced with defamation or praise; having no discrimination in mind whether hearing good or evil; and regarding both the foolish and the wise with equanimity."

With a heart of compassion, one’s mind should always remain equanimous toward all classes of beings—superior, middling, and inferior; one’s mind should be free from duality regarding contempt or honor;
one should not perceive the faults of others’ deficiencies; one should see that all various vehicles are but the One Vehicle;
one should not be terrified even upon hearing of the three evil realms; and one should conceive the thought of Tathāgatas toward all Bodhisattvas, for a Buddha appears in an age of five corruptions.
"O Brahmā, you should conceive a sense of wonder and, by means of these ten dharmas, travel through that world. [Note:
When the Buddha Sūryaprabhāsa instructs him with these ten dharmas of practice, he is manifesting the true mark (*dharmatā*) through the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Throughout the subsequent various inquiries and debates, none of them contradict this principle.
The Brahma-deva Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I do not dare to utter the lion’s roar before the Tathāgata;
that which I am able to practice, the Buddha knows himself. Now, by means of these ten dharmas, I shall travel to those worlds and cultivate them with a single mind.
At that time, in the land of the Buddha Sūryacandraprabha, there were various bodhisattvas who addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we have attained..."

Great benefit does not arise among such evil sentient beings. [Note] Because they hear these ten dharmas and are exhorted to practice them, they realize that the Sahā world is defiled and turbid and difficult to endure;
thus, each gives rise to self-congratulation.
That Buddha said, "Good son, do not speak such words. Why is this?

If a bodhisattva were to practice the pure brahma-conduct in this land for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, it would not equal the merit of one who, in that land, maintains a mind free from anger and obstruction from morning until the meal;
the latter's merit is superior. [Note: The *Jingming jing* states that there are ten unprecedented things in this Sahā world.]

There are dharmas that are difficult to obtain which exist in this world but not in other worlds; namely, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) and so forth for the purpose of overcoming stinginess.
For this reason, practicing for a single day in this world is superior to [practicing] for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas in other worlds.
At that time, twelve thousand bodhisattvas arrived together with the Brahma-king Viśeṣacintin and made this declaration:
"We, too, wish to travel to that world by means of these ten dharmas in order to behold Śākyamuni Buddha. [Note:
They desired to come together because they had heard the Buddha’s praise of that land's excellence.

Thereupon, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, together with twelve thousand bodhisattvas, suddenly vanished from that buddha-field and arrived at the abode of Śākyamuni Buddha in the Sahā world, like a strong man bending or extending his arm;

having arrived, they stood to one side. [Note: "In the time it takes to bend or extend an arm" refers to an interval that cannot be measured; "suddenly arrived" means they reached there in an instant.]
This is not separated [from the ultimate], for it comes by means of the characteristic of non-coming and arrives by means of the characteristic of non-arrival;
one may say that its skillful means are not inferior to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
At that time, the Buddha said to Jālinīprabha Bodhisattva: "Do you see this Brahmā Viśeṣacintin? "It is so, World-Honored One; I have seen him."
[Note] Previously, when Jālinīprabha wished to invite those from other directions who were skilled in posing difficult questions, he saw that they had gathered upon seeing the light;
however, the World-Honored One did not explicitly name them as "those skilled in posing difficult questions. The following section provides the explanation to establish this point.
Jālinīprabha, you should know that among all bodhisattvas who ask correct questions, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin is the foremost.
[Note] This distinguishes him from the śrāvakas.
Among all bodhisattvas who skillfully discern all dharmas, he is the foremost; and among all those who preach sūtras according to what is appropriate, he is the foremost.
He is the foremost among bodhisattvas in terms of mental resolve; he is the foremost among bodhisattvas in terms of loving-kindness;
he is the foremost among bodhisattvas in terms of compassion; he is the foremost among bodhisattvas in terms of sympathetic joy;
he is the foremost among bodhisattvas in terms of equanimity; and he is the foremost among bodhisattvas in terms of gentle speech.
He is foremost among all Bodhisattvas who are free from anger and delusion;
he is foremost among those Bodhisattvas who first inquire with kind intent; he is foremost among all Bodhisattvas who resolve doubts.
[Note] Regarding these eleven kinds of "foremost," the first is the direct response to the meaning of the excellent inquiry, while the subsequent ones separately open up ten [further categories].

This is the primary purpose for which he was born, to repay the Buddha’s instruction through those ten dharmas. The general meaning is that because one asks with skill and correctness, one is able to discern well;
because one discerns well, one skillfully understands the teachings as they were spoken according to what is appropriate;

because one understands the teachings as they were spoken according to what is appropriate, one gives rise to a compassionate mind and bestows happiness upon sentient beings—bestowing happiness upon sentient beings consists in their deliverance.
One guides the suffering of sentient beings through the four immeasurables; desiring to guide them, one encourages them with gentle speech.
When wishing to encourage sentient beings, if they pose difficult questions, one does not give rise to thoughts of anger.
If there is something they have not yet attained, one does not deceive oneself; rather, one first greets them with kind intent and seeks to discern the truth. Once discerned, regarding...
Among all doubts, one attains certainty and is free from delusion; these are all the virtues of the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

At that time, the Brahma-Heaven Lord *Cintavistara*, together with twelve thousand bodhisattvas, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him in verse:
"The World-Honored One of great renown is universally heard throughout the ten directions."
There are no Tathāgatas anywhere who do not praise him. [Note] Śākyamuni’s great name and myriad virtues are not only held in high esteem by those of the Three Vehicles;
they are also praised by all Buddhas.
There are other pure lands where even the names of the three evil realms do not exist; having relinquished such pure lands out of compassion, [the Bodhisattva] was born here.
[Note: This verse explains the meaning of what all Buddhas have praised: to relinquish those pure and wondrous lands and be born in the five turbidities is extremely difficult.

"The Buddha’s wisdom neither increases nor decreases. [Note: This commentary on the preceding verse is intended to prevent sentient beings from falling into dualistic views—namely, that there is a pure land to be abandoned and a defiled land to be reborn in—failing to realize that the Buddha-land is eternally pure.
While sentient beings perceive it as defiled due to their ignorance, how could the Buddha’s wisdom ever increase or decrease?
Together with all Tathāgatas, by virtue of their great compassion and original vows, they dwell in this defiled and evil land. [Note:
Whenever Buddhas appear in a defiled land, it is invariably through their great compassion and original vows that they manifest their presence in such an evil land.
If a person maintains the precepts in a pure land for a full kalpa, practicing loving-kindness in this land for even a brief moment is most superior.
[Note] To re-explain the preceding meaning: For what reason do the Buddhas dwell in this evil land by virtue of their original vows? It is because their merit is transcendent and supreme;
maintaining the precepts in a pure land for a kalpa does not equal the merit of practicing loving-kindness in this land for a brief moment. Its merit is superior.
To surpass others is supreme.

If a person has committed offenses of body, speech, or mind in this land that would otherwise cause them to fall into the three evil realms, they shall experience their retribution in the present life instead.
Bodhisattvas born in this land should not harbor anxiety or fear; even if they have the sins that lead to the evil realms, such as headaches, these shall be immediately eliminated.
[Note] To restate the previous point: since the Pure Land and the land of evil have been compared, their merits over days and kalpas are mutually superior;
one should not seek elsewhere for a pure and wondrous realm while feeling weary of this defiled and evil one. Some may harbor doubts, saying:

"It is possible for the Buddhas to manifest birth through their supernatural powers, but for us, the power of ignorance is great and the power of wisdom is slight; we are not only unable to save sentient beings, but [cannot even perform] our own practice."
The Master said: "One may incur offenses of body and speech that lead one to fear falling into the three miserable realms (*trāya*).
[However,] the commentary states that these can also be eliminated in the present life, and one need not harbor such anxiety. Why can they be eliminated in the present life? The commentary states:
'Even if one has committed offenses, they may be removed by means of a headache. Formerly, the Dharma Master Śīlabhadra suddenly suffered from a headache and intended to take his own life."
Lü addressed him, saying, "Do not seek death. Because you served as king for three lifetimes, your killing was excessive;
now that your karmic retribution has sought you out, you should have fallen into the evil realms. Now that you practice the Way, your headache shall be removed. The next day, he indeed recovered.
If the bodhisattvas of this land can protect the Dharma, they will not lose right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) in every place where they are born throughout their successive lives.
[Note: Having heard that the merit of the former [practices] is superior, one desires to dwell here and practice; it is possible that all evil karma will be eliminated in the present life.
However, if it is not eliminated, one will be obscured by the subsequent aggregates (*skandha*) and lose right mindfulness—what then? The commentary says:
Do not worry about the darkness of the future life; worry only that you cannot protect the Dharma.
If you can protect the Dharma, then not only in future lives but in every birth thereafter, you will never lose right mindfulness. What is called the Dharma is precisely one's own mind;
because this mind is subtle and wondrous, no names or characteristics can reach it. Sentient beings are unable to realize their own minds.

Although it is said that one practices cultivation, in reality, this often increases forgetfulness and defilement; if one can attain wondrous awakening and constantly guard and cherish it, what cause for loss need there be?
An ancient saying goes: "When the Great Matter is not yet clarified, it is as if one has lost one's parents; when the Great Matter is already clarified, it is as if one has lost one's parents.
This is precisely that meaning.
If a person wishes to sever their bonds, extinguish afflictions, karma, and transgressions, and protect the Dharma in this land to augment all-encompassing wisdom—[Note]:
A doubt arises: "It may be sufficient to guard one's own mind so as not to lose right mindfulness;
yet if one does not eliminate the afflictions, by what means can one be liberated from bondage and increase all-encompassing wisdom? The explanation states: "You need only guard your own mind."
Then, while afflictions are not severed, they will be severed of their own accord; and while wisdom does not increase, it will increase of its own accord.
To uphold and explain the Dharma in this Sahā world from dawn until the meal is superior to doing so in a Pure Land for many billions of kalpas.

[Note] The previous statement that "pure lands and evil lands differ by factors of ten thousandfold in terms of the days and kalpas for upholding the precepts and practicing compassion" explains that pure lands and evil lands differ by factors of ten thousandfold in terms of the days and kalpas for preaching the Dharma.
I have seen the Land of Joy and seen the Land of Peace and Bliss; herein there is no suffering, nor even the name of suffering.
To perform meritorious deeds therein is not yet to be considered extraordinary. [Note] This reiterates that practicing in a Pure Land is not yet sufficient to be deemed marvelous.
To be able to endure what is unbearable within this realm of afflictions, and to teach this Dharma to others—this merit is supreme.
[Note] Re-explaining the superiority of practicing the Way and preaching the Dharma in this land over other lands:
observing this verse, it is entirely because, among the long prose passages, there are bodhisattvas before the Buddhas Candrasūryapradīpa who rejoice that they were not born amidst evil assemblies.
Although it is said that this was spoken while in the midst of birth to praise Śākyamuni, it is in fact addressed to those indolent bodhisattvas who aspire to be born in a Pure Land:
"I pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One, the Greatly Compassionate Savior from Suffering, who is able to preach the Dharma for evil sentient beings— this is truly most difficult."
[Note] This is a concluding eulogy for Śākyamuni.
The Buddha gathers an immeasurable assembly of Bodhisattvas whose names are renowned throughout the worlds of the ten directions; they listen to the Dharma without ever feeling satiated.
The Buddha gathers these Bodhisattvas whose names are renowned throughout the worlds of the ten directions; they listen to the Dharma without ever feeling satiated. [Note] One world constitutes...

Taking the worlds of the ten directions as his companions—meaning that each and every one of those worlds of the ten directions individually possesses its own ten directions—to express the extreme limit of the vastness of his assembly.
It is like the ocean swallowing all streams. [Note] This explains that the Bodhisattva Renowned Name Heard Everywhere possesses great wisdom and is able to receive the Buddha’s...
The Dharma is like the ocean swallowing all rivers.

For such people as these, he extensively expounds the Buddha-way. [Note: That the Tathāgata manifests birth in an evil land yet gathers bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions is the principle that there is no duality between them;
it is for those of such great capacity that he speaks.
"Dharma" refers to those whose faculties are capable of hearing the Dharma.
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the various devas, nāgas, and spirits have all assembled, desiring to seek the Dharma.

According to their respective faiths and inclinations, [the Buddha] speaks to the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—who have gathered together; he prays that you will now expound it for them.

[Note]: These devas, nāgas, and the fourfold assembly each have their own inclinations; the Buddha should know their profound intentions and sever all their doubts, ensuring that none are left behind or neglected.
There are those who delight in the Buddha-vehicle, as well as pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas; the Buddha, knowing their profound intentions, resolves all their doubts for them.
[Note] The previous was requested by those of great capacity; this is requested by those of the three vehicles.
Those who do not sever the lineage of the Buddha are able to give birth to the Triple Gem. [Note] This summarizes what has preceded:

although the inclinations of the two types of practitioners—the Great and the Small—differ, they are both capable of ensuring that the lineage of the Buddha is not severed and that the Triple Gem is brought forth.
"For the sake of these bodhisattvas, I now entreat the Dharma King. [Note: Although the faith and inclinations of those of the three vehicles differ, in reality they are all bodhisattvas;
therefore, I exhort the Dharma King to preach the Dharma.
The fame [of this teaching] spreads throughout the ten directions; when Bodhisattvas hear it, they all gather together, and for them he preaches the Unsurpassed Way.
[Note: The World-Honored One has long kept this unsurpassed Great Dharma secret and did not speak of it, fearing that those of the Two Vehicles would be startled and terrified.
The request made by Brahmā was not merely for those present who are capable of receiving the great transformation; rather, the name of this Great Dharma has spread throughout the ten directions.
Since those bodhisattvas have all come to hear and receive [the teaching] upon hearing of it, I exhort you to preach this Great Dharma.
This unsurpassed Great Dharma is beyond the reach of the two vehicles. [Note: This is why [Brahmā] made his request three times.

Fearing that the fourfold assembly might harbor doubts, thinking the World-Honored One was being parsimonious with the Dharma, [Brahmā] explained that it was not out of parsimony for the Dharma; rather, it is because this Dharma...
This is truly beyond the capacity of the followers of the two vehicles to illustrate.
It is by the power of our faith that we have been able to enter into such a Dharma. [Note: It is not only the followers of the two vehicles who cannot fathom it;
even we ourselves do not yet possess the portion of wisdom required, and can only enter through faith.
"Inconceivable wisdom is beyond our reach; although the Buddha is free from weariness, we now have a request to make.
We repent before the World-Honored One and pray that you will expound the path of the bodhisattva. [Note: These are the words of this Brahmā in self-deprecation, meaning:
"We truly know that we are overstepping our station in troubling the World-Honored One; though the Buddha is untiring, we must offer our repentance."]
Having fulfilled his vows, he shall preach the Great Dharma.
Chapter Two: On the Four Dharmas.
[Note] The first chapter is titled "On Radiance" because radiance is beyond words; as there is no gate for question and answer, the intermediate section merely...
To speak of the names of the radiance while not manifesting the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) would cause their traces to vanish;

therefore it is said that Prajñā is like a great mass of fire, into which one cannot enter from any of the four directions. Yet, through the Buddha’s majestic empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), one is able to see and to inquire.
Thus, there is no seeing and yet one is able to see; there is no questioning and yet one is able to question—without being entangled [in contradiction].
Not lingering in the two extremes but abiding in the middle current—this is the source from which these four dharmas arise;
hence it is said that Prajñā is like a cool pond, into which one may enter from all four sides.
At that time, after the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what is meant by a bodhisattva whose mind is firm and free from weariness? What is meant by a bodhisattva whose words are definitive and not subject to regret?
What is meant by a bodhisattva who increases their roots of goodness? What is meant by a bodhisattva who is without fear and whose dignified deportment remains unshakable? [Note]
"Non-retrogression" means that even when encountering objects that oppose one's will, one's deportment remains sovereign and is not moved by external sensory conditions.
What is meant by a Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the pure dharmas (*śukladharma*)? What is meant by a Bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of proceeding from one stage (*bhūmi*) to the next?
[Note] From "firmly stabilizing one's own mind" to "accomplishing one's own Dharma" concerns the cause-stage practice (*hetu-caryā*).
From "one stage to another stage" concerns the fruit-stage (*phala-avasthā*). Knowing the cause-stage practice well prevents the error of confused cultivation;
knowing the fruit-stage well prevents the fault of overweening pride (*abhimāna*). These six questions above all belong to the gate of self-benefit (*svārtha-mukha*).
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of means among sentient beings? What is meant by a bodhisattva’s skillful transformation of sentient beings?
[Note: These two questions concern the practice of benefiting others.

What is meant by a bodhisattva not losing the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) from lifetime to lifetime? What is meant by a bodhisattva being able to unify the mind and remain free from mixed conduct?
What is meant by a bodhisattva skillfully seeking the treasure of the Dharma? What is meant by a bodhisattva skillfully emerging from the transgression of violating the prohibitions?
What is meant by a bodhisattva skillfully obstructing the afflictions (kleśa)? What is meant by a bodhisattva skillfully entering among the great assemblies?
What is meant by a bodhisattva skillfully opening the gift of Dharma? What is meant by a bodhisattva obtaining the power of prior causes so as not to lose their roots of goodness?
What is meant by a bodhisattva being able to personally practice the six pāramitās without relying on the instruction of others?

What is meant by a bodhisattva being able to relinquish dhyāna and samādhi and return to birth in the desire realm? What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining non-retrogression regarding all Buddha-dharmas?
What is meant by a bodhisattva not severing the lineage of the Buddhas? [Note: These twelve questions above involve both self and others together;
they constitute the essential means for reaching far into the future, and no one other than a great bodhisattva could pose them.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
You are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a matter. Listen attentively now and reflect upon it well. "So be it, World-Honored One; I wish to hear it with joy," [he replied].
The Buddha told Brahmā Viśeṣacintin: "There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva makes their mind firm and remains without weariness. [Note: The preceding section concerns Brahmā.]
This concludes the general statement of the inquiry; hereafter, the World-Honored One unfolds and explains it in detail, which may be called the height of compassion.
"What are the four? [Note: This interrogates and explains the wording; subsequent instances follow this pattern.]
First, to give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all sentient beings. [Note: Seeing the suffering and affliction of sentient beings, one thinks of how to rescue them;

thus, great compassion is generated. Second, to be diligent and untiring. [Note: In rescuing others, there is nothing that precedes benefiting oneself; as for the essential means of benefiting oneself, nothing surpasses diligence.
If one does not practice diligently on the path of cultivation, compassionate vows are in vain.

Third, one must have faith and understanding that birth and death are like a dream. [Note] If one believes that birth and death truly exist and can be escaped, then to resolve to cultivate and exert effort becomes a deluded thought and is not true diligence.
If, however, one understands that birth and death are like a dream and does not abandon cultivation, this is true diligence.
To practice in this way is true diligence.
Fourth is right contemplation of the Buddha’s wisdom. [Note: The first three are distinct and serve as aids; this one is comprehensive and constitutes the core.
Otherwise, even those of the Three Vehicles and non-Buddhists may possess compassion and so forth, yet they are unable to contemplate the Buddha correctly.
If wisdom is excessive, one will likely fall into decline; however, if one can contemplate the Buddha-wisdom, their mind will become firm and free from regression.
When a bodhisattva possesses these four dharmas, they stabilize their mind and remain free from weariness. [Note: Conclusion.]
Brahmā Bodhisattva, there are four dharmas by which that which is spoken is definitive and free from subsequent regret. What are these four?
