First, one definitively teaches that all dharmas are without self. [Note: "All dharmas" refers to the aggregates, bases, and elements, as well as mundane and supramundane dharmas such as bodhi and nirvāṇa.
If one were to say that there is a self, then what would that self be?
When one investigates that the self is fundamentally non-existent, what is spoken becomes definitive.
Second, it is definitively taught that among all places of birth, there is nothing to be delighted in. [Note: If phenomena possessed a self, then there would be places of birth to be delighted in;
but when one investigates and finds no self, it is definitive that there are no places of birth to be delighted in.

Third, one must resolutely and constantly praise the Mahāyāna. [Note: If one clings to the fixed notion that there is no self and no place of birth, one still falls into doubt and descends to the path of the Two Vehicles.
One must know that while all phenomena are without self, there is no "non-self" apart from them; while all phenomena are without birth, there is nothing that does not arise.
Only when one accords with the perfectly interfused true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Mahāyāna, free from all doubts, can one be said to have attained it.
The definitive teaching consists of four points;
the fourth is the definitive teaching that the karma of transgression and merit is never lost—this constitutes the four. [Note] The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"There is no agent, no creator, and no experiencer, yet the karma of good and evil does not perish. This may indeed be called a definitive teaching.
Brahmā Bodhisattva, there are four dharmas that increase the roots of goodness. What are the four? First, upholding the precepts; second, extensive learning; third, giving. [Note:
The precepts can produce concentration, and extensive learning produces wisdom. Concentration encompasses the five perfections, while wisdom possesses the single gate.
The five perfections increase merit, and the single gate increases wisdom. When wisdom is complete, it possesses the dharma of giving; when merit is complete, it possesses giving.
Because it concerns material wealth, generosity follows after concentration and wisdom. As for what is called generosity, it is the relinquishing of all that one possesses;
as the Sūtra says, it is giving without attachment to sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, and so forth.

The fourth is renunciation; these constitute the four. [Note: There are three types of renunciation: first, renouncing the worldly household, as exemplified by the fourfold assembly currently present;
second, renouncing the household of the triple world, as exemplified by the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; third, renouncing the household of ignorance, as exemplified by the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
Regarding the first, one is encouraged to cultivate concentration and wisdom; once concentration and wisdom are perfected, one is encouraged to practice the distribution [of merit].
To practice giving is to relinquish all that one possesses; to relinquish all that one possesses is to be unattached to everything.
This lack of attachment is called "leaving home. One who thus leaves home is able to increase their roots of goodness.
Brahmā-deva Bodhisattva possesses four dharmas by which he is without fear and his majestic deportment remains unshakable.
What are these four? First, loss of profit; second, ill repute; third, humiliation; and fourth, suffering and affliction. These are the four. [Note:
These four are all circumstances contrary to one's wishes; when a practitioner encounters them, it is easy for their mind to be moved and for fear to arise. If there is loss...
If gain is not a cause for anxiety, ill repute not a cause for distress, and humiliation not a cause for shame;

if suffering does not oppress and one does not give rise to fear when encountering adversity, then one will not be moved or shaken when encountering favorable conditions, and one’s dignified demeanor will remain ever as it was.
Brahmā Bodhisattva has four dharmas by which he accomplishes the pure dharmas (*śukladharma*). What are these four? First, teaching others to believe in sin and merit;
second, practicing giving without seeking karmic retribution; third, guarding and protecting the true Dharma;
fourth, instructing all bodhisattvas with wisdom. These are the four. [Note: By believing in sin and merit, the wondrous path may be expected. Seeking retribution...
To respond with karmic retribution is conditioned; to personally take responsibility for protecting the True Dharma ensures that Māras and heretics cannot interfere;
and to instruct Bodhisattvas causes the Buddha-wisdom to gradually unfold. First, one teaches people to believe in the laws of sin and merit; finally, one uses wisdom to instruct Bodhisattvas.
Although these two teachings are divided into beginning and end, they share the same ultimate aim: the Buddha-wisdom that benefits others. Second, one practices giving without seeking reward.
Third, guarding the True Dharma; and second, although these two practices follow one another in sequence, they both lead toward the Buddha Vehicle for the benefit of oneself.
Māra-deva, there are four dharmas by which a Bodhisattva well knows how to proceed from one stage to the next. What are the four? First—
First, having long planted roots of goodness; second, being free from all faults and transgressions; third, skillfully knowing the means of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*);
and fourth, practicing with diligent vigor. These are the four. [Note: These are causes from the past.

If there were no past causes, it would not be easy to resolve the mind [for enlightenment], as there would be many obstacles and much affliction. Since one already possesses roots of goodness from the past, one shall now be free from them in the present.
Faults are remedied through cultivation; yet while it is said that one must cultivate and advance, one must know the skillful means of dedication and remain unattached to seeking for oneself.
If one seeks for oneself, it becomes a delusion. Although it is said not to seek for oneself, one must not dismiss or ruin one's progress in cultivation.
If one dismisses it and does not practice, how can one proceed from one stage to the next?
In these aforementioned six chapters, the sequence of arising begins first with making the mind firm; when the mind is firm, one’s words become decisive;
when one’s words are decisive, one increases the roots of goodness; when the roots of goodness increase, one is not moved by favorable or adverse conditions;
when one is not moved by favorable or adverse conditions, one is able to accomplish the white dharmas (pure qualities). The white dharmas...
When these are accomplished, one can proceed from stage to stage, moving from cause toward fruit; thus, self-benefit is perfected.
Brahmā, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva skillfully understands the means (*upāya*) among sentient beings. What are the four? First, to accord with the inclinations of sentient beings;
second, to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) regarding the merits of others; third, to repent and eliminate [faults]; [fourth, to practice dedication].

The fourth transgression is to exhort and entreat the Buddhas; these constitute the four. [Note: Skillfully adapting to and meeting the needs of others without opposing their capacities, one rejoices in and praises them so that they may progress, repents of their offenses so that dark karma may be silently extinguished, and entreats the Buddhas so that the lamp of the Dharma shall not be extinguished.
Within the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), these four matters do not originally exist; yet, from the perspective of transforming sentient beings, one does not lose the skillful means.
Brahmā Bodhisattva possesses four dharmas for skillfully transforming sentient beings. What are these four? First, constantly seeking to benefit sentient beings.
[Note: One who wishes to transform sentient beings should regard all sentient beings as being like an only child;
regarding them as an only child, one should constantly contemplate how to bring them benefit.
Second, one personally relinquishes one’s own happiness. [Note] The reason for benefiting others is that one must first relinquish one’s own happiness and then cause them to find joy;
this is because sentient beings are blinded by pleasure, as in the case of the World-Honored One who left home to practice the Way and so forth.
Third, mental harmony and patience. [Note] Mental harmony means dwelling together without contention; patience means not retaliating against arrogance.
Fourth, the relinquishing of pride. These are the four. [Note] By relinquishing pride, those who study will hold one dear and affectionate. These are the four.
These are all matters concerning the transformation of sentient beings.
Brahmā, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva does not lose the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) from lifetime to lifetime. What are these four?
First, constantly recollecting the Buddha; second, dedicating all performed merits toward enlightenment; third, drawing near to virtuous [friends].
The four kinds of spiritual friends are: praising the Mahāyāna; these constitute the four. [Note: To mindfully recollect the Buddha is to have illumination and awakening without obscuration;
to take bodhi as one's goal is to ensure that one’s cultivation and progress do not falter; to rely on spiritual friends is to receive instruction without weariness;
and to praise the Mahāyāna is to not scheme for minor paths—what loss could there be?
Brahmā, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva can unify their mind so that it is free from mixed practices.
What are these four? First, to be free from the mind of a śrāvaka; second, to be free from the mind of a pratyekabuddha; third, to seek the Dharma without weariness;
and fourth, to extensively explain the Dharma as one has heard it for the sake of others. These are the four. [Note: Not to accept the nirvāṇa with remainder, nor to find it pleasing.]

Solitary liberation is what is called "the ocean swallowing all streams. To preach according to what one has heard means that one’s own practice and the transformation of others are never two different paths;
their minds are always one. The first three [aspects] refer to making one's own mind one, while the latter one refers to transforming the minds of others into one.
Brahmā-deva Bodhisattva, there are four dharmas for skillfully seeking the treasure of the Dharma. What are the four?

First, one should conceive the thought of a jewel regarding all dharmas because they are difficult to obtain. [Note] This refers to the fact that throughout immeasurable kalpas one has never before heard such a Dharma as this;
it is called "difficult to obtain. It is like the constant offering of the mind, the Medicine King, the Great Being who burned his own arm, and the one who offered his entire body.
When the Wheel-Turning King sits thus seeking the Dharma, he regards it in all cases as a precious jewel.
Second, he conceives the thought of medicine regarding all dharmas, because they cure all illnesses. [Note: Of the eighty-four thousand diseases of affliction, only the Dharma serves as the remedy.
Third, one should conceive the thought of wealth and profit regarding all dharmas because they are never lost. [Note: Worldly wealth and profit are easily gained but easily lost;

the wealth and profit of the Dharma-treasure, once gathered and stored within the *ālayavijñāna*, remains inexhaustible for eternal kalpas. An ancient saying goes: "In studying the Way, one must seek enlightenment;
in providing for one's livelihood, one must seek abundance. If one studies the Way and studies the means of livelihood together, each and every person will achieve success.
The Buddha acts as the patriarch.
Fourth, because one gives rise to the perception of suffering within arising and ceasing among all phenomena until reaching nirvāṇa—these are the four. [Note:

Sentient beings are tormented by the eight sufferings and long remain submerged in birth and death; only the wondrous Dharma of the Buddha is called that which can extinguish them and lead to nirvāṇa.
Because of this turning back.
Brahmā, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva skillfully emerges from the offense of violating the prohibitions. What are these four?

First, attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), because all dharmas have no coming; second, attaining the patience of the non-extinction of dharmas, because all dharmas...
First, because there is no going, one attains the patience of conditions (*pratyaya-kṣānti*), for one knows that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions.

Second, one attains the patience of non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita-kṣānti*), because there is no continuity of distinct mental states. These are the four. [Note: Since all phenomena come from nowhere and go nowhere, one knows they are all produced by causes and conditions.
When that which arises from conditions is understood as a conjuncture of illusions, one attains non-abiding. That which is non-abiding—
Not abiding in the past, not abiding in the future, not abiding in the present; not abiding within, not abiding without, not abiding in between;
since the nature of the three periods of time is empty and nothing is to be obtained internally or externally—who is it that upholds the precepts, and who is it that violates them?
To realize this thoroughly is to be able to skillfully emerge from one's offenses.
Brahmāvatī Bodhisattva, there are four dharmas that effectively obstruct the afflictions. What are these four? First, right mindfulness;
second, restraining the sense faculties; third, attaining the power of wholesome dharmas; fourth, dwelling alone in seclusion. These are the four.
[Note] Afflictions arise from a deviant mind; if one recollects the correct, the deviant does not arise. When the deviant does not arise, afflictions are not produced.

Although afflictions may arise, deviant thoughts are actually due to the six sense organs falsely perceiving their objects. If the six sense organs are blocked and stilled, external攀缘 (pān-yuán—clinging to objects) is severed, and one becomes profoundly tranquil in that very place.
When clinging is severed, afflictions cease; this is what is meant by "the faculties being blocked. Since the faculties are thus... [text truncated]
Regarding the forms and characteristics of the objects of perception, these two [factors] counteract their causes.

Speaking in terms of their correspondence, when the mind attains the power of wholesome dharmas, by what means could afflictions arise? Speaking in terms of severing conditions, one who dwells alone always values sitting in meditation;
through seclusion, one abandons all sensual desires.
Brahmā Bodhisattva possesses four dharmas for skillfully entering great assemblies. What are these four? First, seeking the Dharma and not seeking victory;
second, possessing a mind of reverence free from arrogance; third, seeking only the benefit of the Dharma and not manifesting oneself;
fourth, teaching others the wholesome Dharma and not seeking fame or profit. These are the four. [Note: Not seeking victory prevents contention.
Only by severing inferior learning can one attain higher realization; how could arrogance ever be permitted?
When one’s inner state is manifest as truly real, there is no further reception of dharmic benefits. If one seeks fame and profit, likes and dislikes will arise;
once likes and dislikes arise, even if one uses wholesome teachings to instruct others, they will not be believed.
Brahmā Bodhisattva possesses four dharmas by which he skillfully opens the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).

What are these four? First, guarding the Dharma; second, benefiting one’s own wisdom while also benefiting others; third, practicing the dharma of virtuous persons; and fourth, showing people the distinction between defilement and purity.
These are the four. [Note: "Dharma" refers here to the Mahāyāna single mind (*ekacitta*); this mind is beyond all dependence and transcends the person.
Our current state is largely due to being obstructed by beginningless false habitual tendencies; thus, we merely provide protection.
As the ancients said, "Like a hen brooding over her eggs," and as the Book of Documents says, "As if standing on the brink of a deep abyss, as if treading upon thin ice.

Furthermore, the expressions "cautious and reverent" and "apprehensive fear" all convey the meaning of cherishing and protecting. If one can thus guard this mind, it will not only benefit oneself but also be able to benefit others.
Since he himself lacks the desire for goodness, it is impossible for him to transform others toward goodness; such a thing cannot exist. As for what is called defilement and purity:
attachment to the five desires is defilement, while detachment from the five desires is purity. Attachment to a self is defilement, while non-attachment to a self is purity.
Discrimination is defilement, while non-discrimination is purity. Furthermore, that which involves apprehension is defilement, while that which is without apprehension is purity.
Purity, etc.
Brahmā-deva Bodhisattva, there are four dharmas by which one obtains the power of prior causes and does not lose one’s roots of goodness. What are the four?

First, seeing the deficiencies of others, one does not regard them as faults. Second, toward those who are angry, one constantly cultivates a mind of loving-kindness. Third... [text continues]... Fourth... [text continues].

These four are: first, constantly contemplating the causes and conditions of all phenomena; second, constantly contemplating the Dharma; third, constantly recollecting the causes and conditions of evil; and fourth, constantly keeping bodhi in mind. [Note] This is self-exhortation.
To speak of the causes and conditions of evil is to take them as precepts; to speak of the causes and conditions of good is to take them as the Dharma.

To keep the awakening mind in mind means that in every birth one does not lose clarity through the power of prior causes. When one does not lose clarity in every birth, the roots of goodness flourish.
How could there be any error?
Brahmā-deva Bodhisattva possesses four dharmas by which he is able to practice the six pāramitās spontaneously without relying on the instruction of others.
What are these four? First, leading people through giving; second, not speaking of the transgressions of others who have violated the precepts; third... [text truncated]
First, skillfully knowing how to gather disciples through the Dharma to transform sentient beings; second, understanding and penetrating the profound Dharma—these are the four. [Note:

One must first give away what one possesses before others will submit to one’s transformation. This is as the Great Master Shandao taught when he used money to encourage people to recite the Buddha’s name.
To speak of another’s transgressions while taking those transgressions upon oneself is not the way to save oneself; therefore, this is not permitted.

It is not the case that speaking is categorically forbidden; rather, if a person who has transgressed the prohibitions comes to a Bodhisattva seeking earnest repentance, the Bodhisattva must rely on the methods of guidance (*saṃgraha-vastu*) or determine the nature of the offense according to the Vinaya to induce a sense of shame and remorse.

Alternatively, by directly pointing out the true nature of reality so that they realize the emptiness of the nature of offenses, the Bodhisattva may also preach the Mahāyāna Six Perfections for the sake of transforming sentient beings.

Because it is not something known by those of the two vehicles, it is called the "profound Dharma. If one can understand and penetrate it, then one will practice spontaneously without relying on the instruction of others.

Brahmā-devaputra, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva is able to relinquish meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and return to birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). What are these four?
First, their mind is supple and soft; second, they have attained the power of all roots of goodness; third, they do not abandon any sentient beings;

fourth, they skillfully cultivate the power of wisdom and skillful means. These are the four. [Note: In the Hīnayāna, because one loathes the coarse and seeks the sublime, one subdues the distracted mind to enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
In the Mahāyāna, once the mind has attained suppleness and softness, the coarse and the sublime are equalized.

When observing that meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and desire (*kāma*) are non-dual, if one does not obtain the power of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), one will become attached to and fail to relinquish meditative concentration;
how then could one be reborn in the realm of desire? To obtain the roots of goodness, sentient beings alone are the object of focus (*ālambana*).

Therefore, one must not abandon sentient beings in order to be born in the realm of desire. This requires skillful wisdom and means (*upāya*). As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Only when there is wisdom..."

Thus, one is bound by wisdom lacking skillful means, and liberated by skillful means accompanied by wisdom; one is bound by skillful means lacking wisdom, and liberated by wisdom accompanied by skillful means.
Brahmā, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains non-retrogression regarding all Buddha-dharmas.
What are these four? First, undergoing immeasurable births and deaths; second, making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas; third, practicing immeasurable...
The four aspects of the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*) are: having faith and understanding in the immeasurable wisdom of the Buddhas; these are the four. [Note:

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are deluded regarding birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and thus suffer retrogression; those of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*) fear birth and death and thus fail to achieve progress.

The Bodhisattva undergoes immeasurable births and deaths without weariness toward the Buddha-dharma and does not suffer retrogression. By making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) become deep.

When the heart of profound compassion is extensively spread, there will be no conditions for regression; because the heart of compassion is immeasurable, one can undergo immeasurable births and deaths;
because one serves immeasurable Buddhas, one can realize the immeasurable wisdom of the Buddhas.
Brahmā Bodhisattva, there are four dharmas that do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas. What are these four? First, not retreating from one’s original vow;
second, ensuring that one’s words are necessarily put into practice; third, possessing great aspiration and diligence; and fourth, practicing the Buddha-way with a profound mind. [Note:
Although one may arouse diligence, if it is not in accord with the Buddha-way, it is not true diligence. This is because [the diligence] of the two vehicles...
Because all non-Buddhists (tīrthika) claim to be diligent,
these four dharmas constitute the means by which a bodhisattva does not sever the lineage of the Buddhas. When these four dharmas were being taught,
twenty-two thousand devaputras and humans all resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and five thousand [others likewise did so].

When those who have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) arrived from the ten directions, the bodhisattvas who had come to pay homage to the Buddha scattered celestial flowers,
which completely covered the great trichiliocosm until they reached the height of the knees.
Chapter Three: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Correct Inquiry [Note]:

Regarding the origin of this chapter, because the World-Honored One praised Brahmā for being the foremost among those who could correctly inquire concerning bodhisattvas, Brahmā raised twenty-one questions, to which the World-Honored One answered point by point in accordance with them.
This is the intent of his coming; yet Jālinīprabha interrogates him as to why he has come. Is it not certain which of these constitutes the "correct question"?

If being able to ask is the correct question, then one is attached to the notions of self and person (*ātman-pudgala*). If being unable to ask is the correct question, then one falls into mere cleverness.
Apart from these two, what is it that constitutes the correct question? Therefore, this chapter is titled "The Correct Question," for there is indeed such a thing as the correct question.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha asked the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin: "The Buddha has declared you to be the foremost among those who ask questions correctly regarding bodhisattvas.
What is it that constitutes a bodhisattva’s question as being 'correctly asked'? Viśeṣacintin replied: "Jālinīprabha..."

If a bodhisattva asks questions based on the distinction between "self" and "other," this is called a wrong question. [Note] To have a "self" who asks and a "other" who answers is what is meant by a wrong question.

To ask questions that involve conceptualizing phenomena is called a wrong question. [Note] Regarding phenomena which are fundamentally without subject or object, to falsely give rise to conceptualization is so stated.
To give rise to delusive desire by discriminating phenomena is an erroneous question.
If one asks without [the notions of] self and other, it is called a correct question; to ask without discriminating phenomena is called a correct question. [Note:
If one does not discriminate phenomena, then both self and other are forgotten; internally there is no mind that asks, and externally there is nothing that is asked.
Regarding this Dharma, there has been no master before who could answer it; unattached in the three locations, it is tranquil in the middle, falling neither into subject nor object.
This is called the "correct question. This serves as a general revelation that all that is opened up in the following text is nothing other than an explanation of this:
one should not differentiate regarding phenomena, and one should not be attached to questions concerning self and other.
Furthermore, Jālinīprabha, to ask by way of arising is called an erroneous question; to ask by way of cessation is called an erroneous question;
to ask by way of abiding is called an erroneous question. To not ask by way of arising, not to ask by way of cessation, and not to ask by way of abiding is called a correct question.
[Note: Arising, abiding, change, and cessation are the characteristics of the mundane world, not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is without arising, abiding, or ceasing; therefore, if one asks while clinging to worldly characteristics, it is called a "deviant question.
If one asks without clinging to worldly characteristics, only then does it accord with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); this is called a "correct question.
For example, Layman Pang asked Mazu, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion? Mazu replied, "Wait..."
If you were to draw up all the waters of the Western River with a single mouthful, this would be an instance of not being subsumed by the four marks.
Furthermore, Jālinīprabha, if a bodhisattva asks for the sake of defilement, it is called an erroneous question; if they ask for the sake of purity, it is called an erroneous question.
[Note: Regarding the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), what is defiled and what is pure? To ask in this manner is to contradict the reality limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
These are erroneous questions.
To ask for the sake of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is called an erroneous question; to ask for the sake of transcending birth-and-death is called an erroneous question;
to ask for the sake of *nirvāṇa* is called an erroneous question. [Note: Birth-and-death is that which causes delusion; transcending birth-and-death is that which constitutes cultivation.
Since taking *nirvāṇa* as that which is realized involves both the subject and the object, how could it not be erroneous?

If one does not ask for the sake of defilement or purity, does not ask for the sake of birth-and-death or transcending birth-and-death, and does not ask for the sake of *nirvāṇa*, this is called a correct question.
[Note] The following provides the explanation and establishment of this point.
Why is this so? Within the station of dharmas (*dharmapada*), there is neither defilement nor purity, neither birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) nor nirvāṇa.

[Note: This directly reveals that within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), such names and characteristics do not exist; for to give rise to the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of the reality of nirvāṇa and birth-and-death as opposites is itself a fabrication.
[Question: In the preceding text, it was stated that arising, abiding, change, and cessation are the characteristics of the movement of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
In this context, birth and death are the conditions for the beginning and end of sentient beings. Sentient beings wander in delusion and do not return;
the Buddha has revealed this to enable them to know how to weary of birth and death and seek nirvana—this is what the Buddha taught. Now you ask:
since this is a false teaching, how can it be a correct answer? Even within the teachings of the Three Vehicles, there are provisional explanations that do not destroy the means [of liberation].

In the teaching of the True One Vehicle, if one does not establish expedient means, the question becomes erroneous; yet if one does not destroy expedient means, they serve as a provisional method for guidance.
If one does not establish expedient means, one points directly to the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
If one remains stuck in the provisional, one is deluded regarding the real—how could this be considered a correct question?
Furthermore, Jālinīprabha, if a bodhisattva asks for the sake of vision—[note: this refers to the Path of Vision (darśanamārga)]—or asks for the sake of abandonment—[note:
this refers to the abandonment of afflictions (kleśaprahāṇa)].
He asks for the sake of realization; [Note: this refers to realizing nirvāṇa.
He asks for the sake of cultivation; [Note: this refers to cultivating the holy life (brahmacarya).
He asks for the sake of attainment; [Note: this involves calculating that there is something to be attained.]
One asks for the sake of the fruit. [Note] To reckon that there is something realized is called a false question.
[Note] This is a refutation directed at the three vehicles.
If there is no view, [Note] this explains right view.
There is no abandonment. [Note] Delusion has no intrinsic nature.
There is no realization. [Note] Nirvāṇa is unconditioned.
There is no cultivation. [Note] The holy life is signless.
There is no attainment. [Note] The essence is fundamentally complete.
There is no fruit. [Note] It ultimately does not exist.
Therefore, to inquire thus is called a correct inquiry. [Note] This is shown in response to the One Vehicle.
Furthermore, because Jālinīprabha [asks] whether this is wholesome or unwholesome, his inquiry is termed a "perverse question"; it is a worldly dharma. [Note:
This refers to the dharmas of the three realms of existence.
It is a supramundane dharma. [Note: This refers to the dharmas of the four noble ones.

These are dharmas of transgression; these are dharmas without transgression; these are dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava*). [Note: Because all three realms of existence (*bhava*) in the world possess outflows.
These are dharmas without outflows (*anāsrava*). [Note: Because the four noble ones (*ārya*) who have transcended the world are all without outflows.
These are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). [Note: This is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
These are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). [Note: This is ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

To ask questions regarding these two types of phenomena based on such [dualistic] attachments is called a wrong question (*mithyā-praśna*). [Note: This refers to the very intention [behind the question].]
A single movement of thought immediately deviates from it.
If one does not perceive duality—[Note] the immeasurable is itself the one—one does not perceive non-duality either. [Note] even the one does not exist.
This is called the "Correct Question. [Note: When a non-Buddhist asked the Buddha whether he spoke of existence or non-existence, the World-Honored One remained seated.
The non-Buddhist praised him, saying: "The World-Honored One’s great compassion has cleared away the clouds of my delusion!
To not ask about 'existence' is to not see duality; to not ask about 'non-existence' is to not see non-duality. To question in this manner is indeed to be without [conceptualization]."
Question: "The World-Honored One took his seat; this was neither an answer nor a question.

By saying 'no answer,' he opened the clouds of my delusion, whereby the non-Buddhists lost both their eyes. Nevertheless, if one can understand this, it may be called a correct understanding of the question."
Furthermore, Jālinīprabha, if a bodhisattva discriminates when inquiring about the Buddha, it is called an erroneous inquiry. [Note] "Buddha" means awakening;
if one is attached to discrimination, one does not awaken.
Discriminating dharmas. [Note: "Dharma" means equality; if one clings to discrimination, it is no longer equal.
Discriminating the Sangha. [Note: "Sangha" means harmony; if one clings to discrimination, it is no longer harmonious.
This serves to exclude the arising of views regarding the Triple Gem and so forth when posing questions.
Distinguishing sentient beings. [Note: Primary retribution.
Distinguishing Buddha-lands. [Note: Secondary retribution.
Distinguishing the various vehicles. [Note: The gate of practice.]
To ask whether phenomena are identical or different is called a false question; to not ask whether phenomena are identical or different is called a correct question. [Note:
This distinguishes that one should not give rise to discriminative questioning regarding the gate of relying on correct practice. As an ancient said:
"If you wish to attain the primary correspondence, do not bring questions to ask."
Furthermore, Jālinīprabha said: "Brahmā, what is meant by 'all dharmas are correct' and 'all dharmas are erroneous'?
[Note: If a dharma is correct, it cannot admit the erroneous; if a dharma is erroneous, it does not receive the correct.
Why is it that the erroneous and the correct are both the same single dharma, yet give rise to mutually contradictory characteristics?"
Brahmā said: "Because there is no mind within the nature of all phenomena, all phenomena are termed 'correct' [samyak]. [Note:

If one realizes that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, then the mind has nothing upon which to rely; when the mind has nothing upon which to rely, conceptual discrimination is extinguished, and thus they are termed 'correct.
This may be called the abiding of phenomena in their own place."
If one uses the mind to conceptually discriminate within phenomena that are themselves mindless, all such phenomena are termed "erroneous. [Note:

All phenomena are originally mindless; not knowing them to be so, one employs the mind to engage in discrimination, and thus they become erroneous—just as when clouds move, the moon appears to move, or when a boat travels, the shore seems to shift.

The fact that all dharmas are devoid of characteristics is called "correct. [Note: For example, a mountain has height as its characteristic, water has depth as its characteristic, the eye has seeing as its characteristic, and the ear has hearing as its characteristic. Yet each of these is without mind:

the mountain does not say, "I am high," and thus it is devoid of the characteristic of height; water does not say, "I am deep," and thus it is devoid of the characteristic of depth; the eye does not say, "I..."
Seeing is simply the departure from the characteristic of seeing; it does not mean that hearing departs from the characteristic of hearing.
Yet the mountain remains thus high and the water thus deep, the eye thus sees and the ear thus hears, without leaving their original positions; therefore, this is called "correct."
If one does not have faith and understanding that this is the state of being free from marks, one is then discriminating among all phenomena.
If one discriminates among all phenomena, one enters into overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Whatever is thus discriminated is called "erroneous. [Note:

Not understanding such a state of being free from marks, one uses the mind to discriminate, saying of the mountain, "I am high," of the water, "I am deep," of the eye, "I see," and of the ear, "I hear."
To hear it thus is called the discrimination of dharmas that results in the attainment of a mind of existence, leading one to enter into overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Therefore, whatever is discriminated is termed "erroneous. As the ancients said: "If this is so, you are adding a head upon a head;
if this is not so, you are cutting off your head to seek life. Because one discriminates and grasps at the marks of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it is not [the truth].

This attachment to the characteristic of detachment while severing conceptualization is also not the reason why it is said that one is "skillfully able to discern," for such a person remains unmoved regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Jālinīprabha asked, "What is meant by the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena? Brahmā replied, "All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and devoid of desire."

This limit is called the "Right Nature" (*samyaktva*). [Note: To be free from intrinsic nature means there is no self-substance internally; to be free from the limit of desire means there is no functional characteristic externally.
Since both internal and external are detached, the middle must transcend all dependence; this is termed the "Right Nature."
Jālinīprabha said, "Few are able to understand such a true nature. Brahmā said, "This true nature is neither one nor many. [Note:
What is called the "true nature" is that which is inherently possessed by every person; it is so for all phenomena (dharmas). Because there is no one who can understand it, it is not many;
because there is no one who cannot understand it, it is not few. Since there is no one who can understand it, it is not many; since there is no one who cannot understand it, it is not few.
Jālinīprabha, if a son or daughter of good family can thus know the true nature of all phenomena—whether they have known it, are now knowing it, or will know it—[note:
such knowledge is precisely the knowledge of non-knowing. How can there be knowing in non-knowing?
When knowing is non-discriminative, [true knowing occurs].
This person has no dharma that has already been attained, no dharma that is being attained now, and no dharma that will be attained in the future.
[Note: The previous explanation was "knowing thus," while this explanation is "knowing thus. Since there is no knowing, it is known as knowing;
since there is no attaining, it is attained as attaining.
Why is this so? [Note] This is a reiterated explanation of the meaning of "no-knowledge" and "no-attainment.
The Buddha taught that being without attainment and without discrimination is called the mark of one who has completed what was to be done.

[Note] "Without attainment" means not attaining the attainment of all dharmas, but rather attaining the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas. "Without discrimination" means attaining such knowledge.
If a person, upon hearing this true nature of all phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam*), exerts themselves with diligent effort, this is called "practicing according to the teaching.

[Note: Since it is said that taking what is non-knowing as knowing and what is non-attaining as attaining constitutes diligence where there is no diligence—such that the absence of diligence is itself called diligence—this is practicing according to the teaching.
"One does not proceed from one stage to another stage. [Note] At the very moment of speaking, it is practice; at the very moment of practicing, it is speaking.
Since speaking and practicing are simultaneous, there is immediate understanding and immediate realization; therefore, one does not proceed from one stage to another stage.
If one does not proceed from stage to stage, this person is neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa. Why is this?
[Note] This explains the meaning of why they are not situated therein.
The Buddhas neither attain birth-and-death nor attain nirvāṇa. [Note: The Buddhas have no separate object of realization;
they realize only that the nature of birth-and-death is empty, which is itself nirvāṇa. This establishes the meaning of non-attainment.
Since birth-and-death and nirvāṇa possess no dual nature, discrimination is thereby extinguished.
Jālinīprabha asked, "Does the Buddha not preach the Dharma for the sake of crossing over birth and death? Brahmā replied, "Is there any Dharma shown by the Buddha that crosses over birth and death?

[Note: If one were to say that the Dharma preached by the Buddha is for the sake of crossing over birth and death, then the Buddha would possess the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, and so forth.

Jālinīprabha said, "It is non-existent. Brahmā said, "For this reason, one should know that the Buddha does not cause sentient beings to emerge from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) or enter into nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa*).
[Note: Regarding the question, "If he acts neither for the sake of birth-and-death nor for the sake of nirvāṇa, what is the meaning of his preaching the Dharma? the explanation says:
It is solely for the purpose of transcending false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). [Note] What is meant by "false conceptualization"? The commentary states:
it refers merely to the discrimination between the two characteristics of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Within this context, [the note] indicates the state of true nature (*bhūtatathatā*).
In reality, there is no one who crosses over from birth-and-death to nirvana. Why is this? [Note] This explains that there is no intentionality. All phenomena are equal;
there is no coming or going, no emerging from birth-and-death, and no entering into nirvana. [Note] The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"This Dharma abides in its own place, and the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. To abide in the place of the Dharma means not to emerge from birth-and-death.
And thus entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, saying: "Excellent, excellent! You have spoken of the true nature of all dharmas;
it should be as you have said. [Note: If the Buddha did not provide such confirmation, it would be difficult for others to gain faith.
When this Dharma was being taught, two thousand bhikṣus did not grasp at any dharmas. [Note] Because they attained non-attainment, their outflows were exhausted.
[Note] Because they did not fall into the two extremes.
The mind attains liberation. [Note] Because of thorough discernment.

The Buddha told Brahmā: "I do not attain birth-and-death, nor do I attain nirvāṇa. [Note] Why did the Tathāgata summon and address Brahmā after previously granting his request, when there had been no explanation yet?
It was because he feared that the assembly might harbor doubts that remained unresolved.

"Birth and death, and entry into nirvana—these are what the Buddha has always taught. That one neither attains birth and death nor attains nirvana is something that the multitude has not yet realized.
Therefore, the commentary explains:
"Although the Tathāgata speaks of birth and death, in reality there is no person who comes and goes through birth and death; although he speaks of nirvana, in reality there is none."
There are those who attain extinction (*nirvāṇa*). [Note: Therefore, what the Buddha has taught is merely for the purpose of crossing over the delusive thoughts of these two.
If there is one who enters this Dharma-gate, such a person possesses neither the characteristic of birth-and-death nor the characteristic of extinction. [Note: An ancient said:
"It is not the Buddha, it is not the mind, it is not an object—what then is it?"
At that time, five hundred bhikṣus in the assembly rose from their seats and spoke thus: "We have practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) in vain.
We now clearly see those who have attained parinirvāṇa, yet you say there is no such thing as parinirvāṇa. For what purpose, then, should we cultivate the path and seek wisdom? [Note:
Those who see one attaining parinirvāṇa do not realize they must extinguish their own deluded thoughts; they fail to extinguish themselves.]
Because of their nature, they give rise to doubt.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if there are those who give rise to views regarding the Dharma, then for such persons, the Buddha does not appear in the world.
[Note: When the mind is blinded by views and knowledge, true awakening remains hidden.
World-Honored One, if there were anyone who held a fixed view of nirvana, that person would not transcend birth and death.
[Note] To see that there is extinction is, in itself, precisely birth and death.
Why is this so? Nirvāṇa is defined as the eradication of all marks (*nimitta*) and the distancing from all restless thoughts and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
[Note: Nirvāṇa is called "that which can extinguish," yet it merely extinguishes the marks of conceptual proliferation and discrimination regarding all phenomena;
the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is in fact not extinguished. If one gives rise to knowledge and views regarding all phenomena, then the Buddha does not appear in the world.
If one conceives of the arising and cessation of all phenomena as *nirvāṇa*, one will not attain liberation from birth and death.

World-Honored One, these bhikṣus have left the household life within the Buddha’s True Dharma, yet they now fall into the heterodox views of non-Buddhists, perceiving a fixed characteristic of *nirvāṇa*.
[Note: First, the cause for their falling into error is established; subsequently, the fallacy of their attachment to heterodoxy is refuted.

It is, for example, like oil being extracted from sesame seeds and clarified butter (*sarpis*) being extracted from curd. [Note: The crushing of sesame seeds to produce oil is a metaphor for those who, having extinguished false views, enter *nirvāṇa* by ending birth and death.

As for the extraction of clarified butter from curd—the curd does not itself become the butter, yet the butter truly emerges from the curd—this is a metaphor for how the True Dharma does not itself cease birth and death, yet one realizes *nirvāṇa* through it; thus, *nirvāṇa* truly transcends birth and death.
World-Honored One, if there are those who seek nirvāṇa within the characteristic of cessation among all phenomena, I say that such people are all characterized by overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
[Note: It was previously stated that "nirvāṇa is named the extinction and removal of all characteristics," meaning the extinction of characteristics such as knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).
If one clings to this characteristic of cessation while seeking nirvāṇa, then one has not yet transcended knowledge and vision.
The World-Honored One, the practitioner of the true path, does not bring about the arising of dharmas nor their cessation; there is neither attainment nor fruit. [Note:
The first two sections establish that knowledge and vision are neither subject to extinction nor yet unarisen.
As for the practitioner of the true path—referred to as a "false man"—he does not produce the characteristic of arising in all dharmas, nor does he produce the characteristic of non-arising.

One does not produce the mark of cessation, nor does one produce the mark of non-cessation; there is neither attainment nor fruit. One merely remains far removed from such conceptual proliferations and discriminations.
Jālinīprabha said to Brahmā: "Regarding these five hundred bhikṣus who have risen from their seats, you should provide them with a method."
He then guides their minds into this Dharma-gate, causing them to attain faith and understanding and to be free from all false views.
Brahmā said, "Good son, even if one were to go away for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, one could not escape from such a Dharma-gate.
It is like a foolish person who fears empty space; abandoning space and fleeing, wherever he goes, he does not leave empty space behind."

These bhikṣus are also like this: although they travel far away, they do not depart from the mark of emptiness (śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa), they do not depart from the mark of signlessness (animitta-lakṣaṇa), and they do not depart from the mark of wishlessness (apraṇihita-lakṣaṇa).
[Note: For example, it is like those with wrong views who, fearing birth and death, desire to escape;
yet not knowing that birth and death are themselves the marks of emptiness and so forth, what could they possibly escape?
Furthermore, it is like a person who, seeking empty space, runs hither and thither, saying, "I wish to obtain space; I wish to obtain space.
This person merely utters the name of space but does not obtain space; though he moves within space, he does not perceive space.
These bhikṣus are just the same: desiring to seek nirvāṇa, they move within nirvāṇa yet do not attain it.
Nirvāṇa. [Note: One might suppose that Nirvāṇa definitely has a location and seeks it therein, yet fails to realize that its own nature is originally quiescent.
Failing to realize that its own nature is originally quiescent, one acts within quiescence while remaining unaware that it is quiescence.
Why is this so? Nirvāṇa exists only as a name, just as space exists only as a name and cannot be grasped;
nirvāṇa is likewise, existing only as a name and being ungraspable.

At that time, having heard this teaching of the Dharma, five hundred bhikṣus did not grasp at any dharmas. [Note: This refers to what is called "being far removed from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)."
The outflows are exhausted. [Note] One does not fall into the two extremes;
the mind attains liberation. [Note] This refers to the severance of the fetters and latent tendencies.
One attains the path of the Arhat. [Note] This is called "one beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
He spoke thus: "World-Honored One, if a person seeks nirvana within the mark of the ultimate cessation of all dharmas, then for that person, a Buddha does not appear in the world.
[Note] Because this arises from the view of arising, it is not the view of cessation; yet since it is also a form of negation, it is as previously stated:
"If one gives rise to views regarding dharmas, then a Buddha does not appear in the world. Now it is said that seeking within the mark of cessation likewise results in no appearance of a Buddha.

World-Honored One, we who are now here are neither ordinary beings, nor those in training (*śaikṣa*), nor those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); we do not abide in saṃsāra, nor do we abide in nirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because the Buddha has appeared in the world, we are said to be far removed from all stirring thoughts and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
[Note] That which is called "Buddha" is precisely one's own mind. As it has been said of old:

"If one does not understand that all phenomena are but mind, various discriminations arise—namely, the categories of sage and ordinary person, birth-and-death and nirvana. Once one realizes that all phenomena are but mind, discrimination no longer arises;
this is what is meant by being far removed from stirring thoughts and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Because one is far removed from discrimination, one's own mind...

Because it manifests with perfect clarity, it is said that "a Buddha has appeared in the world. Because true mind becomes obscured if one clings to knowledge and views, it is said that "a Buddha has not appeared in the world.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Have you now attained right wisdom for your own benefit?"
The five hundred bhikṣus said, "Venerable Śāriputra, we have now attained that which is 'that which should not be done' among all afflictions.
[Note: This means that those who have attained right wisdom do not act for their own benefit;
rather, they understand that although it is "that which should not be done" within the context of afflictions, they engage in it to give rise to the sublime function of benefiting others.
Śāriputra asked, "For what reason do you say this? [Note: Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom;
that he now does not know the bhikṣu’s answer indicates that within the gateway of the True Nature (bhūtatathatā), there are matters beyond the reach of his wisdom.
The bhikṣus said: "Because they know the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all afflictions (*kleśa*), it is said that they have 'attained' all afflictions. [Note:

If one does not know the true nature of the afflictions, one is turned by them; because one knows the true nature, one is able to employ the afflictions, and thus it is said that they have "attained" them.
Because we have already realized that nirvāṇa is of an unconditioned nature (*anabhisaṃskṛta*), it is said to be "acting through non-action. [Note:
The essence of nirvāṇa is unconditioned and has been thus from the beginning; therefore, one speaks of "realizing" it rather than "attaining" it.

Since afflictions arise based upon this essence and are not inherently existent, one speaks of "attaining" them rather than "realizing" them. Since they arise based upon the essence, one knows that [the essence] is non-existent [in terms of arising].
"Because it is their nature, they act though there is nothing to be done.
Śāriputra said, "Excellent, excellent! You all now abide in the field of merit and are able to consume offerings."
[Note] Śāriputra praised the bhikṣu for having attained that which cannot be contrived yet manifested wondrous functions through illusion to benefit and deliver all beings;
he is a field of merit for humanity, capable of consuming offerings.
The bhikṣus said, "Even the Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, cannot fully digest such offerings; how much less can we?

Śāriputra asked, "For what reason do you say this? The bhikṣus replied, "Because the World-Honored One knows and perceives the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and because that nature is eternally pure.

[Note] Regarding "because the nature is eternally pure": it means that because the World-Honored One knows and perceives the nature of phenomena and has entered into right nature (samyaktva), he remains far removed from [defilement].

False conceptualization—this false conceptualization itself, within all phenomena, consists of fields of merit and non-fields of merit, those that can digest offerings and those that cannot digest offerings.
Once false conceptualization is abandoned, there is neither benefit nor merit within all phenomena.
Where there is no benefit, there is neither a field of merit nor a non-field of merit; there is no merit.
Thus, because it neither consumes offerings nor fails to consume offerings, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"If there is one who gives, there is no great merit and no small merit; it neither causes loss nor brings benefit."
Thereupon, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintī addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, who is worthy of receiving offerings?
The Buddha told the Brahmā, "One who is not led astray by worldly dharmas. [Note: One who is not led astray by worldly dharmas has neither receiving nor non-receiving;
because there is no receiving, such a person is one who should receive offerings.
“World-Honored One, who is able to digest offerings? The Buddha said, “One who grasps at nothing regarding the Dharma. [Note:

One who grasps at nothing does not grasp at the mind internally nor grasp at objects externally. When both internal and external are forgotten, there is neither that which can be digested nor that which cannot be digested.
“World-Honored One, who is the field of merit for the world? The Buddha said, “One who does not destroy the nature of bodhi. [Note:
To not destroy the nature of bodhi means that one constantly benefits others through the nature of awakening, rather than by way of inferior paths; therefore, such a person is a field of merit.
“World-Honored One, who is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to sentient beings? The Buddha said, “One who does not abandon a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward all sentient beings.
[Note: One who treats others with loving-kindness is looked up to by people and transforms them.
“World-Honored One, who knows how to repay the Buddha’s kindness? The Buddha replied, “It is one who does not sever the lineage of the Buddhas.
[Note] To protect and mind one’s own mind so that it remains uninterrupted is to know how to repay kindness.
“World-Honored One, who is able to make offerings to the Buddha? The Buddha said: “One who can penetrate the limit of non-arising. [Note:

The Dharma of non-arising is the fundamental intention for the Buddha’s appearance in the world; one who can penetrate this is truly making offerings, and the four material requisites are not involved.
“World-Honored One, who is able to draw near to the Buddha? The Buddha said: “One who, even for the sake of losing their life, does not violate the prohibitions.
[Note: To lose one’s life without violating the prohibitions means to remain far removed from Māra and externalists while constantly drawing near to the Buddha.]

“World-Honored One, who is able to pay respect to the Buddha? The Buddha said, “One who well covers the six sense-faculties. [Note] To cover the six sense-faculties means that the mind is not negligent;
when the mind is not negligent, one will always maintain the thought of reverence.
"Bhagavān, who is called 'Wealthy'? The Buddha said, "One who has accomplished the seven riches.

[Note] The seven meritorious qualities are faith, diligence, precepts, shame, remorse, learning, relinquishment, concentration, and wisdom. Worldly wealth and treasures, though they exist, are not real; when life ends, they end with it.
The supramundane wealth of the Dharma is inexhaustible throughout birth and kalpas; this is what is called being "wealthy."
“World-Honored One, who is called one who is content? The Buddha said, “One who has attained supramundane wisdom. [Note:

Mundane wisdom is deluded regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), and thus one greedily grasps at them without satiety. Supramundane wisdom, however, thoroughly realizes the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and perceives that there is not a single thing to be grasped;
this is what is meant by being content.
“World-Honored One, who is it that distances themselves from the Buddha’s words and has no aspirations within the three realms? [Note:
When there are no aspirations, the攀緣心 (pariṣaṇḍana-citta / ālambana-citta) is severed; when the pariṣaṇḍana-citta is severed, one is then loftily and eternally parted.]
"Bhagavān, who is it that is endowed with the Buddha’s words and is able to sever all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)? [Note:
"Fetters" refers to the six fetters, such as the eye and its objects; "underlying tendencies" refers to the ten underlying tendencies, such as greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt.
When these fetters and underlying tendencies are severed, one has accomplished what was to be done; therefore, one is said to be "endowed."]
“World-Honored One, who is the person who possesses happiness? The Buddha said, “One who is free from craving and attachment. [Note:
The happiness of craving and attachment is subject to destruction; the happiness of non-craving is indestructible.
“World-Honored One, who is it that has no greedy attachment? The Buddha replied, “One who knows and sees the five aggregates.

[Note] Here, the previous question is restated because there was a fear that one might still engage in grasping or rejecting regarding the objects of the six sense-fields. The Buddha’s answer causes people to illuminate and shatter the deluded mind of the five aggregates;
once this deluded mind is shattered, one will have nothing to which to become greedily attached among the external six sense-fields.
“World-Honored One, who crosses the river of desire? The Buddha said, “One who is able to relinquish the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). [Note:
Because the six sense organs are entered by the six objects, they are called the six bases. Since the organs and their objects are bound together, one drifts in the river of desire;
if both organs and objects are relinquished, then the river of desire is crossed.
"Bhagavān, who dwells on the other shore? The Buddha said, "One who is able to know the equality of all paths. [Note: The equality of all paths means neither "that" nor "this.
Since there is neither "that" nor "this," there is likewise no conceptualization of crossing over or not crossing over.

Within this, the conditions for arising are not without their sequence; it was through this that the five hundred bhikṣus attained the true nature of all dharmas (dharmatā), and Śāriputra [attained it as well].
He considered that those dwelling in the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) are able to consume offerings, and the bhikṣus understood his intention.
However, since the gateway of right faith cannot be exhausted through a single path, Brahmā followed in his footsteps to inquire further, thereby expanding upon his meaning.
Previously, Brahmā had criticized them, saying: "Five hundred bhikṣus have gone forth into the Buddha’s true Dharma..."
Why is it that these non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to such false views? There are three kinds of "homes" from which one renounces:

first, the worldly home; second, the home of the triple world (*tridhātu*); and third, the home of ignorance (*avidyā*). It was previously stated that those who renounce within the Buddha’s True Dharma leave the worldly home;
here, the bhikṣu who attains the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) leaves the home of the triple world. Therefore, it is said:

Having attained arhatship, the bodhisattva below [the rank of] the *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) cultivates the six perfections, the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), and so forth, thereby emerging from the house of ignorance.
Because he realizes the true nature (*bhūta-dharmatā*), he emerges from the triple world (*tridhātu*). Having emerged from the triple world, he is worthy of receiving offerings;

being worthy of receiving them, he is able to digest them; being able to digest them, he becomes a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for the world; being a field of merit for the world, he brings about the welfare of sentient beings.
If one regards knowledge as a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), then one will know how to repay its kindness; knowing how to repay its kindness, one will know what it is to offer worship;
knowing what it is to offer worship, one will know whom to draw near to; and knowing whom to draw near to, one will know how to show reverence, and so forth—these can be inferred by analogy.
“World-Honored One, what is it that enables a bodhisattva to be a donor? The Buddha said, “A bodhisattva is able to transform sentient beings with the mind of omniscience.
[Note] Between the two kinds of giving, the gift of Dharma is supreme; there is no gift greater than transforming sentient beings with the mind of omniscience.
“World-Honored One, what is it that enables a bodhisattva to uphold the precepts? The Buddha said: “It is being able to constantly never abandon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). [Note:
In the Hīnayāna, one maintains discipline through non-violation of the ritual codes (*vinaya*); in the Mahāyāna, one maintains oneself through the path-concomitant restraint.]
“World-Honored One, what is meant by a bodhisattva being able to practice patience? The Buddha said: “It is seeing that the characteristics of the mind perish moment by moment.

[Note] Seeing the characteristic of the mind’s cessation, one externally severs all dependence on conditions. When one externally severs all dependence on conditions, there is neither patience nor impatience.
“World-Honored One, what is it that allows a bodhisattva to practice diligence? The Buddha said: “One seeks the mind and does not find it.
[Note: Both diligence and indolence are produced by this mind. Since the mind cannot be found, there is neither diligence nor non-diligence.
“World-Honored One, what is it that enables a bodhisattva to practice meditative concentration? The Buddha said, “By eliminating the coarse characteristics of body and mind. [Note:

Because those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) practice concentration, they become attached to it and do not relinquish it; whereas the meditative concentration of the Great Vehicle nature is neither fixed nor unfixed—it merely eliminates coarse characteristics.
"Bhagavān, what is it that allows a bodhisattva to practice wisdom? The Buddha said: "To be without conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding all phenomena.
[Note: Ordinary persons lack wisdom and formulate the dualistic views of existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena; this is conceptual proliferation.
If one does not form these two views regarding phenomena, this is practicing wisdom.

“World-Honored One, what is meant by a bodhisattva being able to practice a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*)? The Buddha said, “It means not giving rise to the notion of sentient beings (*sattvasaṃjñā*).

“World-Honored One, what is meant by a bodhisattva being able to practice a mind of compassion (*karuṇā*)? The Buddha said, “It means not giving rise to the notion of dharmas (*dharmasaṃjñā*). [Note: Loving-kindness is able to bestow happiness, while compassion is able to extract suffering.

If one gives rise to the notion of sentient beings, one cannot equally bestow the bliss of a Tathāgata; if one gives rise to the notions of dharma or non-dharma, [one fails to realize the ultimate nature].
Then one would not think to uproot the suffering of sentient beings.
World-Honored One, what is meant by a bodhisattva being able to practice a mind of sympathetic joy? The Buddha said: "It is the non-arising of the notion of self. [Note:

If one gives rise to the notion of self, seeing the goodness in others leads to jealousy, while seeing their lack of goodness leads to anger. If the notion of self does not arise, then one sees neither the faults nor the virtues of others.
When one encounters those who suffer, one contemplates how to rescue them; when one encounters people of virtue, talent, and sagehood, one contemplates how to praise them.

World-Honored One, what is it that allows a bodhisattva to practice the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*)? The Buddha said: It is the non-arising of the notions of "self" and "other. World-Honored One, what... [text ends]
This refers to the Bodhisattva who dwells securely in the purity of the mind of faith and understanding regarding the Buddha’s words, a state free from turbidity.

[Note]: When ordinary beings place their faith in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), it is termed defiled. For a Bodhisattva, perfect faith in the unturbid nature of one's own mind leads to the distancing from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and dwelling securely in pure faith.
“World-Honored One, what is meant by a bodhisattva dwelling securely in emptiness? The Buddha replied, “It means not clinging to any verbal expressions.
[Note] Previously, having realized the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), Jālinīprabha asked about being worthy of receiving offerings, the six perfections, and the four immeasurable minds;
he now specifically asks about dwelling in emptiness because all differentiated names and characteristics are but one’s own mind.
It is merely a shadow; therefore, the World-Honored One replied: "One does not cling to words. When one does not cling to words, then all things are empty.
What did the World-Honored One mean when he said that a bodhisattva is called "possessed of shame"? The Buddha said: "One who knows and perceives internal dharmas. [Note: To know the dharmas within.]
Possessing [this quality], one feels shame for former delusions.
The World-Honored One said: "What is meant by a bodhisattva being called 'possessed of a sense of shame'? The Buddha replied: "It means abandoning external dharmas. [Note:
To abandon external dharmas is to sever the limits of the past and future; when the limits of the past and future are severed, one feels shame for formerly grasping at objects of perception.
“World-Honored One, what is meant by the ‘universal practice’ (paryāpanna-caryā) of a bodhisattva? The Buddha said: “It is the ability to purify the karma of body, speech, and mind.

[Note: All karma arises from these three types of action; if these three are pure, this is the universal practice of a bodhisattva, whereas if they are impure, it is the universal practice of an ordinary being (*sattva*).
The verse provides a detailed explanation of this.

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse: "If the body is pure and free from evil, If the mouth is pure and always speaks truthful words, If the mind is pure and constantly practices compassion— This is the universal conduct of a bodhisattva.

[Note: "The body being free from evil" encompasses killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. The mouth, through truthful speech and the other three [wholesome modes of speech], remedies the four faults of speech;
namely, truthful speech remedies false speech and so forth. The mental karma consists of three [unwholesome types], which are treated individually.
The practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can overcome hatred; because the Bodhisattva considers anger to be the most harmful of all, it is said:
"When a single thought of anger arises, a million gates of obstacles open. Thus, by practicing loving-kindness, the other virtues are also fully realized.
This verse comprehensively presents the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome paths of action, as their texts mutually encompass one another.

Practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*) without attachment, contemplating impurity (*aśubha*) without aversion, and practicing equanimity (*upekṣā*) without delusion—this is the universal practice of the Bodhisattva.
[Note] The preceding passage enumerates the ten karmas in general; here, the three mental karmas are specifically singled out because the mind is that which is capable of encompassing them.

There are two types of practicing loving-kindness: first, objectless loving-kindness (*anālambana-maitrī*); second, loving-kindness based on affectionate views (*snehadṛṣṭi-maitrī*). If one practices loving-kindness with attachment...

If one clings, one falls into attachment and views; it is not without an object. When contemplating the impurity of the body, if one does not immediately give rise to revulsion or anger, yet if revulsion or anger should arise, one falls into the practice of the Two Vehicles.
If one practices equanimity (*upekṣā*) without seeking karmic retribution, yet if one seeks retribution, one forms greedy attachment.
Greedy attachment leads to delusive craving. If one is without greed, without anger, and without delusion regarding the three karmas, this is called...
The universal conduct of a bodhisattva cannot be compared to that of the two vehicles.
Whether in an empty village, in the wilderness, or amidst a great assembly, his majestic deportment never wavers; such is the universal conduct of a bodhisattva.
[Note]: Through the purity of the mind, one dwells alone without it being a secluded place, and dwells among the multitude without it being a clamor;
one is not turned by external objects, for there is neither "acceptable" nor "unacceptable.
To know phenomena is called the Buddha; to know detachment is called the Dharma; to know non-existence is called the Sangha—this is the universal practice of the Bodhisattva.
[Note] By attaining the non-duality of movement and stillness, one realizes the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) free from all conceptual discrimination;
thus, one penetrates the mind of signlessness (*animitta-citta*) and perceives therein the oneness of the Triple Gem.
To know the conduct arising from desire, to know the conduct arising from hatred and delusion, and to know well how to transform this conduct—this is the universal conduct of a bodhisattva.
[Note] Since one has realized that the Three Jewels are fundamentally rooted in the single mind, greed, hatred, and delusion are never distinct from liberation;
because one does not cling to them nor loathe them, one perfectly attains their true course. Therefore, it is called "knowing well."
Not relying on the desire realm and not dwelling in the practices of the form or formless realms—such meditative concentration is the universal practice of a bodhisattva.
[Note: Once the three poisons and the three virtues have been skillfully transformed, one does not abide in the three realms but dwells in meditative concentration.
To resolve with faith that all phenomena are empty, signless, and wishless, yet not to exhaust the outflows—this is the universal practice of a bodhisattva.
[Note: Practicing such meditative concentration, one neither clings nor becomes weary; because of non-clinging, there is signlessness and wishlessness;
because of the absence of weariness, one does not exhaust the outflows.
Skillfully knowing the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, while penetrating the Buddha vehicle, is the universal practice of a Bodhisattva.
[Note: The vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas involve attaining the exhaustion of outflows by realizing that all phenomena are empty, signless, and wishless;
the Buddha vehicle, however, involves knowing emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness without exhausting the outflows.

To clearly understand all dharmas without doubt regarding what is the path and what is not the path, and to have no distinction between love and hatred—this is the universal practice of the Bodhisattva. [Note:

"The Path" refers to the Three Vehicles; "that which is not the Path" refers to the six classes of ordinary beings. To clearly understand the nature of dharmas and to be equanimous toward both the Path and that which is not the Path, such that one does not give rise to aversion or attachment—and because greed and so forth constitute that which is not the Path—is the meaning.
To be entirely without discrimination regarding all things in the past, future, and present worlds is the universal conduct of a bodhisattva.
[Note] Whereas previously it was the equality of what is the path and what is not the path, here it is the equality of the three periods of time;
there is nothing in saṃsāra or nirvāṇa that is not equal.
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is meant by a bodhisattva transcending worldly dharmas and penetrating worldly dharmas?
Having penetrated worldly dharmas, how does one deliver sentient beings from worldly dharmas, act within the world, and yet not destroy the world?
[Note: There are three kinds of worlds: first, the vessel-world; second, the world of sentient beings.]
There are three worlds in the world: the world of sentient beings, the world of the vessel (the physical environment), and the world of the perfectly awakened wisdom.

To "transcend the world" means to surpass the world of the vessel and the world of sentient beings and enter the world of the perfectly awakened wisdom. "Thoroughly penetrating the world" refers collectively to all three worlds.
Regarding "delivering sentient beings from the phenomena of the world," although one knows that the phenomena of the world are without marks and...

To manifest through the means of "sameness of purpose" (*samānārthatā*) and thereby deliver sentient beings by this very method, while acting within the world without destroying the world, arises from knowing that the world is like an illusion. By skillfully applying the Middle Way, one is neither defiled nor destroyed;
it is just as the sun and moon move through the sky, illuminating the world without being obstructed by the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse: "The five aggregates are called 'the world,' for they are that upon which the world relies.

Relying upon the five aggregates, one does not escape the worldly dharmas. [Note: The five aggregates are form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

"Aggregate" (*skandha*) has the meaning of "covering" or "obscuring," for it can cover True Suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, internally it forms the root-body, and externally it constitutes the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), revolving [in saṃsāra].

Because they rely on mutual dependence, they cannot attain liberation; taking the five aggregates as the creator and the world as the created, the interaction between subject and object gives rise to worldly dharmas.
The Bodhisattva possesses wisdom that knows the true nature of the world—namely, that the five aggregates are like worldly dharmas—and thus remains unstained by them.
[Note] Sentient beings, being obstructed by ignorance and failing to realize the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), do not achieve liberation within the world.
Bodhisattvas, possessing great wisdom and skillfully knowing the suchness (*tathatā*) of phenomena, abide therein without defilement;
this is what is meant by "transcending the world."
Gain and loss, defamation and fame, praise and blame, suffering and pleasure—these eight worldly dharmas constantly entice the world.
Yet the Bodhisattva of Great Wisdom scatters and extinguishes these worldly dharmas; seeing the world’s state of decay and ruin, he remains unmoved.
When gaining profit, his mind does not exalt; when losing profit, his mind does not sink. His mind is firm and unshakable, like Mount Sumeru.
Regarding gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, and suffering and pleasure—among these eight worldly dharmas, his mind remains ever equanimous. [Note:

These eight dharmas, such as gain and so forth, are also known as the "Eight Winds. Sentient beings, failing to understand their emptiness and falsity, are constantly pulled and disturbed by them, like the ocean of the mind.
The Bodhisattva, through the contemplation of wisdom, skillfully attains the state of reality and remains unmoved therein.
Like Mount Sumeru, they know that the world is illusory and arises entirely from perversion; such persons do not follow the worldly path.
[Note] This explains why the Bodhisattva remains unmoved while dwelling therein: because the Bodhisattva knows the world...
Because false imaginings arise from inversion, they are immovable; this answer concerns the thorough penetration of worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*).
Since the Bodhisattva recognizes all paths within the world, he is able to deliver sentient beings from their suffering and affliction within that world.
