[Note] This answer concerns the thorough penetration of worldly phenomena (*lokadharma*) and the deliverance of sentient beings from worldly phenomena.
Although they act within the world, they remain unstained like a lotus; yet, because they do not destroy the world and have thoroughly penetrated the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they do so.
[Note] This answers [the question of] how one acts within the world without destroying the world.
While acting within the world, the world does not know it is the world. [Note] Because ordinary worldlings do not know it is illusory, they cling to it with firm persistence and do not relinquish it;
therefore, they dwell perpetually in birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The Bodhisattva practices within the world, clearly understanding the characteristics of the world, the world’s characteristic of being like space, and that space itself is without characteristics.
Knowing it thus, the Bodhisattva is not defiled by the world. [Note: The followers of the Two Vehicles do not understand that the world is false and arises from inversion;
they grasp at it as truly existent and apply their minds to its destruction. If one grasps at what is falsely existent as real, then that falsity...
Inversion is the attachment to marks; the Bodhisattva who skillfully knows that the markless nature of the world is identical to empty space—being neither real nor unreal—is simply like this.

According to what is known of the world, he expounds it accordingly. [Note: It was previously stated that he delivers sentient beings from suffering and affliction; however, this has not yet been fully examined.
By what means does a bodhisattva cross over? By non-crossing as the crossing. According to what he knows, he expounds it for others, enabling them to cross over by themselves;
it cannot be crossed over by another.
Because he knows the nature of the world, he does not destroy the five aggregates of the world; their lack of self-nature is itself the nature of the world.

[Note] The nature of the world’s lack of intrinsic nature is precisely like the lack of intrinsic nature of the five aggregates; because one knows them to be without intrinsic nature, one dwells therein without being destroyed.
This reiterates the previous meaning.
If a person does not know this, they remain in the world; yet if they see and know that the five aggregates are neither born nor extinguished, [they likewise abide in the unconditioned].
This person walks in the world yet does not rely on the world;

while ordinary people do not know the Dharma and give rise to disputes and litigation regarding what is real and what is unreal, dwelling within these two characteristics, I always do not engage in disputes with the world, because I have fully understood the true nature of all worldly phenomena.
Thus, all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas are entirely free from dispute and litigation.
Because one knows the equality of the world, it is neither real nor false. [Note: This verse concerns the gate of the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;
its true aspect (*lakṣaṇa*) is thus neither real nor false. It is not that I alone say this, for all Buddhas are likewise. If one dwells in dualistic characteristics, then disputes will arise;
the following passage refutes such errors.
If the Buddha-dharma were definitively characterized by either reality or falsehood, it would be no different from the attachments of non-Buddhists;
yet within the true meaning, there is neither reality nor falsehood. Therefore, I have always taught that the supramundane dharma is non-dual.
If one knows the suchness of the nature of the world in this way, one will not grasp at these evil views regarding what is real or what is false.
One who thus knows that the world is pure like space is a person of great renown; one who illuminates the world like the sun is such a person.
If a person perceives the world as I perceive it, such individuals are able to see the Buddhas of the ten directions.
[Note] This verse states that if one can perceive the true reality of the world as the Buddha perceives it, then one can perceive the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas of the ten directions.
All phenomena arise from conditions and possess no inherent nature of their own; if one understands these causes and conditions, one will penetrate the true reality of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
If one knows the true nature of phenomena (*dharmas*), then one knows the characteristic of emptiness; if one can know the characteristic of emptiness, then one sees the Teacher. [Note:
This explains the meaning of the preceding verse—that knowing the true nature is to see the Buddha. All phenomena arise from causes and conditions;
because they arise from causes and conditions, they lack a fixed nature. This absence of a fixed nature is the true nature, and this true nature is emptiness.
This is precisely the characteristic of emptiness; to be able to know the characteristic of emptiness is to see the Buddha. Thus, a verse from the *Mādhyamaka-śāstra* says:
"Phenomena produced through causes and conditions—I declare them to be empty. They are also designated as provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.
This refers to the nature of non-fixity.
If there are those who hear such teachings on the characteristics of the world, they may act within the world yet do not dwell in the world.
[Note: It was previously stated that being able to know and see refers to the realm of self-realization; thus, one can attain such a state.
This, however, means that by hearing from others, one also attains the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Those who rely on various views cannot reach this matter. [Note] This distinguishes those outside the Way (tīrthikas) who, relying on false views, give rise to the sixty-two views;
they cannot reach it within the gateway of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
How does one practice in the world yet not dwell in the world?
If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there are those who delight in this Dharma, the Buddha will constantly manifest his Dharma-body before such persons.

If a person understands and penetrates this, they protect my Dharma, they make offerings to me, and they are a teacher of the world. [Note: To have faith in this true reality is to see the Dharma-body. Understanding...
This is the merit of protecting and making offerings for one’s own benefit; it is the practice of benefiting others as a guide for the world.
If a person hears of the nature of the world in this way even for a moment, that person will never again fall into the grasp of the evil Māra.
[Note] This verse intends to manifest the superior by means of the inferior:

if even hearing for a mere moment—a duration of time that is extremely brief—brings protection and benefit, how much more so for those who see, hear, believe, and understand, and practice for a long period, yet fail to obtain sublime benefits?
If one can penetrate this meaning, they are a donor of the great wealth of the Dharma of wisdom; they are also one who possesses the prohibitive precepts.
If one knows the world to be thus, they possess the power of patience, are courageous and robust, are endowed with all meditative concentrations, and have attained penetration into wisdom.
[Note] To be able to penetrate this true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) is called being fully endowed with the six *pāramitās*.
In whatever place one hears this Dharma, there is a Buddha in that direction. Such bodhisattvas will before long sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
If one has deep love and joy for such a nature of the world, one can subdue all Māras and swiftly attain the unsurpassed path.

[Note] Regarding the passage beginning with "How does one proceed oneself," which generally clarifies the meaning of faith, understanding, practice, and realization throughout the world, the text is explicit and thus not further explained here.
Jālinīprabha’s initial question—"What is the correct inquiry of a bodhisattva?"—is followed by his subsequent question—"What is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena?
To this, Brahmā replies that being free from the discrimination of self and other constitutes the correct inquiry, while being devoid of false discrimination constitutes the true nature.
As bright as the sun and stars, this truth is naturally understood without words. Five hundred bhikṣus, harboring doubts and agitation, were on the verge of withdrawing from their seats;
Jālinīprabha requested a skillful means, whereupon Brahmā declared: "Even if you were to retreat for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges, you could not escape this Dharma-gate.
He then drew forth two analogies—escaping into space and searching for space—to illustrate this point.
The entire assembly knows where to turn; one may say that although Brahmā did not grant him expedient means, his own expedients were already perfected.
While the bhikṣu had nothing to believe or understand, his faith and understanding were suddenly clear. Śāriputra offered praise for his own benefit regarding what wisdom cannot know;
the bhikṣu replied that the root of afflictions is empty and karma has no reality. Contemplating their roles as guest and host, their dialogue was like clouds.

The Venerable Bhikṣu Śāriputra asked thirty questions, such as: "Who is it that excels in the fearlessnesses and eloquence? "With whom can these be compared? "How does one attain this state? and "Who is worthy of receiving offerings?
It appears as though he did not know the answers to each question and thus questioned the Buddha;
could it be that even Brahmā has limitations? Surely there must be someone who knows. The answer is: "Entering samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation—this is the Dharma of all Buddhas."

The method for bestowing [this teaching] upon all bodhisattvas is the gateway for entering the Path: through questioning one receives an answer; through the answer one hears; through hearing one understands.
Thus, it is seen here that the bhikṣu attained awakening from Brahmā through hearing, reflection, and faith-based understanding.
That both of these were initiated by Jālinīprabha indicates they equally rely upon fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). The following text should...

The thirty questions beginning with "receiving offerings" and extending to the "five aggregates" and the "world," constitute the gateway for cultivation and realization that transcends the reach of intellectual wisdom (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

Whether posing the questions or providing the answers, all are addressed to the Honored Brahmā; thus, faith, understanding, practice, and realization all emerge from the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
Indeed, this sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna is a single mind that is absolute and beyond dependence, wherein there is neither question nor answer.
Answer: Since there is no realization and no cultivation, by what means could the wisdom that is not a skillful method be initiated? Therefore, it is indicated by means of an elephant.
Chapter Four: The Four Noble Truths.
[Note] By virtue of the preceding chapter, one who perceives and realizes the true nature (*dharmatā*) is one who sees the Buddha.

Abiding immovably in the world like Mount Sumeru, illuminating the world like the sun, acting as a guide for humanity, and being fully endowed with the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), such a one subdues the enemies that are the māras.
What is the destination (*gati*) for these merits? It is the Noble Truths (*āryasatya*). Previously, the true nature was taken as the correct nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
According to this principle, the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) takes the noble truths (*āryasatya*) as its goal; the true mark takes the signless (*animitta*) as its characteristic;
and the noble truths take the truthlessness (*asatya*) as their truth. How can there be four? These four are merely the characteristics of the world.

To realize that the essence of these four characteristics is empty and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is precisely what constitutes the noble truths. Therefore, following the correct inquiry, the noble truths are subsequently presented.

Knowing this to be his inclination, the Buddha further addressed the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin: "The Tathāgata transcends the world, yet he also teaches the suffering of the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world.
[Note: Previously, the Brahmā asked what it means for a bodhisattva to transcend the world.]
While the Tathāgata guides sentient beings through worldly dharmas, his intention is this: it is not only the bodhisattvas who transcend worldly dharmas;
I, too, have transcended worldly dharmas, yet I also teach worldly dharmas to guide sentient beings within worldly dharmas.

The five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are called the suffering of the world. [Note: The five aggregates constitute that which is created by the world, while the world constitutes that which creates the five aggregates.
Because the subject and object depend upon one another, revolving without ever escaping each other, this is the characteristic of the suffering of the world.

Clinging to the five aggregates is called the origination of the world. [Note] Because the causal origination of the five aggregates of the past brings about the fruit of suffering in the present world,
and because one fails to realize its falsity and repeatedly constructs karmic causes that bring about the fruit of the future,
this is the origination of the world.

The exhaustion of the five aggregates is called the cessation of the world. [Note] The present physical body’s disintegration at the moment of death is the mark of the exhaustion of the five aggregates;
because there is no consciousness in subsequent aggregates, one does not perceive arising or ceasing, which is the cessation of the world.
To seek the five aggregates by means of the non-dual dharma is called the mundane path to cessation. [Note] Within this, there are two cases:
if one seeks the true mark of the five aggregates by means of the non-dual dharma, and the five aggregates remain as they are, then the mundane world is likewise so;
this is the supramundane Truth of the Path. If, within the non-dual dharma, one clings to the existence of the five aggregates that are to be severed, this is the mundane [path].
The preceding section explains the meaning of "cessation," while the subsequent section clarifies the correct interpretation of this passage.

Furthermore, as the Brahma-king stated, the five aggregates exist only as verbal designations; [note: in reality, no intrinsic nature can be apprehended, for one does not perceive the attainment of a non-existent nature.
Within this, grasping at signs and giving rise to conceptual discrimination constitutes what is called "worldly suffering. Not abandoning these views constitutes what is called "worldly origination.

The self-characteristic of these views constitutes what is called "worldly cessation. [Note: To give rise to views, engage in conceptual discrimination, and observe the self-characteristic of the five aggregates as being moment-to-moment impermanent—this is called "cessation."

Whichever path one follows, not grasping at these views is called the Path to the Cessation of the World. [Note: Whichever path one occupies, not grasping at discriminative views is called the Path to Cessation.
Because one does not realize that discrimination also lacks intrinsic nature, it is not termed a "Truth" (satya).
Whereas previously the Four Truths arose from the five aggregates, here the Four Truths are complete within a single thought-moment.
The five aggregates (pañca-skandha) pervade the three periods of time, and the four noble truths (catur-āryasatya) are divided into effect and cause;
these are all characteristics of the mundane world (*loka-dharma*). For this reason, Brahmā, I have said to the non-Buddhist seers (*ṛṣi*):

"O Seer, within your very body, you already speak of the suffering of the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world. [Note: The preceding section was...]

To manifest this through mindfulness is to manifest it within the very body itself. What is meant by the Four Noble Truths within the body? Birth, old age, sickness, and so forth—these eight sufferings are collectively termed "Suffering.

Seeking that which cannot be obtained and the separation from what one loves constitute "Origination. The intense burning of the five aggregates and the flux of the eight sufferings constitute "Cessation.
To distance oneself from the five aggregates and the eight sufferings is the "Path to Cessation. Furthermore, there is the collection of the four great elements.

That is to say: the arising of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct in the world is the worldly truth of suffering (*duḥkha*); the decay of the four great elements is the worldly truth of origination (*samudaya*);

the exhaustion of the four great elements is the worldly truth of cessation (*nirodha*); and the aversion to suffering and the seeking of happiness constitute the worldly truth of the path (*mārga*)—these two aspects of body and mind being the four truths of the sentient world (*sattvaloka*).
Why does the Tathāgata provide such detailed and thorough exposition of these, yet alone fail to speak of the four truths of the vessel world (*bhājanaloka*)?
Furthermore, the sentient world (*sattva-loka*) and the vessel world (*bhājana-loka*) are two yet non-dual.

If one speaks according to the principle of "the primary encompassing the secondary," then by speaking of the sentient world, the vessel world is already included; therefore, it is not mentioned separately.

Moreover, the Four Noble Truths are established because the deluded minds of sentient beings grasp at signs and engage in discrimination; the vessel world, being insentient and devoid of discrimination, is not [so established].

Because characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are inherently non-existent, there are no Four Noble Truths to be expounded; even though the Buddha does not preach [in terms of] characteristics, because the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*) are fully present and gathered together, this is the world’s suffering (*duḥkha*).
Because strife and contention are firm and solid, this is the world’s origin (*samudaya*). Because months and years pass and flow on, this is the world’s cessation (*nirodha*).
To trace back to the beginning and return to the end is the world’s path to cessation (*mārga*). The "Noble Truths" mentioned below are precisely wisdom (*jñāna*) and correctness (*samyak*).
[He] awakened to the world.
At that time, the Brahma King Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding the Four Noble Truths spoken by you, which among them are the true Noble Truths?
Is 'suffering' not called a Noble Truth? Is 'the origin of suffering' not called a Noble Truth? Is 'the cessation of suffering'..."

That which is called the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the Cessation of Suffering is not [itself] called a Noble Truth. [Note: That all four truths are termed "suffering" is a characteristic of the mundane world;
the following provides the explanation for this.
Why is this so? If suffering were the Noble Truth, then all cattle, donkeys, and animals would likewise possess the Noble Truth of suffering.
If the origin of suffering were the Noble Truth, then all sentient beings in whatever place they are born would likewise possess the Noble Truth of the origin;
for it is because of the origin that one is born into the various realms of existence. If the cessation of suffering were the Noble Truth...
Regarding the Truths: those who contemplate cessation and those who speak of annihilation should both possess the Noble Truth of Cessation.
[Note] Those who contemplate cessation are individuals who practice for themselves; those who speak of annihilation are those who preach the Dharma to others.
As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Kātyāyana and Vairaṭīputra both said: "The annihilation of this body after death is called Nirvāṇa. Furthermore...
In this system of natural philosophy, it is taught that after death the physical form decays and the spirit disperses;
even if one were to perform acts such as cutting or burning the body, they would have no effect whatsoever—all of which is said to be total annihilation.
If the path leading to the cessation of suffering were the Noble Truth, then all paths pertaining to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) should likewise constitute the Noble Truth of the Path.
[Note: "Conditioned paths" refers to those of worldly non-Buddhists and immortals, as well as the various arts and crafts, each of which claims to possess a path;
it also includes the two vehicles of the transcendental realm and even Bodhisattvas who rely on the provisional means (*upāya*) and have not yet exhausted the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is called the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Brahmā, for this reason you should know that the Noble Truths are neither suffering, nor its origin, nor its cessation, nor the path. As for the Noble Truth of Suffering:
knowing that suffering does not arise is called the Noble Truth of Suffering. [Note] Explaining the above "neither suffering" and so forth: what is meant by "neither"?
Suffering arises from suffering; if there were no suffering, how could suffering arise? If it does arise, does it arise in the mind or in the object?
If it arises in the object, then that object is suffering, and what concern is that for me? If it arises in the mind, is it one with the mind or different from it?
If it is one with the mind, then it cannot be known as suffering, because the mind does not know itself. If it is...
When the mind differs, it returns to being the same as the preceding object; investigating in this manner, one finds that ultimately there is no arising—this is called the Noble Truth.
Knowing that accumulation (*samudaya*) is without conjunction is named the Noble Truth of Accumulation. [Note: What is meant by "non-accumulation"?
It refers to how past causes of accumulation invite the fruit of suffering in the present, and how present causes of accumulation invite the fruit of suffering in the future. Is this not so?
The past does not reach the present, and the present does not reach the future. Why is this? Because the past has already ceased, the future has not yet arrived, and the present does not abide.
When one investigates the three time periods, no accumulation can be found.
Since there is no accumulation, what is there to be called "conjunction"? Because there is no conjunction, this is called the Noble Truth.
Within the dharma of ultimate cessation, to know that there is neither arising nor ceasing is called the Noble Truth of Cessation. [Note: What is meant by "neither arising nor ceasing"?
The five aggregates, such as form (*rūpa*), do not abide for even a single moment;

yet outsiders (*tīrthika*) reckon this to be annihilation, while those of the Two Vehicles apply their minds to subdue it and grasp it as ultimate cessation. Both of these lack the Noble Truth; it is only in the Mahāyāna that it is truly so.
The place of its cessation does not obstruct its arising; because one realizes non-arising and there is no attainment of cessation, it is called the Noble Truth of Cessation.
To attain the Way through the dharma of non-duality by means of equality toward all phenomena is called the Noble Truth of the Path. [Note: Equality]
One who neither attains birth-and-death nor attains nirvana remains far removed from the two extremes; the five aggregates remain as they are, and the world likewise remains as it is.
Because suchness is suchness, there is no attainment and yet there is attainment; thus one attains the Noble Truth of the Path.
The Brahma-true holy truth is devoid of falsehood. [Note] The four kinds of holy truths mentioned above consist in realizing that suffering and the other [truths] are without self-nature;
this is called the holy truth. If one were to say that there are four holy truths, it would be equivalent to falsehood and not the true holy truth.
The true holy truth is such that it is not merely devoid of the four characteristics of suffering and so forth, but is even devoid of a self, a person, a life-span, and a soul.
Furthermore, all that is false and illusory is entirely non-existent.
That which is called "false and illusory" refers to attachment to a self, attachment to sentient beings, attachment to a person, attachment to a life-sustainer, and attachment to a nourisher.
[Note] Non-Buddhists claim that the self is nourished by Brahmā, Puruṣa, and so forth; this is comparable to the local calculation that nature [is the source].

"Those attached to what is bestowed by heaven," and so forth—those who are attached to existence, attached to non-existence, attached to arising, attached to cessation, attached to birth-and-death, and attached to nirvana.

[Note] This is a further explanation establishing that if one is attached to such names and marks as these, they are not the true Noble Truths; it serves to refute the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
Brahmā, if a practitioner says, "My knowledge and vision of suffering is false; my abandonment of the origin of suffering is false;
my realization of cessation is false; my cultivation of the path is false. Why is this? Because such a person has lost the Buddha’s protective mindfulness;
therefore, it is said to be false. [Note: This refutes the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). It is because they regard conditioned phenomena as permanent.
To view the unconditioned as nihilism, or to hold views of both existence and non-existence, is the view of superimposition;

to hold views of neither existence nor non-existence is the view of conceptual proliferation. If these four views arise such that even a small portion of the sixty-two false views remains unextinguished, one will lose the seed of the Buddha and shall not be protected by his mindful care.
What is it that constitutes being protected by the mindfulness of the Buddha? [Note] Having refuted the heterodox, one should now manifest the orthodox:

namely, not recollecting any dharmas whatsoever is called being protected by the mindfulness of the Buddha. [Note] Regarding the four propositions and the hundred negations, none of them are recollected.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "Neither think of good, nor think of evil—what is it? At this very moment, one returns to oneself.
However, when the mind enters non-arising, it is profoundly still and eternally quiescent.
If a practitioner abides within this mindfulness, they do not abide in any phenomena (*nimitta*). If they do not abide in any phenomena, they abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
To abide in the limit of reality is called "non-abiding of the mind. One who does not abide in the mind is called a [true] person.

"Neither true speech nor false speech. [Note]: When all external marks are eliminated and internal mental states—the mind that dwells upon them—are likewise extinguished, then it is neither real nor unreal.
Brahmā, for this reason you should know that that which is neither real nor unreal is called a Noble Truth.
Brahmā, what is real never becomes unreal. [Note: Because it does not become unreal, it is not false; because it does not establish itself independently, it is not real.
Whether there is a Buddha or not, the dharma-nature (dharmatā) is eternally abiding. [Note: This further explains the meaning of being neither real nor unreal.
"Whether there is" or "whether there is not" refers to worldly phenomena; however, the dharma-nature eternally abides, never having existence or non-existence.
What is called the nature of birth-and-death and the nature of nirvāṇa is the eternally real nature. Why is this so? Because one does not attain nirvāṇa apart from birth-and-death;
this is what is called the Noble Truth. [Note] The preceding passage, in its dual negation of the characteristics of the mind, stated that it is "neither real nor unreal.
Here, in the dual negation of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, it is stated that their "intrinsic nature is eternally real. This is what is meant by "directly pointing at the person."
That the mind does not rely on words is seen here.
If a person realizes these Four Noble Truths in this way, they are called one who speaks the truth of the world. [Note: These Four Noble Truths are neither realized nor unrealized;
that is to say, when one wishes to speak them with the mouth, the words fail; when one wishes to contemplate them with the mind, the thoughts vanish. It is simply this.
It may be left at that.
Brahmā, there will be bhikṣus in the future who do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate ethical discipline, do not cultivate the mind, and do not cultivate wisdom;

such persons will say that the characteristic of arising is the truth of suffering, the conjunction of various conditions is the truth of origination, and the cessation of phenomena is the truth of cessation.
Regarding the second point, seeking characteristics within the two dharmas as being the Truth of the Path, the Buddha said: "I declare that these foolish people are followers of external paths;
I am not their teacher, nor are they my disciples. Because these people have fallen into false paths and have destroyed and lost the Dharma, they claim that there is a 'Truth'.
[Note: The Buddha intended to cause the bhikṣus of the final age to cultivate precepts regarding the body and wisdom regarding the mind.

Having taught the four characteristics such as suffering so that they might know [phenomena] are unreal, if a bhikṣu not only fails to cultivate the precepts and wisdom but further speaks in such a manner, how can he be a disciple of the Buddha?
He is merely a member of the faction of true non-Buddhists.
"Brahmā, furthermore, observe that when I sat at the site of enlightenment, I did not apprehend a single dharma as being either real or illusory.
If I did not apprehend any such dharma, how could there possibly be speech, discourse, or instruction among the assembly?"

[Note] The previous refutation of the bhikṣu’s reckoning was merely not done out of mere formality; [the bhikṣu implies that] "I truly did not obtain a single dharma while sitting at the site of enlightenment.
The World-Honored One seems almost like one who confesses his own guilt while still clutching the stolen goods.
Brahmā said, "No, World-Honored One. Because all dharmas are unattainable and because all dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), my awakening is characterized by the absence of craving.
[Note: Within the Deer Park, the World-Honored One turned the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths three times;
at that time, Cunda and others first attained understanding, while the rest had not yet awakened to the Four Truths.

Because sentient beings fail to understand that phenomena are unborn and instead engage in conceptual proliferations such as existence and non-existence, the World-Honored One revealed the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) within the very Four Noble Truths.
Following the section on the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, he subsequently expounded the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths;

like a flash of lightning followed by a sweeping rain, names and marks (*nāmanimitta*) no longer remain. This may truly be called "directly abandoning expedient means. (Question: Regarding the four [teachings] of Tiantai...)

Question: Among the four truths, to which one does this correspond? Answer: It is the teaching of the single mind in its sudden aspect, which cannot be contained within the categories of names and forms;
since it is not even "one," how could there be "four"? Yet, within the process of pointing toward and expressing it, there is no lack of a target.

The initial statement that the five aggregates are called the "world" and so forth refers to the four truths of arising and ceasing, encompassing the immeasurable. The subsequent statement regarding "knowing that which is without arising" and so forth [refers to the truth of cessation].
This refers to the Four Noble Truths of Non-arising combined with the Unconditioned (Anabhisaṃskṛta).

At the end, it is called the "Truth of the True Sage" because it transcends names and words, simultaneously negating both the empty and the real, and ultimately lacks any verbal expression, discussion, or teaching that could encompass it.
How could Tiantai possibly attempt to fathom such a truth, which is the Tathāgata’s own repayment of his verbal debts?
Chapter Five: Praising Merit [Note]:
Because one hears that the Tathāgata did not attain a single dharma when sitting at the site of enlightenment, one knows that meritlessness constitutes merit.
Praise can never exhaust this merit; since merit is taken as merit through meritlessness, it is thus praised.
"Non-praise is itself praise, for all things ultimately return to one’s own mind.
At that time, the Brahma Heaven King Siyi addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, if the Tathāgata has no attainment regarding the Dharma, what benefit is there in saying that the Tathāgata attains Bodhi and is thus called a Buddha? [Note: The Brahma Heaven King feared that those in the assembly would not...]
The realization that there is nothing to be attained while yet attaining it is also a form of indicative expression;
therefore, this difficult question was raised. The Buddha said: "Brahmā, what do you think?

Regarding the dharmas I have taught—whether conditioned or unconditioned—are these dharmas real or are they false? Brahmā replied: "These dharmas are false, not real. [Note: Ordinary beings are attached to them.]

The Buddha spoke of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) to shatter their attachment to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and he spoke of skillful means (*upāya*) to inspire the resolve of those attached to the unconditioned of the two vehicles.
Since both existence and non-existence were spoken of as expedients to suit specific capacities, what relevance do they have for me?
Thus, Brahmā knew them to be false and not real.
What do you think? If a dharma is false and not real, does that dharma exist or not exist? [Note:
There are four permutations for distinguishing dharmas: namely, whether conditioned dharmas exist as existent, or whether unconditioned dharmas exist as non-existent.
Brahmā said: "World-Honored One, if a dharma is illusory, that dharma should not be said to exist, nor should it be said not to exist.
What do you think? If a dharma is neither existent nor non-existent, can that dharma be attained? Brahmā replied: "There is no one who attains it.
"Brahmā, when the Tathāgata sat at the site of enlightenment, he realized only that which arises from illusory inversion and affliction."

The nature of ultimate emptiness is free from affliction. [Note] The preceding chapter stated that when I sat at the site of enlightenment, I did not apprehend a single dharma that was either real or illusory, reaching a state beyond words, speech, and debate. Thereupon, a Brahma-king raised an objection, saying:
"If you do not apprehend a single dharma, how can you attain bodhi and be called a Buddha? The World-Honored One questioned him in response and replied:
He said: "While sitting at the site of enlightenment, I did not attain any dharmas, but only attained the emptiness of the nature of all dharmas.
As previously stated, nirvāṇa and space possess only names, yet lack any real nature.
Because there is nothing to be attained, one attains; because there is nothing to be known, one knows. [Note:

"Attaining because there is nothing to be attained" means realizing that all phenomena are empty and attaining one's own mind. "Knowing because there is nothing to be known" means that afflictions are unreal, and knowing that the self-nature is eternally sublime.
Why is this? The Dharma I have attained cannot be seen—just as the eye cannot see itself—and it cannot be heard—just as the ear cannot hear itself.
It cannot be awakened to. [Note] The mind does not awaken itself.
It cannot be cognized. [Note] Consciousness does not cognize itself. These four points convey the meaning that internal realization is unattainable.
It cannot be grasped. [Note] It is like the moon in water or an image in a mirror;
it cannot be clung to. [Note] It is like a mirage on land or an object within a dream.
It cannot be spoken. [Note] I am unable to speak it.
It cannot be challenged. [Note] You are unable to challenge this; these four points externally demonstrate its unattainability.
It transcends all characteristics of dharmas; it is without speech, without discourse, without letters, and without the path of verbal expression.
[Note] Since neither internal nor external can be apprehended, one knows that this dharma transcends all characteristics of dharmas.

It is without words or discourse, which realizes the aforementioned absence of verbal expression; it is without letters, which realizes the aforementioned absence of deliberation; it is without the path of verbal expression.
This demonstrates that there was no prior instruction.
Brahmā, this Dharma is like space; do you wish to obtain benefit within such a Dharma? Brahmā replied, "No.
[Note: These words were spoken by the World-Honored One when his power of reasoning could not fully subdue him, and he thus employed a metaphor.
Taking empty space as witness, one has not yet attained even half; if you wish for the public case to be complete, you must realize it within yourself before you can attain it.
When Brahmā asked, "If not a single dharma is attained, what benefit is there in attaining Bodhi?
the World-Honored One first answered that it is by having nothing to attain that one attains it, and subsequently challenged him on how one could attain it through having nothing to attain.
One should seek benefit therein.
The World-Honored One, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are most rare and marvelous in that they have accomplished unprecedented dharmas;

having entered deeply into great loving-kindness and great compassion, they have attained such dharmas of the mark of quiescence, yet they teach people by means of words and letters so that they may attain them as well. [Note]

Within the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is not a single dharma; yet, although there is not a single dharma, it does not obstruct verbal expression or written characters used to teach people about quiescence—that which is neither arising nor ceasing.
Because it is non-ceasing, one teaches people so that they may attain non-arising;
thus, in reality, there is not a single dharma.
"Bhagavān, those who hear this Dharma and are able to believe and understand it—know, Bhagavān, that such persons have not come from small merit.
This Dharma is difficult for all the world to believe. Why is this?
Because the world clings to reality, yet this Dharma is neither real nor false; the world clings to dharmas, yet this Dharma is no-dharma."
The world clings to nirvāṇa as being contrary to the Dharma, yet this Dharma has neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa;
the world clings to wholesome dharmas, yet this Dharma is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; the world clings to pleasure, yet this Dharma is neither suffering nor pleasure;
the world clings to the appearance of a Buddha in the world, yet this Dharma has neither the appearance of a Buddha nor its absence.

Although there is the teaching of the Dharma within *nirvāṇa*, this Dharma is not a phenomenon that can be expressed through words. [Note] In the preceding "Chapter on the Proper Inquiry," it was stated:
"If one gives rise to views regarding phenomena, the Buddha does not appear in the world; if one seeks *nirvāṇa* within the dharma of ultimate cessation, the Buddha does not appear in the world.
It further states: "The appearance of the Buddha in the world is called the distancing from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)," yet there is concern for the masses...
The "reality within" refers to the appearance of a Buddha in the world and the presentation of understanding by Brahmā, both of which have been swept away. A doubt arises:
"If no Buddha has appeared in the world, why is there currently one who preaches the Dharma? The explanation states: "Another says that there is no preacher;
if one were to say that there is something to be preached, it would constitute frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)."
Although one may praise the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha itself is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

[Note] Since the unconditioned is equal with respect to both praise and blame, this Dharma is difficult for all the world to believe. [Note] This demonstrates that the ultimate, non-referential single mind constitutes the reason it is difficult to believe;
because it is non-referential, it is neither empty nor real, neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa, and neither...
Good is not, evil is not, suffering is not, pleasure is not; all phenomena are "not," while the true mind alone shines brightly.
When the skin and flesh have fallen away, only the reality remains—this is called that which is difficult to believe.
It is like fire emerging from water or water emerging from fire; it is difficult to find anything that can be believed, yet such is the nature of the Buddha-nature within afflictions.
That within *bodhi* there are afflictions (*kleśa*) is likewise difficult to believe. [Note: That within afflictions there is *bodhi* does not destroy the *dharmatā*;
that within *bodhi* there are afflictions does not sever the nature of evil afflictions.

If viewed through their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are like water and fire, which cannot coexist; if viewed through their essence (*svabhāva*), they are wondrously contained within one another.
Furthermore, those who follow the three vehicles mostly lose sight of the nature because they cling to appearances;
thus, enlightenment and afflictions are perceived as being diametrically opposed, such that one desires to extinguish afflictions in order to attain enlightenment.
Within the teaching of the One Vehicle, afflictions and enlightenment are wondrously harmonized with one another, never reaching a state of duality. This is what is called "difficult to believe."
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata has realized the nature of these illusory afflictions; there is neither a dharma that exists nor one that does not exist. [Note:
The first phrase reveals the nature of true emptiness, while the second phrase manifests the reality of wondrous existence. Because it is true emptiness, afflictions are fundamentally suchness;
because it is wondrous existence, there is no dharma that cannot be attained.
Whatever Dharma is taught is likewise without form. [Note: Because no dharma can be apprehended, there is no obstruction to what is taught;
yet although there is that which is taught, no fixed essence can be found.

Although there is that which is known, there is no conceptual discrimination. [Note] Because knowing accords with *tathatā* (suchness) and is far removed from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is without discrimination.
Although one realizes *nirvāṇa*, there is no one who extinguishes. [Note] *Nirvāṇa* is called "extinction and transcendence" because it transcends afflictions and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, in this realization of the Dharma of the perfectly wondrous self-mind, there is no birth-and-death to be extinguished, nor is there any nirvana to be realized.

World-Honored One, if there are good sons or good daughters who are able to believe and understand such meanings of the Dharma, you should know that these people have attained liberation from all views.
[Note: Such meanings of the Dharma are far removed from the two extremes, namely, neither being real nor...

If the empty were identical to the real, then the empty would be existence; if the empty were identical to non-existence, then existence and non-existence would form two views, which in turn compound into the sixty-two views.

Therefore it is said that when one is detached from these various views, one is liberated from them all. Once one is free from the two views of existence and non-existence, then all views are thereby transcended.
One should know that such a person has already drawn near to immeasurable Buddhas; one should know that such a person has already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas.

[Note: To be liberated from all views is for the mind to accord with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Because it accords with the true mark, this is called "drawing near" and this is called "making offerings."
One should know that such a person is protected by spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). [Note: They are cherished by those whose minds accord with reality and who share the same path.
One should know that such a person’s resolve is vast; one should know that such a person’s roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are profound.
[Note: When the roots are great, they naturally aspire to the stage of a Buddha; when the roots are thick, they naturally sustain the Great Dharma.
It should be known that such a person guards the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas; it should be known that such a person is able to contemplate well and give rise to wholesome karma.
[Note] To shoulder the great Dharma is to guard the Dharma-treasury; to claim for oneself the stage of Buddhahood is to give rise to the wholesome fruit of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

It should be known that such a person is of noble lineage, born into the family of the Tathāgata. [Note] By a single thought of faith and understanding in the true reality (*dharmatā*), one is immediately called a son of the Buddha;
this differs from the gradual cultivation of the three vehicles.

Just as a prince is born with innate nobility and differs from a minister’s son who achieves status only after long study, it is said that a bodhisattva ascends [to the stage of realization] by the mere arousal of the mind in a single thought.

One who attains perfect enlightenment should be known as one capable of practicing great relinquishment (*mahopekṣā*) and abandoning all afflictions (*kleśa*); one should know that such a person possesses the power of ethical discipline (*śīla-bala*), not the power of afflictions.
[Note: The ethical discipline of the Hīnayāna, consisting of the observance of prohibitions and precepts, gives rise to many afflictions; whereas in the Mahāyāna, the mind is in accord with reality.
The true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is then called "concomitant with the Path" (mārgasahagata).
One should know that such a person attains the power of patience (kṣāntibala), not the power of anger (vyāpādabala). [Note: When mind and objects confront one another, anger arises;
if the mind is free from dependence (nirapekṣa), there is neither patience nor anything to be endured.
It should be known that such a person attains the power of diligence and is free from weariness;

it should be known that such a person attains the power of meditative concentration and extinguishes all evil thoughts. [Note: In the Hīnayāna, because the mind dwells upon attainment, one remains attached and does not relinquish it—this is called an "evil thought.
In the Mahāyāna, the mind dwells in equanimity, utterly devoid of attachment.
It should be known that such a person attains the power of wisdom and is freed from evil, false views. [Note: Among the non-Buddhists, there is no wisdom;
they contradict the true nature of reality and cling to various false views. If a person can have faith in this Dharma, then their false views will be abandoned.
One should know that no evil Māras can gain any advantage over such a person, and one should know that they cannot be destroyed by any enemies or thieves.
[Note: Within the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), both loss and gain are forgotten; therefore, neither evil Māras nor enemies and thieves can do anything to them.

One should know that such a person does not deceive the world; one should know that such a person is a speaker of truth, because they skillfully explain the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*);
one should know that such a person is a speaker of reality, because they speak of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);

one should know that such a person is well-guarded by the mindfulness of all Buddhas; and one should know that such a person is gentle, mild, and virtuous, dwelling in peace and harmony with others. [Note] By...
Because they have faith and understanding in this Dharma, they are born into the family of the Tathāgata and practice what the Buddhas practice;
thus they are endowed with the six pāramitās. Being endowed with the six pāramitās, they are not moved by adverse conditions.
Because they are not moved by adverse conditions, whatever they teach is neither deceptive nor false. Because it is not false, the characteristics of the Dharma they teach are true and not deceptive.
Therefore, that which he teaches is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
because it is indeed reality itself, he is protected and sustained by all Buddhas, dwells together with the assembly, and is fully endowed with the six points of harmony (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*).
One should know that such a person is called "greatly wealthy" because they possess the noble riches (*ārya-dhana*);

one should know that such a person is always able to practice contentment because they cultivate the noble lineages (*ārya-vaṃśa*). [Note: Both the noble riches and the noble lineages are born from within one's own mind;
if one can have faith in one's own mind, then the noble lineages and noble riches will be complete therein.

It should be known that such a person is easy to satisfy and easy to nourish because they are free from greedy attachment. [Note] Because they are free from greed, Bodhi is easy to satisfy and the Dharma-body is easy to nourish;
because they are free from attachment, they are easy to satisfy; because they are free from clinging, they are easy to nourish.
It should be known that this person attains a mind of peace and security because they have reached the other shore. [Note] All that precedes concerns self-confidence and one's own practice;
what follows concerns the work of benefiting others.

It should be known that this person delivers those who have not yet been delivered; it should be known that this person liberates those who have not yet been liberated; it should be known that this person...

One who brings peace to those who are not yet at peace should be known as one who has extinguished what was not yet extinguished. [Note] Herein, the four phrases are presented in pairs concerning oneself and others.

Regarding oneself, although afflictions are difficult to overcome, one is able to cross over; regarding others, although one has not yet crossed over one's own afflictions, one causes them to cross over.

Based on this, it should be understood that, with respect to oneself, this establishes the meaning of the preceding "self-confidence" and "self-understanding," while with respect to others, it is as follows below.
This refers to the intention of showing people the right path.
One should know that such a person is able to show the right path; one should know that such a person is able to explain liberation;
one should know that such a person is a great king of physicians who skillfully knows all medicines; one should know that such a person is like a fine medicine that effectively cures all ailments.
[Note] The "right path and liberation" refers to the Dharma that has been taught; the "physician-king’s excellent medicine" refers to the capacities of those for whom it is intended.
The medicine is a metaphor for the true nature (*dharmatā*), which effectively cures the various distinct ailments.
One should know that this person’s wisdom is courageous and robust; one should know that this person possesses great power, being firm and ultimate;
one should know that this person has the strength of diligence and does not follow the words of others. [Note: "Wisdom is courageous and robust" means there is neither doubt nor indecision.
"Firm and ultimate" means there is neither delusion nor failure. "Having one's own position" means not following others.
Regarding the three teachings: because one relies on faith and understanding of the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one is able to shoulder the burden of both self and others;
this is called being courageous and strong, this is called being steadfast, and this is called being diligent.
You should know that such a person is like a lion, free from all fear; you should know that such a person is like a king of elephants.
One whose mind is disciplined and supple should be known as being like an aged elephant; one whose mind is compliant should be known as being like a bull-king capable of leading the great multitude.
[Note] Fearlessness is the excellence of attaining its essence; discipline and suppleness are the excellence of attaining its function;
compliance is the excellence of attaining its skillful means. When these three are complete, one is excellently able to lead the great multitude.
The assembly is like a king of oxen.
One should know that such a person is greatly courageous and capable of destroying the enmity of Māra. [Note] The former passage states that the enmity of Māra does not disturb them;
this passage states that they can subdue the enmity of Māra; thus, the texts are presented from different perspectives.
One should know that such a person is a great man (mahāpuruṣa) who dwells among the multitude without fear;

one should know that such a person has nothing to dread or avoid, because they have attained the dharma of fearlessness; one should know that such a person has no difficulty in speaking the dharma of true reality, because they are fearless.
[Note] "Having no dread" means being without envy, and "being fearless" means being without timidity; this explains the meaning of the great man’s fearlessness.
One should know that such a person is endowed with pure and white dharmas like the full moon; one should know that the light of this person’s wisdom shines like the sun and moon;
one should know that this person dispels all darkness like one holding a torch. [Note]:
Just as the full moon is utterly free from dust and obscuration, so too is the radiance of wisdom like the sun and moon when it is utterly free from dust and obscuration.
The sun illuminates the day, the moon illuminates the night, and the torch illuminates places where the sun and moon do not reach;
these three function in succession to reveal the true nature (dharmatā), for the light of wisdom shines everywhere without exception.

One should know that such a person delights in practicing the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*), remaining free from all hatred and attachment. [Note: When the mind has faith in the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), enemies and kin are equalized, and thus hatred and attachment are distanced.
One should know that this person nurtures and sustains sentient beings like the earth; one should know that this person washes away all defilements like water;
one should know that this person burns away all restless thoughts like fire; one should know that this person is unobstructed regarding the Dharma like the wind.
[Note: Only the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) can purify sentient beings, and only the true mark can eliminate restless thoughts.
Exhausting all obstacles, only the true mark (*dharmatā*) can penetrate and believe in this Dharma; once one believes in this Dharma, what could earth, water, fire, and wind not encompass?
One should know that the mind of such a person is unmoving like Mount Sumeru; one should know that the mind of such a person is as firm and solid as...
Vajragiri, you should know that such a person cannot be moved by any of the proponents of competitive debate among the various non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas). [Note:
The debates of the non-Buddhists do not transcend the views of existence and non-existence; since one who has faith and understanding in this Dharma is free from all such views, they cannot be moved.
It should be known that this person cannot be fathomed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. [Note:
Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have realized partial emptiness, they have not yet glimpsed the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); therefore, they are unable to do so.
One should know that such a person abounds in the treasures of the Dharma like the great ocean; one should know that the afflictions of such a person do not manifest, like the *pāṭala* flower;
one should know that such a person seeks the Dharma without weariness; one should know that such a person is content through wisdom;
and one should know that such a person is able to turn the wheel of the Dharma like a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*). [Note: The wheel-turning monarch turns the ten wholesome paths of action.]
The practitioner who turns the wheel of resolute faith turns the wheel of the true mark (*dharmatā*).

One should know that the physical form and color of such a person are as exquisite as those of Śakra, Lord of Devas; one should know that the mind of such a person has attained mastery like that of Brahmā, King of Gods;
one should know that the sound of such a person’s preaching of the Dharma is like the roar of thunder; one should know that this person...

The descent of the Dharma-nectar is like timely rain; one should know that such a person is able to increase the untainted faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), and factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

[Note] The faculties refer to the five faculties, the powers to the five powers, and the seven factors of enlightenment together with the eightfold noble path are collectively termed the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*).
All these are benefits conferred by the preaching of the Dharma; the sound is like thunder, startling and awakening the various capacities of sentient beings.
They cause sentient beings to awaken according to their capacities and provide them with nourishment, like a timely rain that causes the sprouts of the Path to grow.
One should know that such a person has already crossed the mire of birth and death; one should know that such a person has entered the wisdom of the Buddha;
one should know that such a person is close to the Bodhi of the Buddha; one should know that such a person is able to study extensively, such that none can equal them. One should know.
One should know that this person is immeasurable and has transcended all measure; one should know that this person’s wisdom and eloquence are without obstruction;
one should know that this person’s mindfulness is firm and they have attained dhāraṇī; one should know that this person knows the deep inclinations and actions of all sentient beings;
and one should know that this person has attained the power of wisdom to correctly contemplate all phenomena and thoroughly understand their meanings and purports.
[Note] Above, by transcending birth and death, one draws near to the Buddha’s Bodhi;

by drawing near to the Buddha’s Bodhi, one’s learning emerges from the Three Vehicles, surpassing all numerical measures and exceeding all calculations. Thus, through unimpeded wisdom and discernment, one attains *dhāraṇī*;
having attained *dhāraṇī*, one is able to know the conduct of sentient beings and, through correct contemplation, ensures that what is seen is not erroneous.
Because they have attained thorough understanding, they demonstrate non-differentiation; herein, both self-benefit and benefit for others are entirely the merit of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
One should know that such a person practices with diligent vigor to bring benefit and peace to the world; one should know that such a person transcends the world.
One should know that such a person cannot be defiled, just like a lotus flower; one should know that such a person is not obscured by worldly dharmas.

[Note] Those who wish to benefit and bring peace to the world must first benefit themselves. Because they first benefit themselves, they transcend the world and are not stained by it, just like a lotus flower;
furthermore, by means of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), they are not obscured by worldly dharmas.
Their principle is not like that of the world, yet they act within the world without destroying the world.

One should know that such people are beloved by those of sharp faculties; one should know that such people are revered by those of great learning; one should know that such people are remembered by the wise;
one should know that such people are honored by gods and humans; one should know that such people are seated [in the ultimate state].

One should know that those whom practitioners of dhyāna pay homage to are virtuous persons esteemed by the worthy; one should know that they are the objects of longing and admiration for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
[Note: When one has faith and understanding in such Dharma principles and is thus honored by the multitude, who would not look up to them and emulate their learning?
One should know that such a person does not crave minor practices; one should know that such a person does not conceal their faults nor flaunt their virtues.

[Note: Since even the reality of the Dharma’s meaning is not encompassed by the Mahāyāna, who would crave minor practices? Since the essence of both fault and merit is non-arising (*anutpāda*), what is there to conceal and what is there to flaunt?

One should know that this person’s deportment is fully perfected, inspiring pure faith in others; one should know that this person’s physical form is upright and handsome, bringing joy to all who see them;
one should know that this person possesses great majestic power, revered and honored by the multitude;
one should know that this person adorns their body with the thirty-two marks of a great man. [Note: The preceding section concerns the sound of preaching the Dharma, up to the śrāvakas.]
To praise their verbal karma out of greedy admiration is not to practice the minor deeds; this [passage] praises their bodily karma.
One should know that such a person can continue the lineage of the Buddhas; one should know that such a person can protect the Jewel of the Dharma; one should know that such a person...
One should know that those who are able to make offerings to the Sangha are beheld by all Buddhas; one should know that such persons have attained the Dharma-eye;
one should know that such persons receive the prediction of enlightenment through the wisdom of the Buddha; and one should know that such persons are fully endowed with the three kinds of patience.

[Note] The three types of patience—patience regarding the practice of austerities (*duṣkaracaryā-kṣānti*), patience regarding the arising [of phenomena] (*utpatti-kṣānti*), and patience regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*)—are also termed "dharma-patience" (*dharmakṣānti*); this meaning is derived from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
One should know that such a person dwells securely in the place of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*); one should know that such a person destroys the armies of Māra; one should know that such a person...
One who attains all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) should be known as one who turns the wheel of Dharma;
one should be known as one who performs immeasurable Buddha-works. [Note: The preceding eulogistic passages appear out of sequence;
their general meaning is solely the single reality-mark (lakṣaṇa). Do not let the words obscure the meaning by seeking separate interpretations.

If there are people who believe in and understand the meaning of such dharmas without being startled, doubtful, or terrified, they shall obtain such merit. These people, regarding the unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) of all Buddhas— which is profoundly deep, difficult to understand, difficult to know, difficult to believe in, and difficult to enter—
are able to believe and accept it, read and recite it with mastery, uphold it, explain it extensively for others, and practice according to the teaching.
If one practices this oneself and also teaches others to practice as taught, even if I were to spend an eon—or slightly less than an eon—speaking of such a person’s merits, I could not exhaust them.
[Note: This chapter was originally extracted from the "Four Noble Truths" chapter;
while there appear to be some discrepancies, the aforementioned statement that "my enlightenment is characterized by the absence of craving" was followed by Brahmā.]
Question: Since not a single dharma can be found upon sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), what benefit is there in speaking of attaining *bodhi*?
Thus, through these successive interrogations, do you wish to obtain a benefit within such dharmas?
[This matter] should be connected to the subsequent text in the "Chapter on the Noble Truths" (*āryasatya-paṭala*), where the World-Honored One [states]: "All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas..."
The arrival [of this text] is truly rare; it belongs to the "Chapter on Praising Merit," and its meaning is thus well-established.
