Because they are free from conceptual construction, all phenomena are without activity; because they have transcended the three realms, [this is] the illumination of the Dharma shown by means of the three gates of liberation.
Because all phenomena are by nature free from desire and are quiescent, all phenomena are free from hatred and are without obstruction, and all phenomena are free from delusion.
Because there is no darkness. [Note: This demonstrates that phenomena are free from the three poisons.
All phenomena come from nowhere, for they are fundamentally unarisen; all phenomena go nowhere, for they have no destination;
all phenomena abide nowhere, for they have no support; all phenomena transcend the three periods of time—past, future, and present—for they do not exist therein.
Therefore. [Note] Because the three limits—the three periods of time—are all non-appropriated;
because all phenomena have no difference as their nature is one; and because all phenomena are unarisen as they are free from retribution.
[Note] This is shown based on the four characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing to demonstrate that phenomena do not exist.
All phenomena (dharmas) are without karma, because neither karma, its retribution, nor an agent can be apprehended. [Note: "Without karma" means that within phenomena there is no cause;
"karma-retribution and agent" refers to the absence of karmic fruit within phenomena.
All dharmas do not act because they have no arising; all dharmas are without arising because their nature is unconditioned;

all dharmas are unconditioned because they are free from birth and extinction; all dharmas are true because they do not arise from combination; all dharmas are real because they are the gateway to the single path.
[Note] Since all phenomena do not act, they do not arise; since they do not arise, they are without birth or cessation.
This is because, within the gate of true emptiness, it has been thus from the very beginning. Nevertheless, although it is thus, one must not fall into the view of nihilistic annihilation;
therefore, it further states, "This is reality," to demonstrate its wondrous existence.
All dharmas are without sentient beings because sentient beings cannot be apprehended; all dharmas are without self because they are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). [Note:
The characteristics of a self, a person, and so forth are all characteristics of ignorance. The true nature of all dharmas is precisely the ultimate truth.
Since it is the ultimate truth, how could there be any characteristics therein?

Because all phenomena (*dharmas*) are dull and lack cognition. [Note] "Dull" means having the nature of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); because the essence of phenomena is fundamentally indeterminate.
Because all phenomena abandon hatred and love; because all phenomena are free from afflictions (*kleśa*) and thus lack feverish distress. [Note] Afflictions...
The nature of anger is heat; this heat arises from love and hatred. If one relinquishes love and hatred, then afflictions are abandoned.
All phenomena are by nature stainless, for they are not defiled. [Note: The nature of phenomena is identical to empty space; it is fundamentally without essence.
Since it lacks essence, it cannot even be called "pure," so how could there be "stain"?

All phenomena have a single characteristic because they are the limit of detachment from desire. [Note] The ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all desires is itself the ultimate reality of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), for the nature of phenomena is non-dual;
therefore, it is said to have a single characteristic.

Because all phenomena are eternally quiescent due to their detachment from characteristics. [Note] This means that because they possess a single characteristic, even while detached from characteristics, they are eternally quiescent.

Because all phenomena abide in the nature of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and are indestructible. [Note] If one gives rise to a view that is detached from characteristics, it cannot be called "real."

It is ultimate; if one abides in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one does not depart from signs, yet one constantly dwells in meditative concentration because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) does not destroy signs, and because the suchness-signs (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena are non-discriminative.
[Note: "Non-destruction" is due to the suchness of the characteristics of phenomena; thus, there is no discrimination.
It is the destruction and non-destruction [of all phenomena].

This is because all phenomena enter into and pervade the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). [Note: That which is called "non-discrimination between destruction and non-destruction" is due to the pervasive entry into the dharma-nature;
for both destruction and non-destruction enter into the dharma-nature.
All phenomena are without conditions (*anālambana*), because they do not conjoin with conditions. [Note: Although it is said that they pervade all things, they do not conjoin with conditions.
All phenomena are *bodhi* because they are seen as they truly are; all phenomena are *nirvāṇa* because they are without causes or conditions. [Note:
*Nirvāṇa* is defined as the severing of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). When conceptual discrimination is severed, how could there be any causes or conditions? Thus ends the section.
The thirty-two kinds of Dharma gates are collectively the gate of the single true reality and correct nature;

because these are skillful means employed for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they have many names. When one brings them together and returns to their source, they are seen to be nothing other than one's own mind—different in name but identical in essence.
This can be understood through reflection.
The light of the Tathāgata Universal Radiance Sovereign King constantly issues forth such pure sounds of the Dharma, which are also able to cause all bodhisattvas to perform the work of Buddhas.
In that Buddha-land, there are no demonic activities, and the lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
[Note: Although the light lacks the faculty of speech, it is able to produce such sounds of the Dharma; this Dharma is not ordinary speech.
It is that which is reached by words and sounds; though light itself lacks mind or consciousness, it can cause Bodhisattvas to perform the Buddha-work.

This is a phenomenon (*dharma*) and not something that can be achieved by the mental faculties of the heart, intellect, or consciousness. One who can thus awaken and enter this state will be free from demonic activities and attain the ground of non-birth (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Having attained the ground of non-birth, one's lifespan becomes immeasurable.
Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "If anyone wishes to attain a pure buddha-field, they should take up the merit cultivated by the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha to fulfill a pure land.
It is because, Kāśyapa, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha has fulfilled his vows by cultivating merit in the presence of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddhas. [Note: *upādāya* (to take up)]

The Buddha-land should be like that of Jālinīprabha; one must practice by relying on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) to be able to achieve what is called the "fulfillment of merit cultivated according to vows under immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* Buddhas.

This refers to the characteristic of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which transcends all numerical calculation. A Buddha is one who is awakened; if one awakens to one's own mind, one realizes there is no vow.
When there is no vow, no cultivation of what is not cultivated, and no merit in that which is without merit, only then is one said to be "fully endowed.
At that time, Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha, saying: "Virtuous One, you have already received a prediction from the Buddha.
Jālinīprabha replied: "All sentient beings have received a prediction from the Buddha. [Note: If one were to say, "I have received the Buddha's prediction,"...
If sentient beings do not attain it, then the cause and effect of all phenomena would not be established;

yet, the law of retribution for causes and effects is such by its very nature, like a shadow following a form or an echo following a sound—how could it be that I alone attain it while sentient beings do not?
Brahmā asked, "In what matter does one receive a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa)? Jālinīprabha replied, "One receives a prediction in accordance with the retribution of karma.
[Note: To receive a prediction according to the retribution of karma means that cause and effect are spontaneous; it is a prediction without being predicted.
To be designated as a Buddha is to be recorded so that one may have prior knowledge [of the future].
Brahmā said, "What kind of karma have you performed to receive this prediction?
Jālinīprabha replied, "If there is karma that is not performed by body, not performed by speech, and not performed by mind—can such karma be demonstrated? Brahmā said, "It cannot be demonstrated.
Jālinīprabha asked, "Is awakening (bodhi) characterized by arising and activity? Brahmā said, "No. Why? Because awakening is non-existent (anupalabdha)."
"Brahmā, can one attain unconditioned bodhi by means of the characteristics of conditioned activity? Brahmā replied, "No.
"Brahmā, therefore you should know that if there is no karma, no retribution for karma, no formative activities (*saṃskāra*), and no arising of formative activities, this is called bodhi.
Just as it is with the nature of bodhi, so too is its attainment; just as it is with the nature of attainment, so too is the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*)."
Likewise, one cannot receive the prediction of enlightenment through the performance of conditioned dharmas. [Note:

If karma is produced by body, speech, or mind, it is conditioned and can be demonstrated as "this is killing" or "this is stealing," and so forth; such things do not constitute receiving the prediction of Bodhi.
If karma is not produced by body, speech, or mind, it is the true mark (*dharmatā*); therefore, it cannot [be demonstrated].

It is shown that because it is characterized by non-arising and non-activity, one who possesses the characteristic of non-arising and non-activity receives the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhivyākaraṇa*).
"Bodhi" means awakening; because all phenomena are awakened to as being unattainable, the Buddha receives the prediction of non-attainability. Question:
If one explains this dharma of non-attainability, the Buddha grants them a prediction. If a person commits evil deeds, will they also receive a prediction?

Answer: There are indeed cases where [the Buddha] provides a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), such as when the Buddha predicted to King Virūḍhaka that this man would fall into hell after seven days, and so forth.
Nevertheless, while sentient beings who create karma must inevitably encounter its retribution, it is not strictly necessary for it to be predicted;

for instance, how could one predict that a straight form will cast a straight shadow or that a harmonious sound will produce a concordant echo? In what way, then, does it require a prediction? It is because the Buddha wishes to urge on and inspire those of the Two Vehicles.
Because of the mind of the Way, Brahmā manifested as if he did not understand and asked questions, so that the great assembly would know that there is no recording in what is recorded.
Why is there no recording in what is recorded? The Buddha, by means of the practitioner’s own mind, bestows upon the practitioner the prediction (vyākaraṇa);

it is not a matter of something being given from without. It is like a worldly physiognomist who grants a person nobility or lowliness exactly according to what he has said—it is not [an external act].
When a physiognomist bestows [a prediction] upon someone, the actual nobility or meanness arises from that person’s own self;
yet the physiognomist does not grant them nobility or meanness, but merely enables them to know it in advance.
Brahmā said, "Noble son, do you not receive the prediction [of enlightenment] without practicing the six pāramitās?
Jālinīprabha replied, "It is as you have said: a bodhisattva receives the prediction by practicing the six pāramitās.
Furthermore, Brahmā, if a bodhisattva relinquishes all afflictions, this is called the dāna-pāramitā; that which does not arise with respect to any phenomena is called the śīla-pāramitā."
To be without injury toward any phenomena for the sake of the śīla-pāramitā is called the kṣānti-pāramitā;
to be free from the marks of all phenomena is called the vīrya-pāramitā; to have no dwelling in any phenomena is called the dhyāna-pāramitā;
and to be without conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena is called the prajñā-pāramitā. [Note] As previously stated:
"Non-action and non-arising are the prediction of enlightenment" means that it refutes the attachment of the two vehicles to the notion of "attainment.
Since within the Mahāyāna they constantly disparage such attainment as being false, how could it be that the Bodhisattva here also receives the prediction of enlightenment?
Is this not indeed an attainment? Therefore, the Brahmā asks about illumination so that he may know that by attaining non-attainment, one receives the prediction. This is why.
The question posed herein is intended to refute the attachment of Bodhisattvas of the provisional vehicle (*neyārtha-yāna*) to the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*). They ask:

"If there is no arising and no activity for one to attain the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhi-vyākaraṇa*), does one not still practice the six perfections? If one practices the six perfections, does this not amount to arising and activity? How then can it be said that there is none?
Now, the six perfections are for the purpose of crossing over all that is false and illusory; they are not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena. Therefore [there is no contradiction].
If there were no arising and yet there were truly conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*), it would be called false; how then could one receive a prediction [of enlightenment]? Why is this?
Because giving is not called a *pāramitā*, morality is not called a *pāramitā*, and even wisdom is not called a *pāramitā*.
For what reason? A *pāramitā* is that which "crosses to the other shore. If giving were a *pāramitā*, [it would follow that all givers have already crossed over].

If all conditioned giving were to be called the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), then all non-Buddhists who observe the vows of cows, dogs, and so forth would have to be called those who possess the perfection of morality (*śīlapāramitā*).

If patience were the perfection, then all lowly laborers and slaves who constantly endure their hardships would have to be called those who possess the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*). If diligence were the perfection...
If "honey" refers to the diligent exertion of all followers of the Two Vehicles in severing the accumulation [of suffering], it should be called the Perfection of Diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

If meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) were a *pāramitā*, then all the devas of the realms of form and formlessness who are able to collect their minds should be called the Perfection of Concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
If wisdom (*prajñā*) were a *pāramitā*, then all worldly knowledge and eloquence that possess penetration and sharpness should be called... [the Perfection of Wisdom].

Why is it that the Prajñāpāramitā regards giving that merely produces heavenly merit as inferior; why does it cast out the precepts of cattle and dogs as false views; why does it treat endurance of hardship as mere sycophancy;
why does it not call the diligence of the Two Vehicles the Bodhi-mind; why does it hold that dhyāna in the form heavens does not transcend the realm of ordinary beings;
and why is worldly cleverness and eloquence categorized among the eight difficulties? It is for this reason that these constitute the practice of a Bodhisattva.
The six perfections are distinct because they are conditioned; how are they distinct as conditioned? Giving up the afflictions is giving;
the non-arising of phenomena is morality; the absence of injury toward phenomena is patience; the detachment from signs regarding phenomena is diligence;
the non-abiding in phenomena is meditative concentration; and the absence of conceptual proliferation regarding phenomena is wisdom. Thus are the six.
To transcend that which is neither bodily action, nor verbal expression, nor mental intention; that which is unconditioned, without arising, without birth, and without cessation;
that which cannot be demonstrated and cannot be described; to accord with the mind’s signlessness and attain non-attainment;
and to practice that which is practiced as nothing—this is called the Bodhisattva’s practice of the six perfections.
The Bodhisattva Brahmā practices the six *pāramitās* in this manner: in what place does he practice? Brahmā said: "He practices in no place. Why is this so?
For whatever is practiced is non-practice; if there is practice, it is non-practice;
if there is no practice, that is practice. [Note: Practice is non-practice because the essence of the six perfections is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Not practicing while claiming to practice is the cessation of delusion. Bodhi is one's own mind;
if one gives rise to thoughts or stirs the mind, intending to seek it outwardly, one will not attain bodhi, but only obtain a net of delusions.
Vimalakīrti asked back in order to make [Mañjuśrī] discern for himself that there is no place [for bodhi to be found]. This is why Brahmā resolved the matter. If one realizes this for oneself...
When the mind is entirely without attachment, all objects of perception (*ālambana*) subside; this is why Jālinīprabha received his prediction.
It is like a madman who, while constantly staying within his house, suddenly goes mad and thinks his home is outside.

He exerts himself to run out the door, believing that taking one step is leaving his home one step, and that going a hundred *li* beyond the door is leaving his home a hundred *li*. If he could [realize this]...
To reflect and retreat even one step is to arrive home in every step;
herein, to act is not to act, and not to act is to act—this is precisely how it should be.
Brahmā, for this reason you should know that non-action is bodhi. As you have asked, you shall receive [the answer].
"The prediction of enlightenment is the suchness of the dharma-nature; the prediction I have received is also like this.

Brahmā said, "Good son, the suchness of the dharma-nature has no receiving of a prediction. Jālinīprabha said, "The characteristics of the predictions received by all bodhisattvas are likewise identical to the suchness of the dharma-nature.
[Note: "Suchness of the dharma-nature" means that each and every dharma is suchness; it is not a prediction.]

When the recording of forms is straight and the reflection of shadows is upright, there is no error in principle; thus, it is not that causes and effects are not recorded, nor is it that they are not recorded without being false.
At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, by what practices do the Buddhas bestow upon Bodhisattvas [the prediction of enlightenment]?"
The prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. [Note: Previously, when asked, "Jālinīprabha, what karma did you perform to receive this prediction?
Jālinīprabha replied that karma is not something produced by body, speech, or mind, and even the practice of the six perfections is "non-practice," which is true practice.
It seems that Brahmā has attained understanding; why, then, is the Buddha questioned about this here?

"How can one receive a prediction [of enlightenment] through such practice, when it seems as though they have not yet awakened? How great is this contradiction between the earlier and later statements!
This is a teaching difficult to believe; it cannot be accepted unless authenticated by the Buddha. Because the doubts of the assembly were not yet fully resolved, he asked this question.

The Buddha said: "If a bodhisattva does not practice the dharma of arising nor the dharma of cessation. [Note: The consciousness of ordinary beings is dark and constantly flows and shifts due to the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).
Because the wisdom of the bodhisattva is profound and thoroughly penetrates the true reality (*tathatā*), the four marks do not operate.
The text mentions the two marks of arising and cessation because these two encompass the marks of abiding and change.
Neither practicing the wholesome nor practicing the unwholesome. [Note: The wholesome and the unwholesome arise in mutual dependence.
If there were no unwholesomeness, from what would the wholesome arise? If one does not practice the wholesome, the unwholesome will not be produced.
This is because within the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, all dualities are transcended; subsequent passages follow this principle.

One does not course in the mundane, nor does one course in the supramundane. [Note] Not coursing in the mundane means not coursing in the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
Not coursing in the supramundane means not coursing in the world of wisdom and perfect enlightenment (*jñāna-samyak-saṃbodhi-loka*).
One does not practice dharmas that entail fault. [Note: This means one does not practice what is unwholesome.
One does not practice dharmas that are faultless. [Note: This means one does not practice what is wholesome.
One does not practice with outflowing dharmas (*sāsrava-dharma*). [Note] Not practicing worldly dharmas also refers to "outflows," of which there are three:

namely, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). The twenty-five states of existence within the three realms are collectively termed "outflows.

Regarding the six heavens of the desire realm, as long as one has not severed the dust of desire, it is called the outflow of desire; the outflow of ignorance, however, encompasses all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the three vehicles in their entirety.
To summarize what is not understood: the principles within delusion involve falling into the two extremes, which are collectively termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).

One does not practice the "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*) dharmas. [Note: This means one does not practice supramundane dharmas. Although those of the Two Vehicles practice the path of outflow-freedom, they merely lack the outflow of desire;
the two other outflows are not yet exhausted. Because ignorance remains as a dharma that can still be practiced, they have not yet attained the exhaustion of all outflows.
The two vehicles do not receive the prediction [of enlightenment], whereas the bodhisattva does not cling to outflows; because all oppositions are thus severed, he receives the prediction.

He does not practice conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), nor does he practice the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), nor does he practice the cultivation of the path. [Note: This is what is meant by "non-doing" and "non-arising."
One does not practice its elimination or severance. [Note] This means neither ceasing nor extinguishing.
One does not practice saṃsāra, nor does one practice nirvāṇa; one does not practice seeing dharmas, nor hearing dharmas, nor awakening to dharmas, nor knowing dharmas.
[Note] Dharmas are not seen, heard, awakened to, or known; if one practices seeing, hearing, awakening to, or knowing them, then one does not attain [the goal].

This is the prediction of enlightenment. One does not practice giving, nor does one practice relinquishment; one does not practice precepts, nor does one practice concealment; one does not practice patience, nor does one practice goodness;

one does not practice arousal [of the mind], nor does one practice diligence; one does not practice dhyāna, nor does one practice samādhi; one does not practice wisdom, nor does one practice practice; one does not practice non-practice.
"Know that one does not practice attainment. [Note] Herein, "not practicing the six perfections" is to repeatedly sweep away their marks.
Previously it was said, "one does not practice knowing dharmas," and here it is further said, "one does not practice knowing the texts. Why is this stated redundantly?

The former refers to not practicing the knowledge of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing; this refers to not practicing wisdom—that which is called "wisdom" is the thought, "I am able to practice."
To speak of the six perfections and the myriad practices as "knowing prajñā" is to mean that there is neither knowing nor attaining; the meaning is identical to this.
Brahmā, if a bodhisattva practices in this manner, the Buddhas will bestow upon them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because all practices have something they affirm, yet there is nothing they affirm—this is bodhi.
[Note]: If there are the six perfections that can be practiced, then there are the six perfections as "is"; if there is this "is," then there is that which can be "not-is.
If there is "is" and "not-is," one does not attain the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*). Not attaining the nature of dharmas is not called Bodhi.
If there is nothing to be practiced, then there is no "is"; if there is no "is," then there is also no "not-is. Where there is neither "is" nor "not-is," [this is Bodhi].
This is called bodhi. All that is practiced is conceptualization;
non-conceptualization is bodhi. All that is practiced is conditioned activity;
non-activity is bodhi. All that is practiced is discursive proliferation; non-proliferation is [bodhi].
Bodhi. [Note] Bodhi means awakening (*bodha*). It is the realization of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena, which transcends all dharmas and remains far removed from the two extremes;
because it eliminates conceptual discrimination, it is called bodhi. If one clings to conceptual discrimination, one does not attain bodhi.

Therefore, one should know that if a bodhisattva transcends all spheres of practice, they shall receive the prediction of enlightenment. [Note: This is the source of the meaning expressed by the ancients when they said:
"Do not deliberate at all upon good or evil; naturally the mind enters non-arising, becoming profoundly still and eternally quiescent."

"Indeed, World-Honored One, what is the meaning of 'receiving a prediction' (vyākaraṇa)? The Buddha said: "To be free from the dual characteristics of all dharmas is the meaning of receiving a prediction.

To not discriminate between arising and ceasing is the meaning of receiving a prediction. To be free from the characteristics of the actions of body, speech, and mind is the meaning of receiving a prediction.

[Note: There are ten characteristics of the actions of body and speech; the Tathāgata, for the sake of transforming humans and devas, provisionally distinguishes names and characteristics for the sake of the Two Vehicles.
Because they do not understand and instead cling to this as being real, they are incapable of advancing toward the Mahāyāna. Regarding this, the Tathāgata specifically says:

"One is detached from the characteristics of bodily, vocal, and mental karma; being detached from the characteristics of bodily, vocal, and mental karma, one does not discriminate between arising and ceasing;
not discriminating between arising and ceasing, one does not give rise to dualistic views regarding all phenomena; and not giving rise to dualistic views, one transcends [all conceptualization]."
The past does not go to the future, and the future does not go to the present; it does not abide in the three periods of time. Its essence is empty, and the ten directions are truly quiescent.
To awaken to and enter into this is called receiving the prediction [of enlightenment].
Brahmā, I recall that in the past there was an eon named Sudarśana; during this eon, I made offerings to seventy-two [buddhas].
After a *nayuta* of Buddhas who did not grant me a prophecy, there was another eon named Suvinīta;
during this eon, I made offerings to twenty-two billion Buddhas, yet these Tathāgatas likewise did not grant me a prophecy.
After that eon, there was another eon named Brahmastuta; during this eon, I made offerings to eighteen thousand Buddhas.

The Tathāgatas did not grant me a prediction either; furthermore, after that kalpa, there was a kalpa named Anavadya (Faultless), during which I made offerings to thirty-two thousand Buddhas, yet these Tathāgatas also did not grant me a prediction.
Furthermore, after that kalpa, there was a kalpa named Vyūha (Adornment), during which I made offerings to four million four hundred thousand Buddhas, and to each of them I [offered] with one...
Even when making offerings with all manner of ritual implements, these Tathāgatas do not grant them a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

[Note] "Kalpa" means stagnation. The first is called *Sudarśana* (Good Vision); because one perceives the purity of phenomena, it is called "Good Vision. If one clings to the capacity for vision, one cannot receive a prediction.
The next is called *Sudharmā* (Good Transformation); this refers to clinging to the capacity for transformation. The next is called *Brahmapraśasta* (Praised by Brahmā).
To be "stuck" in one's ego while praising others; next, to be "without fault" while seeking to purify oneself;

next, to be "adorned" while practicing conduct—wherein there is a dharma to be seen, sentient beings to be transformed, the Three Jewels to be praised, a body to be purified, and conduct to be performed—all of these constitute attachments.
Therefore, none of them received a prediction [of enlightenment].
Brahmā, in the past, I made offerings to all Buddhas, honoring, respecting, and praising them;

I purely cultivated the brahma-faring, practiced all forms of giving, maintained all precepts, and observed the dhūta ascetic practices; I remained free from anger and practiced patience and loving-kindness.
Acting according to what has been taught, one diligently cultivates vigor and is able to receive and uphold everything heard.
Dwelling alone in seclusion, one enters into various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). According to the wisdom heard, one recites, studies, contemplates, and inquires;

yet even all these Tathāgatas do not see such a person receiving a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Why? Because they rely upon their practice. [Note: As previously stated, *nirvāṇa* exists only as a name, just like...
Space exists only as a name; so too, while the names "bodhi" and "nirvāṇa" differ, their essence is the same, existing only as a name whose substance transcends all dependence.

If one relies upon the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), one does not receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of bodhi. As stated above, from "skillful seeing" and "skillful transformation" up to "adornment," none of these constitute receiving the prediction.
Here, it is summarized that the six perfections and myriad practices are all based upon the conditioned.
This is because they are not associated with [conditioned phenomena].
By this one should know that if Bodhisattvas transcend all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), they receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
[Note: "Transcending all formations" means being beyond the reach of all conditioned mental states.
If I were to speak the names of these Buddhas for one kalpa, or even slightly less than a kalpa, I could not exhaust them.
[Note] The number of kalpas and the names of the Buddhas spoken by me during this single interval can all be known;
yet, if I were to speak the names of these Buddhas and the number of kalpas for each period of increase and decrease—each lasting ten trillion years—they would still be inexhaustible.

The meaning of "attaining knowledge" is that even if one were to pass through such kalpas, make offerings to such Buddhas, and cultivate such practices, one would still not obtain a prediction [of enlightenment];
this reiterates the point that what is practiced based on the conditioned is ultimately flawed.
"Brahmā, after that, I saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and immediately attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Buddha bestowed upon me this prediction, saying: 'In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
It was because at that time I had transcended all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) and was fully endowed with the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). So it was.

If a bodhisattva is able to relinquish all signs, it is called the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*); if they are able to extinguish all grasping at sensations, it is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*);
if they are not harmed by the six sense objects, it is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);

if they are detached from all conditioned activities, it is called the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*); and if they do not give rise to recollection of any phenomena, it is called the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna*).
The pāramitās that are able to endure the non-arising nature of all phenomena are called the Prajñāpāramitā.
At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I fully perfected these six pāramitās. [Note: Previously, when Brahmā asked Jālinīprabha, he said:
"If one receives the prediction of enlightenment through this non-practice, non-arising, and non-action, how is it that a bodhisattva does not practice the six pāramitās?"
Madhyavyūhaprabha replied: "The six *pāramitās* are themselves the signless (*animitta*) of one's own mind;
if one awakens to this signless nature of one's own mind, that is the fulfillment of the six *pāramitās*. This is what is called the 'dharma difficult to believe. Therefore, Brahmā asked again:
'World-Honored One, by what practice does a bodhisattva receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*)? The Buddha replied: 'By nothing at all.'"
"If one receives the prediction of enlightenment through practice, yet receives the prediction through non-practice, what is the meaning of 'prediction'?

The Buddha replied, "To not discriminate a single dharma, to be unattached to arising and ceasing, and to be free from the karmas of body, speech, and mind—to practice in such a manner is the meaning of receiving the prediction.
Fearing that Brahmā might not believe him, the Buddha specifically cited a past instance.
Those who have departed from me and practiced based on conditioned phenomena have all failed to receive a prediction [of enlightenment].
It is only now, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, that I have awakened to this non-conceptual nature of my own mind and thereby received the prediction.
Chapter Eleven: Sarvajñatā (The Nature of All-Knowledge)
[Note] Previously, when Brahmā asked about the meaning of receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), the Buddha replied that it consists in the non-differentiation of two dharmas;
he answered regarding its fundamental principle (*mūla-artha*) but had not yet answered regarding its goal (*gati-artha*). Here, he answers regarding its goal.

One should know that receiving the prediction of enlightenment has the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its fundamental principle and the flowing into omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) as its goal. The fundamental principle is like a farmer.
In commerce and industry, each has its own principle; when one achieves their aims and establishes a household, each has its own direction.
Likewise, those of the Two Vehicles take the four truths of arising and ceasing as their principle and the partial realization of *nirvāṇa* with remainder as their goal.
That which is called *sarvajñatā*—in Sanskrit, this term is not translated [into Chinese] because it possesses six meanings—is what is meant by "sovereign majesty blazing intensely."
"Īśvara" and so forth are examples of the "many meanings" (*bahvartha*) category among the five types of non-translation. [The Buddha said:

"Brahmā, the merit from all the acts of giving I have performed since first generating the mind of enlightenment does not equal even a hundredth part, nor a ten-thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth, nor a hundred-thousand-millionth part—indeed, it is beyond any calculation or analogy—of this gift of five flowers."
It can be equaled. [Note] This means that even practicing giving based on conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) over many eons cannot equal this signless (*animitta*) giving.
That conditioned giving involves the thought "I am the one who gives" and "there is another who receives"; since both subject and object are present, it is identical to delusion.
Herein, when the mind accords with non-arising (*anutpāda*), one does not internally perceive a mind that gives, nor does one externally perceive...
The gift in which the internal and external aspects of the object given are both free from signs is a gift that surpasses all previous ones.
Since I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I have received and maintained the precepts and practiced the dhūtas;

compared to this [gift], my constant observance of the precepts does not equal even one hundredth part of it, nor can it be reached by any calculation, number, or analogy. [Note: Regarding "precepts," these refer to those of the Three Vehicles.
The practices one cultivates differ in scale, namely the five precepts, the ten precepts, the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu, and the four hundred precepts of a bodhisattva;
whether in terms of maintaining or violating, permitting or prohibiting, these are all termed "arising and ceasing.

This precept of signlessness, however, involves not seeing the mind that maintains [the precepts] within, nor seeing the discipline that might be violated without; when inner and outer are thus identical, this is called [the precept of signlessness].
It is eternally extinguished.

Since I first resolved upon the path, my gentleness and patience have not been equaled by even one hundredth part of the ultimate dharma of patience (*atyanta-kṣānti-dharma*), nor can it be approached by any calculation or analogy. [Note: There are three types of patience: the first is asceticism (*duṣkaracaryā*).]
Patience (*kṣānti*) consists of two aspects: first, self-restraint and the firming of one’s resolve; second, the patience of harmonious compliance, also called the patience toward living beings.

This involves enduring wicked sentient beings who are difficult to tame and being able to subdue them. Within this, there are three stages: first, calmly accepting the sight of wicked people or fierce beasts;
second, observing them; and third, exercising endurance. Third is the patience of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*), also known as the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The patience practiced throughout many lifetimes belongs to the former two types, as the subject and object have not yet been forgotten;

the dharma of ultimate patience shown here involves the forgetting of both subject and object, where there is neither patience nor impatience—this is precisely the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Since first resolving my mind [for enlightenment], the diligent vigor I have exerted does not approach even one hundredth part of this vigor of non-grasping and non-rejection;
it is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy. [Note: Regarding the vigor exerted since first resolving the mind:

as long as one has not realized the non-arising [of phenomena], the mind still harbors grasping and rejection; once the mind awakens to the true reality (*dharmatā*), gain and loss are viewed with equal perspective.
Neither grasping nor abandoning, the single path is level and smooth.
Since first generating the mind of enlightenment, my meditative concentration in solitary dwelling has not been equaled by even one hundredth part of this non-abiding meditative concentration;
it is beyond the reach of calculation or metaphor. [Note: "Solitary dwelling in meditative concentration" means relinquishing existence.]
If one clings to emptiness, loathes clamor, and seeks stillness, the mind is not yet dwelling in non-abiding.

If one awakens to the true mark (*dharmatā*), then emptiness and existence are viewed as equal, and movement and stillness are non-dual. Because they are non-dual, one has no attachment or dwelling in emptiness, existence, movement, or stillness;
this is called "constant concentration" (*nitya-samādhi*).

Since I first resolved my mind [on enlightenment], the wisdom of my contemplation and deliberation does not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth, nor a hundred-thousandth, nor a ten-millionth, nor a billionth part—indeed, it cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy—of this wisdom free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
[Note: The wisdoms of the three vehicles all involve deliberation because ignorance has not been fully exhausted. If...

To be able, in a single thought-moment, to accord with the primordial source and call it "originally existent," speaking in accordance with the nature of reality—all this is not frivolous discourse (*prapañca*). As the ancients said:
"To know through thinking and to understand through deliberation are merely the livelihood of ghosts; that is, the wisdom of conceptualization and calculation.
When one picks up anything and finds no place where it is not the functioning [of the Way], and thus gives rise to no doubt, then there is no frivolous discourse.
Because it appears to differ from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), it was not mentioned; however, regarding the gift of the five flowers, one asks:
since these too are conditioned gifts, how do they differ from the previous offerings? The answer is:

formerly, when the Great Being *Ratnaprabha* offered the five flowers to the Buddha, the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, whereby he attained realization of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and was immediately granted a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*). Therefore...

This is a gift that transcends the ordinary; how could it be merely a gift that precedes the act? By offering the five flowers to the Buddha, one awakens to the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Thereupon, one perfectly comprehends the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the myriad practices, all of which enter the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This is what is meant by "possessing the six pāramitās in a single thought-moment."
Brahmā, you should therefore know that at that time I was fully endowed with the six pāramitās. [Note:
"At that time" refers to the moment of offering the flowers; the completion of the six perfections was all achieved through this occasion.
The World-Honored One said: "How is it that one is said to be fully endowed with the six pāramitās?

Brahmā, if one does not think of giving, does not rely on precepts, does not discriminate regarding patience, does not grasp at diligence, does not dwell in meditative concentration, and is non-dual regarding wisdom—this is called being fully endowed with the six pāramitās.
[Note]: The intention of Brahmā was that the Buddha had practiced the six perfections throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Question: What is meant by "perfection," such that making offerings of these five flowers to the Buddha is called the perfection of the six pāramitās?
The Buddha replied: Throughout immeasurable kalpas, my cultivation of the six pāramitās was based entirely upon the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);

therefore, it was not called "perfection. Now, this mind accords with the unarisen (*anutpāda*). Where there is no arising, there is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); where there is the unconditioned, there is nothing that is not done. Therefore, it is called "perfection."
"Endowed. He asked again, "Having fulfilled the six *pāramitās*, what dharma can one then fully satisfy?

The Buddha said, "Having fulfilled the six *pāramitās*, one can fully satisfy *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge). [Note: *Pāramitā* means 'crossing to the other shore,' arising from the cultivation of non-..."
Because one practices the marks [of a bodhisattva], one receives the prediction of enlightenment; because one receives the prediction, one then attains the fulfillment of the six perfections.
A questioner asks: "To what destination does one who has fulfilled the six perfections go? The Buddha answers: "One crosses over to the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment.
This points to the goal toward which one proceeds.
"Bhagavān, how is it that having fulfilled the six pāramitās, one is able to satisfy sarvajñatā?
Brahmā, the equality of giving is itself the equality of sarvajñatā; the equality of ethical discipline is itself the equality of sarvajñatā;
the equality of patience is itself the equality of sarvajñatā; the equality of diligence is itself the equality of sarvajñatā..."
If meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is equal, that equality is the equality of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge);
if wisdom (*prajñā*) is equal, that equality is the equality of *sarvajñā*. Because all phenomena are equal by means of this equality, it is named *sarvajñā*. [Note:

The essence of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment is equally and inherently possessed by all sentient beings; it is simply because they are obscured by ignorance that they do not realize it themselves.
Knowing the Way of equality, yet giving rise to false discrimination and stirring thoughts while riding upon the Truth—
if one can turn the light back to reflect within and realize that the causal mind is equal, then the state of fruition will likewise be equal. When cause and effect are equal,
there is not a single phenomenon that is not equal.

Furthermore, the marks of fulfilling generosity, the marks of upholding precepts, the marks of patience, the marks of diligence, the marks of meditative concentration, and the marks of wisdom—these are called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

[Note: If one practices without awakening to the fundamental mind, and instead believes that there are dharmas external to the mind, and that there is an agent, things possessed, grasping, abandoning, attainment, and loss, then it cannot be called "fulfillment."

Regarding the perfection of the feet (*pāda-pāramitā*): if one awakens to the fundamental mind, one knows that outside the body there is no dharma—no right and no wrong, no agent and no object, no gain and no loss.
For this reason, it is called the fulfillment of the *pāramitā*.
Thus, one should know that "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) is precisely one's own mind; when all dharmas reach this [state], it is termed "fulfillment. Therefore, it is said:
This is what is meant by the saying: "The hundred rivers and myriad streams reach their limit in the sea; the myriad phenomena of the universe reach their limit in space;
all dharmas reach their limit in the mind."
Brahmā, in this way, by fulfilling the six pāramitās, one is able to fulfill sarvajñatā (all-knowledge). [Note:
Previously it was stated that the characteristic of the fulfillment of the six perfections is called sarvajñatā; this refers to the culmination of the mind directed toward the six perfections.

Here it is said that by thus fulfilling the six perfections, one is able to fulfill the matter of sarvajñatā. When the principle is perfected and the mind is pervasive throughout all phenomena, this is the inevitable reality.
This is the Way.
World-Honored One, how should one know the fulfillment of *sarvajñatā*?
Brahmā, if one does not grasp the eye nor grasp forms, does not grasp the ear nor grasp sounds, does not grasp the nose nor grasp odors, and does not grasp the tongue nor grasp flavors...

When the body does not receive touch, the mind does not receive mental objects, and one does not receive dharmas—if one does not receive these internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*), it is called the fulfillment of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
[Note: Since the signless nature of one's own mind is fundamentally devoid of form and appearance, its fulfillment is neither spatial nor localized.
If there were a spatial location, it would not be without a specific reference; if there were a specific reference, that very reference would be the fulfillment itself.
The Buddha replied: "This mind is without marks (*animitta*) and cannot be pointed out or described. Internally it does not receive the sense organs; externally it does not receive sensory objects.
Since both internal and external are void, the center is free from dependence. The numinous clarity shines alone, moving spontaneously in all directions.
Therefore it is said: 'In heaven above and on earth below, I alone am honored. This very state is called the mark of fulfillment."
I have attained such fulfillment of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) that I am unattached to the eye and unattached to forms;

I am unattached to the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental objects. For this reason, the Tathāgata is called one who possesses unimpeded knowledge and vision, the *sarvajñā*.

[Note] This explains the aforementioned "non-acceptance" of the sense bases (*āyatana*), such as the eye. It means not accepting the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), and does not mean being separated from the faculties.
To seek omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) apart from the sense objects while remaining attached to the eye and its forms is not the way;

this applies likewise to the ear, sound, and so forth, because the nature of the faculties and their objects is fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*). If one seeks the self-mind apart from the faculties and their objects, one gives rise to the false views of annihilationism or eternalism;
therefore, the Buddha provides this further explanation.
Brahmā, Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) does not receive anything regarding phenomena. Why? Because it is without utility. That which is without utility is the meaning of non-existence;
that which is non-existent is emptiness, having the same meaning as space and the same characteristics as space.
This is Sarvajñā; therefore, it does not receive anything regarding phenomena. [Note: This explains that the nature of the faculties and their objects is like non-attachment.
This is the meaning of "destruction. Why? Because regarding phenomena such as the eye and forms, one does not accept or cling to them.

This is because the characteristics of phenomena such as the eye and forms are unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*); they function by depending on the mind. Since they function by depending on the mind, their essence is fundamentally empty.
Their activity and application revolve according to the mind; and since one realizes that the mind has nothing external to it, there is nothing to be accepted.
Brahmā, it is like this: for example, all that is created depends upon space, yet space has no basis;
likewise, all forms of wisdom arise from *sarvajñatā* (omniscience), yet *sarvajñatā* has no basis. [Note:

For example, the rising of the sun, the setting of the moon, the shifting of the constellations, and the movement of the stars all manifest in dependence upon space, yet space does not depend upon them.
To increase or decrease them accordingly, these five aggregates, six sense bases, twelve bases, and eighteen elements all arise and function based on one’s own mind;
yet the mind does not exist or cease because of their presence or absence.
Rather than speaking of the phenomena of the five aggregates and so forth, it speaks of "wisdom," for they all possess the functional capacity for clear discernment.
Brahmā addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what is meant by 'sarvajñā' (all-knowledge) as spoken by you?
Brahmā, all that is practiced is wisdom; it is true wisdom and not something that can be attained by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Therefore, it is called sarvajñā.
Because it is able to accomplish everything that is practiced, it is called sarvajñā. It is because it can destroy all [obstructions]..."
Because it is mindful of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
All instructions and all regulations, as well as the dharmas practiced by these sentient beings, all emerge from within it; therefore, it is called *sarvajñā*.

It attains the wisdom of the noble ones—whether the wisdom of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the wisdom of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or the wisdom of the *pratyekabuddhas*—all of which emerge from within it; therefore, it is correctly called *sarvajñā*.
Because it practices, it is called sarvajñā; because it can discern all medicines, it is called sarvajñā;
because it can extinguish the illnesses of all sentient beings, it is called sarvajñā; because it can eliminate all afflictions and habitual tendencies, it is called sarvajñā;
because it is always in samādhi, it is called sarvajñā; and because it has no doubt regarding any dharma, it is called sarvajñā.
Because all mundane and supramundane wisdom (*sarvajñā*) emerges from within it, it is called *sarvajña*;
because it skillfully knows the characteristics of all wisdom and expedient means (*upāya*), it is called *sarvajña*.

[Note] The previous passage spoke of "not receiving" sense organs and objects, directly manifesting the absolute, non-referential single mind as its name; thus, there is nothing received. Here, the question concerns its perfect interfusion.
Because of single-mindedness, all things are illuminated and all things are accomplished; therefore it is said that one who has nothing received is one who does not fail to receive anything.
Since one’s own mind is originally thus complete, if one does not achieve a wondrous awakening, one will not realize for oneself that it is complete.
Therefore, Brahmā asked each question to clarify and enable people to understand the truth.
He is a Great Being who bestows the Dharma through compassion.
At that time, the Brahma Heaven King *Saddharmavikurvaṇa* addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is unprecedented, World-Honored One!

The wisdom of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is profoundly deep; with no object of perception in their minds, they know the mental activities and the movements of the hearts of all sentient beings. World-Honored One, [this is] the power of the Tathāgata."
If even a *pratyekabuddha* attains such immeasurable merit, what son or daughter of good family would not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas who resolve upon *bodhicitta* out of a desire for merit and benefit, they cannot be said to have resolved upon the Great [Vehicle]."
This is because it is the vehicle of the mind. Why is this? Because all dharmas possess no merit or benefit, as they have no point of opposition.
[Note] The wondrous mind of signlessness is truly without such idle names.
In response to the inquiry of Brahmā, the Buddha, employing skillful means, praised and extolled that which is thus complete, thus born, and thus transcendent. Brahmā offered his praise.
Within *vibhūti* (all-encompassing wisdom), such merits are fully present; who then would not resolve to attain *bodhicitta*?
Jālinīprabha feared that people might dwell upon signs and thereby deviate from actual virtue, so he specifically elucidated this to make them know the perfect subtlety of their own minds.

Although they can accomplish these things equally, it does not contradict the state of absolute transcendence; therefore, it is said there are "no merits or benefits," because there is no place of opposition.
World-Honored One, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should not resolve upon bodhicitta for the sake of the benefit of merit; rather, it is solely for the sake of great compassion,

for the sake of extinguishing the various sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings, for the sake of not being distressed by one's own suffering, for the sake of giving rise to all wholesome dharmas,
for the sake of liberating oneself from all false views, for the sake of eliminating all illnesses, for the sake of abandoning attachment to "mine," and for the sake of non-contemplation.

One generates the bodhicitta because of aversion to attachment and hatred, because of not being submerged in worldly dharmas, because of weariness with conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*), and because of abiding securely in nirvāṇa.
[Note: If a bodhisattva generates this mind seeking their own benefit and merit, they have not yet forgotten attachment to a self;
such a mind is identical to that of the two vehicles and is not the Mahāyāna. If, however, one takes great compassion as the core of the mind, it is purely for the benefit of others.
In their practice, they do not know themselves; this is what is meant by the so-called "sage who has no self," for there is nothing that is not his own self.
What is called the manifestation of great compassion lies in the uprooting of the suffering of sentient beings. To uproot their suffering, one must forget one's own suffering;
if one cannot forget one's own suffering, then compassion cannot arise. Uprooting suffering consists in bestowing happiness.
To bring them joy, one should preach the Dharma so that they may give rise to goodness; when goodness arises, suffering is extinguished;

when suffering is extinguished, bliss arrives. That which causes goodness to arise is to cause them to abandon wrong views, eliminate all afflictions, detach from craving, dissolve hatred and love, not be submerged by worldly dharmas, grow weary of the conditioned, and abide in the unconditioned—all of which constitute the attainment of liberation from suffering.
Joy is the subtle excellence.
The World-Honored One and the Bodhisattva should not seek recompense for their kindness from sentient beings, nor should they observe whether [others] act or do not act;
furthermore, their minds remain unmoved by suffering or pleasure. [Note: To seek recompense for one's kindness is equivalent to seeking merit and benefit.

This is what is meant by "arousing the mind" (bodhicitta). By observing what is done and what is not done, if the mind harbors feelings of aversion or attachment and does not remain unmoved, then one is said to be "not free from personal sorrow and suffering.
If these three [factors] pass through the mind, then right and wrong are established in thought;
if right and wrong are established in thought, then the great compassion that arises is a compassion born of affectionate views (*sneha-dṛṣṭi*), and is not [the true] non-abiding [compassion].
It is because of his great compassion that Jālinīprabha repeatedly clarifies this so that one does not fall into error.

"World-Honored One, what is meant by 'the purity of a bodhisattva’s family'? The Buddha said, "Good son, if a bodhisattva is born into the family of a universal monarch (cakravartin), it is not called the purity of the family.
If he is born among the Śakras or among the Brahmās, it is likewise not [called the purity of the family]."
The noble family’s purity consists in not losing one's roots of goodness even when born among animals, and in causing other sentient beings to give rise to various roots of goodness;

this is called the purity of the Bodhisattva’s family. [Note: As stated above, through the mind of great compassion, one gives rise to wholesome dharmas in all sentient beings without personal distress or suffering;
furthermore, it is feared that the Bodhisattva might [fall] from the good realms into the evil realms.

Because one gives rise to views of acceptance and rejection and does not save oneself with an impartial mind, thereby damaging one's own roots of goodness, the Buddha specifically asks about the purity of the Bodhisattva family.
He answers that if one is born among the Śakras or as a Wheel-Turning King, yet happens to lose one's roots of goodness, one is merely called "noble and honorable" but is not termed "pure.
Conversely, if one is born among animals or in the evil realms, yet happens not to lose one's goodness, [one is termed pure].

Although the roots [of goodness] may be said to be subtle and lowly, they are called "pure. Since gain and loss both reside within the differentiation of these roots of goodness, there is no distinction made between the paths of good and evil.
As it was said above that the six perfections are equal, so too is all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) equal;
here, since good and evil are equal, all-knowledge is likewise equal. Be careful not to feel either joy or aversion.

Furthermore, Jālinīprabha, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the family mind of a bodhisattva because it is impartial; [Note: because unconditioned loving-kindness does not discriminate between enemies and kin.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is the family mind of a bodhisattva because it is a profound mind of mindfulness; [Note: because with a profound mind of great compassion, one vows to rescue all equally.
Joy is the family of the bodhisattva because it is the joy of the Dharma; relinquishment is the family of the bodhisattva because it is free from attachment;
not abandoning bodhi is the family of the bodhisattva because it does not crave the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. [Note] Question:

How is it known that this sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) is one's own mind? Previously, it was stated that one does not accept the eye, nor does one accept forms, and so forth regarding the sense faculties.

If the sense objects (*viṣaya*) are not received, then consciousness (*vijñāna*) is likewise not received. When these three—root, object, and consciousness—are extinguished, this is precisely the absolute, non-referential self-mind.

Furthermore, it is said that that which can accomplish the causes and effects of the mundane and supramundane, as well as those of the holy and the ordinary, is precisely the perfectly wondrous self-mind.
Combining these two aspects is collectively termed *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), which is its essence and function.
[Question: This refers to an image that is undifferentiated and unmixed. If this is so, why do you not simply say "mind" (*citta*), but instead use the term "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñā*)?
Is there perhaps a specific intention behind this? [Answer: It is because the mind does not name itself.

If the mind were to name itself, it would seem as though there were two distinct entities, like fire not calling itself "fire," or water not calling itself "water," and so forth. As the ancients said: [the mind cannot be its own subject].

Regarding speech, one avoids "ten completions" (shicheng) because one does not wish to sever the continuity. Regarding the pivot (ji), one prizes "reciprocity and alternation" (huixu) because one does not wish to be defiled.
The reason it is not called "mind" (xin) is that one avoids ten completions; the reason it is called "sarvajñā" (omniscience) is that one prizes reciprocity and alternation.

What is meant by reciprocity and alternation? It is like when people of the world fear death and avoid mentioning it, using terms such as "collapse," "end," or "funeral"—all of which are instances of avoidance.
This concludes the second fascicle of the *Simplified Commentary on the Sūtra of the Questions of Brahmā Viśeṣacintin*.

Chapter Twelve: The Non-duality of the Bodhisattva.
[Note] The preceding passage consists of a series of questions and answers concerning the provisional teachings and the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*).
These are integrated without being conflated and distinguished without being separated; they are dual yet non-dual, and non-dual yet dual. Their purport is profound and subtle, difficult to perceive.
Although Brahmā has attained awakening to the meaning of "non-explanation as explanation," he has not yet understood the principle that "non-explanation is itself explanation. This [is the point].
This chapter specifically highlights the non-duality [of all phenomena], for all dharmas previously encountered ultimately converge in non-duality.
At that time, the Brahma-Heavenly Being *Siddhārthabuddhi* addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, this Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta is present in this great assembly, yet he says nothing.
[Note: In the Sanskrit language, Mañjuśrī is translated here as 'Wondrous Auspiciousness' (*Miaojixiang*).]
Having come to this assembly for the sake of the eye that discriminates dharmas, since one who possesses the eye that discriminates dharmas cannot remain without speaking—
considering that on the occasion of the Vaipulya assemblies, Mañjuśrī had each of the thirty-two great beings speak on the dharma-gate of non-duality—
it was impossible for him not to ask questions and speak; yet he waited for questions before revealing his illumination.
The Buddha then addressed Mañjuśrī: "Regarding this Dharma you have preached, you may now speak of it briefly. [Note:
The reason the Buddha had Mañjuśrī speak briefly was to reveal that the Dharma previously preached is itself the teaching of non-teaching;
therein, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be spoken. Why did the Buddha not speak himself but instead have Mañjuśrī speak? It was to provide a counterpart.
This is for the purpose of clarifying the multitude [of doubts].
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, can the Dharma attained by the Buddha be cognized?
The Buddha said: "It cannot be cognized. Mañjuśrī said: "World-Honored One, can this Dharma be spoken, expounded, or discussed? The Buddha said: "It cannot be spoken."
"It may be manifested but cannot be discussed, World-Honored One. If this Dharma is unspeakable, unmanifestable, and undiscussable, then it cannot be shown.
[Note: First, the Dharma of the World-Honored One’s noble awakened wisdom and self-realization is established;
subsequently, its state of being unspeakable, unshown, unmanifestable, and undiscussable is clarified, so that people may wondrously accord with the meaning beyond words.
Because the Dharma of self-realization is unattainable, wisdom cannot know it and consciousness cannot perceive it;
the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. For this reason, Vimalakīrti remained silent at Vaiśālī, and the World-Honored One closed his door at Magadha.
If one can awaken to this essential meaning, then the teaching of the dust and the teaching of the lands will never cease.

Is it only that Mañjuśrī does not speak? Has the World-Honored One ever spoken [of such things]? At that time, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin said to Mañjuśrī, "Do you not expound the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, are there two characteristics within the nature of dharmas (dharmatā)? The Brahmā replied, "No. Mañjuśrī said, "Brahmā, if there are no two characteristics within the nature of dharmas, how could I expound the Dharma for sentient beings? The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if there are no two characteristics within the nature of dharmas, then why do you not expound the Dharma for sentient beings? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, if one were to say, 'I am expounding the Dharma for sentient beings,' this would constitute a duality. Because there is no duality within the nature of dharmas, I do not expound the Dharma for sentient beings. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if there is no duality within the nature of dharmas, then what is the meaning of your saying, 'I am expounding the Dharma for sentient beings'? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, the meaning of my saying 'I am expounding the Dharma for sentient beings' is that I am not expounding the Dharma for sentient beings. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you are not expounding the Dharma for sentient beings, then why do you say, 'I am expounding the Dharma for sentient beings'? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, because I do not see any sentient beings, I say, 'I am expounding the Dharma for sentient beings. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that says, 'I am expounding the Dharma for sentient beings'? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I say, 'I am expounding the Dharma for sentient beings. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that hears you expound the Dharma? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I hear myself expounding the Dharma. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that understands the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I understand the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that attains liberation through the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I attain liberation through the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that practices the path according to the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I practice the path according to the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that realizes the fruit according to the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I realize the fruit according to the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that enters parinirvāṇa according to the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I enter parinirvāṇa according to the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that establishes others in the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I establish others in the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that causes others to enter the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I cause others to enter the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that causes others to abide in the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I cause others to abide in the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that causes others to mature in the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I cause others to mature in the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that causes others to enter the vehicle of the Buddhas according to the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I cause others to enter the vehicle of the Buddhas according to the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that causes others to enter the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas according to the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I cause others to enter the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas according to the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that causes others to enter the vehicle of the Śrāvakas according to the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I cause others to enter the vehicle of the Śrāvakas according to the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that causes others to enter the vehicle of the worldlings according to the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I cause others to enter the vehicle of the worldlings according to the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that causes others to enter the vehicle of the gods according to the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I cause others to enter the vehicle of the gods according to the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that causes others to enter the vehicle of humans according to the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I cause others to enter the vehicle of humans according to the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that causes others to enter the vehicle of animals according to the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I cause others to enter the vehicle of animals according to the Dharma I expound. The Brahmā said, "Mañjuśrī, if you do not see any sentient beings, then who is it that causes others to enter the vehicle of hungry ghosts according to the Dharma you expound? Mañjuśrī replied, "Brahmā, it is precisely because I do not see any sentient beings that I cause others to enter the vehicle of hungry ghosts according to the Dharma I expound. The Bra
Mañjuśrī said, "Do all dharmas not enter into the dharma-nature? Brahmā replied, "Indeed, Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī said, "If the dharma-nature is the characteristic of non-duality, and all dharmas enter into the dharma-nature, how should one preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?
[Note: If it is said that this Dharma is without speech and without demonstration, then Mañjuśrī would be able [to preach it]."
"Does he preach the Dharma to sentient beings? This does not mean that he does not preach; rather, it means that the preaching of the Dharma is without dual characteristics.
If there were even a single dharma that could be spoken of within the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*), such that there was speaking and listening, then one would be attached to a self and others.
To be attached to a self and others is called conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); it is not the attainment of the nature of dharmas. If all dharmas...
All enter into the dharma-nature; since the dharma-nature is non-dual, there is no teaching because it is itself the teaching.
How then could one further teach for the sake of sentient beings?
Brahmā asked: "Is there perhaps a teaching of the Dharma that also possesses the characteristic of non-duality? Mañjuśrī replied: "If it is determined..."

If there is a speaker and a listener, there may be the teaching of the Dharma, yet there is no duality. [Note: Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is non-dual, there is neither speaking nor being spoken to, and thus no duality;
it need not be further explained that since speaking and being spoken to are non-dual, how could there not be the non-duality of speaking and not speaking?
If one can definitively attain the state of both speaker and listener, then [this is so].
"Speech has duality and non-duality; yet because neither speaker nor listener can be definitively apprehended, to what phenomenon could one point as being dual or non-dual?
Mañjuśrī, does the Tathāgata not teach the Dharma? Mañjuśrī replied, "The Buddha, though he teaches the Dharma, [does not do so...]"
"By means of non-dual characteristics. Why? Because the *tathāgatagarbha* is non-dual; thus, although there is that which is spoken, it is without duality. [Note:
"Not by means of dual characteristics" means that there are no characteristics of a speaker or a thing spoken of.
Since there is neither a speaker nor a thing spoken of, both speaking and not speaking enter into the *dharmatā*. In the *Laṅkāvatāra*, there are two kinds of penetration (*sāmānya*), namely:
Regarding the characteristics of the principle-vehicle (zongtong) and the characteristics of the teaching-vehicle (shoutong): the characteristic of the principle-vehicle refers to the noble silence;
the characteristic of the teaching-vehicle refers to the noble preaching of the Dharma. These two—speaking and not speaking—both ultimately converge in the dharma-nature (dharmatā).
Brahmā said: "If all dharmas are non-dual, who is it that creates duality? Mañjuśrī replied:
"It is only because ordinary beings are attached to a self that they conceptually differentiate between two. That which is non-dual never becomes dual.

Although one may conceptually differentiate various things as being dual, in its ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi), there is no characteristic of duality. [Note: All dharmas are such because the noble ones realize their true nature.
There is no duality because ordinary beings, through their attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self," engage in false conceptualization and thus perceive duality.
In reality, the true mark (*dharmatā*) is non-dual; it does not become dual by virtue of the conceptualizations of ordinary beings.
Therefore, while ordinary beings are said to be characterized by falsehood, how could that ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) be rendered dual by such means?
Brahmā asked, "How can one cognize the non-dual dharma? Mañjuśrī replied, "If there were a non-duality that could be cognized, it would not be non-dual.
Why is this? That which possesses the characteristic of non-duality cannot be cognized. [Note:
If there were a non-duality that could be cognized, it would not be true non-duality. Why? Because it would involve the existence of opposites; if there were no opposites, [it could not be cognized].
How could one wait for peace before being able to realize non-duality?
Brahmā, duality is precisely the activity of consciousness; it is the teaching of the Buddha that the nature of dharmas cannot be known through consciousness. [Note:
The Buddha taught that duality is the characteristic of karmic activity and is thus a knowable phenomenon, whereas the nature of dharmas (dharmatā) is not knowable.
This Dharma is not as it is described. Why? Because this Dharma is without letters. [Note:

"This Dharma is not as it is" means it cannot be cognized in the manner that karmic characteristics are cognizable; for what the Tathāgata has taught does not rely on letters or language, and thus it cannot be cognized.
"Mañjuśrī, where does the Dharma taught by the Buddha ultimately lead? Mañjuśrī replied, "The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata leads to nowhere.
Brahmā asked, "Does the Dharma taught by the Buddha not lead to nirvāṇa? Mañjuśrī replied, "Can nirvāṇa be reached?
Brahmā said, "Nirvāṇa has no place from which it comes, nor any place to which it goes."
Mañjuśrī said: "So it is; the Dharma taught by the Buddha reaches that which has no destination. [Note] The Dharma taught by the Buddha ultimately culminates in nirvāṇa.
Because nirvāṇa has no location, and because it has no location, it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
