The "Lion’s Roar" refers to maintaining an impartial mind toward both enemies and kin; the "Lion’s Roar" refers to constantly practicing diligence without abandoning one's original vows.

[Note] "Original vows" refers to the Four Great Vows and the like; although one realizes the true nature of reality (dharmatā) wherein there is neither vow nor action, one nevertheless does not abandon them.

The "Lion’s Roar" is named for its ability to eliminate afflictions (*kleśa*). [Note] Afflictions arise from a distracted mind; only through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) can they be eliminated.

The "Lion’s Roar" is named for wisdom (*prajñā*), which skillfully knows what is to be practiced. [Note] The aforementioned six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are all definitively in accordance with reality.
Because of these characteristics, it is collectively termed the "Lion’s Roar.
When this Dharma of the Lion’s Roar was being preached, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways. [Note:
It is precisely because this true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) effectively destroys ignorance that the world shakes for its sake; the world itself is ignorance.

Because it is bound [by vows], hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resound spontaneously without being struck. [Note: That musical instruments resound spontaneously without being struck serves as proof of effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*), for the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is itself effortless.

Its great radiance universally illumines heaven and earth. [Note] Because the principle of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) penetrates all doubts so that no delusion remains unbroken, it is called "great radiance."

Hundreds of thousands of devas leaped for joy and exclaimed, "Having heard the不退轉 (Avivartika) Devaputra preach the Dharma of the Lion’s Roar, we behold the turning of the Wheel of Dharma once again in Jambudvīpa.
[Note: The Wheel of Dharma can only be turned by a Buddha; others are all incapable of doing so.
Now, having heard what the Devaputra has preached, it is no different from that of the Buddha; therefore, they say they behold it once again.

At that time, the Buddha smiled. When Buddhas manifest a smile according to the Dharma, hundreds and thousands of kinds of light—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, and so forth—issue from their mouths, universally illuminating immeasurable and boundless worlds, passing beyond the Brahma-world and eclipsing the light of the sun and moon;
they then circle the body three times and re-enter through the mark of the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head. [Note: There is a reason why the Buddha manifests a smile.]

There are three reasons for this: first, that which was spoken by Mañjuśrī, praised by Śakra, and recounted by the devaputra all accord with the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and deeply satisfy the Buddha’s intention;
therefore, he smiled. Second, when the various devas praised him, saying they saw the turning of the Wheel of Dharma for a second time, they knew only one and did not recognize the other.
Why? They merely heard what the devaputra said and assumed it was a second turning.
While turning the wheel of Dharma, they do not realize the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*);
yet, in every dust mote, in every land, and throughout the mountains, rivers, and great earth, they preach at all times with unceasing fervor. How could there be any further turning or non-turning?

Because they do not know this, the Buddha manifests a smile. Third, the Devaputra Avivartin has thoroughly understood the profound Dharma and is worthy of receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Therefore, when the Buddha manifested a smile, the Brahmā Siṃhavikrāntagāmin, silently perceiving its cause, fully inquired about the reason for the smile within his verses of praise;
yet the World-Honored One specifically highlighted the occasion of the prophecy while omitting other details, because those of sharp faculties do not require such explanation.
Thereupon, the Brahma-heavenly being Viśeṣacintin joined his palms toward the Buddha and praised him in verse:

"O Most Victorious Honored One, whose wisdom transcends all, You fully know the conduct of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, As well as their wisdom, merit, and liberation; I only pray that you will explain the cause and conditions for your smile. [Note:

Because the Tathāgata has reached the ultimate true reality, he is said to possess "wisdom that transcends all"; because his rank has attained wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), he is so described.
It is said that because the Most Victorious One has exhausted the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), he is able to know the mental activities of sentient beings.
The *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "The Tathāgata thoroughly knows that all minds of sentient beings are 'no-mind. Why?
Because the past mind cannot be apprehended, the future mind cannot be apprehended, and the present mind cannot be apprehended. Since...
One who can liberate themselves and liberate others knows that the three virtues are perfectly luminous and complete in every respect;
such a venerable and supreme being has a specific purpose for every manifestation, which is why Brahmā requests instruction.
The Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable and unobstructed; it is beyond the knowledge of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. He speaks according to the minds of sentient beings as they respond.
I pray that the Most Honored One will explain the cause of his smile. [Note] The first two phrases explain the aforementioned "wisdom that transcends all.
The third phrase explains the aforementioned "knowledge of the intentions of sentient beings. The fourth phrase provides the conclusion.

The Buddha’s light is delightful, pure, and free from defilement; it shines universally upon devas and humans, eclipsing the sun and moon, as well as Mount Sumeru, the Iron Ring Mountains, and all other mountains.
I pray that the Peerless Honored One will explain the cause for this smile. [Note: This verse explains the meaning of the smiling and the emission of light mentioned in the prose section.
The Great Sage is tranquil and free from anger; gods and humans gaze upon him without weariness, and all receive happiness.
We pray that you will explain for us the cause of your smile. [Note] This verse was uttered by Brahmā.
Because the Buddha has abandoned the root of anger, he benefits all sentient beings; he does not become disturbed by questions concerning the mark of self.
He speaks for their sake.

One who has realized that all phenomena are empty and without self—like foam, clouds, dew, dreams, the moon reflected in water, or the appearance of space—should explain the causes of his smile with a wondrous voice.
[Note: Since the essence of all phenomena is empty like foam and the like, by what cause could there be a smile?
To speak is to express joy, anger, sorrow, and delight, yet these are themselves the mark of emptiness; what, then, is there to speak?
Nevertheless, like the moon in water, though the mark of emptiness is invisible, it is seen; and like the cause for the Tathāgata’s smile, which is ineffable, it is spoken.
Therefore, it is called "wondrous sound."
Having abandoned conceptualizations and all false views, you have realized emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and constantly delight in meditative concentration and the tranquil Dharma;

pray tell us the conditions for the emission of this pure light. [Note: Because one enters the three gates of liberation by abandoning all false views, and because one constantly delights in meditative concentration while emitting this pure light, how could it be said that there is no cause? This is why I ask.
Not clinging to words, letters, or vocal sounds, he does not rely on the Dharma nor on sentient beings; each person thinks, "He is speaking to me.
This is the explanation for his smile, spoken through the wisdom of supernormal powers. [Note: When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he does not cling to words or language;
internally he does not rely on the Dharma, and externally he does not cling to sentient beings. It is by means of his supernormal powers that each person thinks they have personally heard it.
What could the Dharma possibly possess that the Buddha lacks?
As the King of Physicians who extinguishes all maladies, possessing the strength of Nārāyaṇa, the Savior of the World, he proceeds toward the ultimate path of radiance;
honored by devas and humans, he explains the causes for his smiles. [Note: Because the Buddha has attained supreme mastery within the wisdom of skillful means.
The title of the Physician King is "Teacher of Discipline" (*Vināyaka*), because he skillfully disciplines the physical and mental illnesses of sentient beings.
Because of this skillful discipline, he possesses great power and function as a Savior of the World. Like Nārāyaṇa, there are two modes of engagement and relinquishment:

either engaging in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) while relinquishing the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), or engaging in the conditioned while relinquishing the unconditioned. He has attained mastery over himself.
Therefore, it is called the Ultimate Path.
Chapter Twenty: The Firm and Strong Perfection of Holy Conduct (*Brahmacarya*).
[Note: All other sutras contain the merit of cultivation and realization; however, because they do not fully exhaust the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), they all rely on attainment.
To have realization, teaching, and learning is not called the "firm and strong Brahma-conduct" (brahmacarya).

Only this sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna, in which the single mind is free from all dependence, exhausts the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and is purely unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); therefore, it is named the "firm and strong Brahma-conduct.

The true mind being free from dependence is called "Brahma-conduct"; its ultimate steadfastness is called "firm"; and its ability to confront and overcome heterodox arguments is called "strong. To enter [this state] is to realize it.
Regarding "effortless practice" (*anābhoga-caryā*), it is said that while the virtues praised in the preceding "Lion’s Roar" chapter are all within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)—
neither established nor destroyed— this present chapter establishes something specific.
At that time, the Buddha said to the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin, "Do you see this Non-regressing Devaputra?

"Indeed, I see him, World-Honored One," replied the Brahmā. "This Non-regressing Devaputra, from this day forward, after the passing of three million two hundred thousand asaṃkhyeya kalpas, shall attain Buddhahood under the name Sumerupradīparāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna."
The One Perfected in Conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
[Note] In the preceding text, the Buddha manifested a smile and Brahmā requested that he explain the cause of this smile; herein, he provides the direct answer to that request.
Because the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is immovable, it is called "Sumeru"; because it illuminates and realizes the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), it is called "Lamp King. This...

Because the Son of Heaven, upon hearing Mañjuśrī’s “arousing of the mind through non-arousing,” suddenly shattered his ignorance and wondrously accorded with the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the Buddha was thus named.

The world was named Wondrous Flower (*Sumanā*) and the eon was named Brahma Praise (*Brahmastava*). [Note: This is because the Son of Heaven, Non-retrogression, [realized this] according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Because he praised the true nature (*dharmatā*), the world was named "Exquisite Flowers" (*Sukusuma*), signifying that the conventional and the ultimate are identical; thus it is called "Exquisite Flowers.
"Flower" (*puṣpa*) refers to the cause, for by praising the true nature, he inspired pure faith in people and led them away from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
therefore, the eon was named "Brahma’s Praise" (*Brahmaghoṣa*).
That Buddha-land has Jambūnada-gold and lapis lazuli for its ground. [Note: "Jambūnada" means gold of supreme color;
"gold" signifies firmness and hardness, while "lapis lazuli" signifies clarity and transparency.
This is because the Non-retrogressive Devaputra, having deeply penetrated the true nature (*dharmatā*), employs firmness and clarity as a recompense for his merit of non-retrogression.
The Saṃgha consists solely of Bodhisattvas. [Note] Because within the Dharma of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), there is no room for Śrāvaka bhikṣus.
There are no māras or adversaries. [Note] When one internally realizes the true mark, external conditions are severed; since conditions are severed, how could there be any harm from māras?
Whatever things were required arrived as soon as they were thought of; the Buddha’s lifespan was immeasurable and incalculable in years.
Thereupon, the Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the Devaputra Avaivartika, saying: "The Tathāgata has now bestowed a prediction upon you, O Devaputra. The Devaputra replied:
"Brahmā, just as the prediction is bestowed through suchness and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), so too is the prediction bestowed upon me. [Note: The preceding net]
The bestowal of prophecy upon Mingshou (明授) was obtained by relying on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*);
the bestowal of prophecy upon the devaputra herein was obtained by relying on skillful means wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). Although skillful means is provisional, it is identical to true wisdom;

therefore, it is said that the prophecy is given "as suchness" (*tathatā*) and according to the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Since the dharma-nature has the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), [the prophecy is so granted].
Cintāviśeṣa said: "Just as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) cannot be predicted, the Devaputra said:
'If the nature of phenomena cannot be predicted, you should know that the prediction of all Bodhisattvas is likewise so. [Note:
Just as the heat of fire and the moisture of water are such by their very nature and do not require a prediction to cause them to be so, so too fire and water do not exist apart from their nature."
If it were hot and damp, then even when a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, it would likewise not be recorded in a prophecy.
Yet, although it is not recorded, the reason for recording it is the intention to benefit beings and not to harm them;
this is what is meant by "recording. The *Suyāma-sūtra* states: "If the Tathāgata does not grant you a prophecy, then your existence before the Buddhas of the past would be in vain."
The Devaputra Abiding in the Brahma-conduct said: "If there is no abiding, that is abiding in the Brahma-conduct.

[Note] What is called 'bestowing a prediction' (vyākaraṇa) refers to the response to causes and the answer regarding results. Regarding the question concerning the transgression of practicing the Brahma-conduct:

if one who practices the Brahma-conduct does not obtain the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, then cause and result would have nothing upon which to rely. The intention of the Devaputra is that if cause and result exist...

To abide [in such a way] is called "conditioned," and one cannot thereby receive a prediction (vyākaraṇa); because there is no abiding in cause and effect, this is the abiding in the holy life (brahmacarya), and it is for this reason that one receives a prediction.
Thus, it is said that the bestowal of the prediction is identical to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Siddhārthabuddhi asked: "How does one dwell in the holy life (brahmacarya) by dwelling nowhere? He replied:
"If one does not dwell in the desire realm, does not dwell in the form realm, and does not dwell in the formless realm, that is dwelling in the holy life.

Furthermore, Brahmā, if one dwells such that one does not dwell in a self, does not dwell in sentient beings, does not dwell in a life-span, and does not dwell in a person, that is dwelling in the holy life. To state it briefly, if—"
"Not abiding in dharmas and not abiding in non-dharmas is to abide in the holy life (*brahmacarya*). [Note:
Regarding the question of how Brahmā abides in the holy life without abiding, the answer is divided into three sections: first, not abiding externally in the triple world;
second, not abiding internally in the four characteristics; third, not abiding in the middle between dharmas and non-dharmas. This is called "abiding by way of non-abiding."
He asked again, "What is the meaning of the holy life (*brahmacarya*)? He replied, "To abide in the path of non-duality is the meaning of the holy life.
He asked again, "In abiding in the path of non-duality, in what does one abide? He replied, "Abiding in the path of non-duality is precisely not abiding in any phenomena whatsoever.
Why is this? Because the various noble ones (*ārya*) have no place of abiding; by not grasping at phenomena, they are able to cross over the many torrents. [Note]
"If there is no abiding, what is the meaning of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) for one who practices it? Your Majesty, you may wonder what the meaning of the holy life is;
the holy life has 'non-abiding' as its meaning. If there were a meaning to non-abiding, then abiding would exist. Because they are non-dual, this is their meaning.
For example, if a bell, a gong, a cymbal, and a drum were all struck at once, if one listens with a discriminating mind, then there is abiding."
Because the mind has no dwelling place, attachment does not arise; thus, although the eight tones play in concert, they are distinct and clear, for there is no duality in hearing.
Again he asked, "What is meant by 'cultivating the Way'? He replied, "Not falling into existence, not falling into non-existence, and furthermore, not making such distinctions."
To have no practice regarding that which is non-existent in this way is called the cultivation of the path. Again, it was asked: "By what dharma is the path cultivated? He replied:
"Not by means of the dharmas of seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing; not by attainment, nor by realization;

to be without marks and without demonstration regarding all dharmas is called the cultivation of the path. [Note: To receive a prediction while receiving nothing received is because one abides in non-abiding.

The Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*) takes non-abiding as its meaning; thus, there should be no cultivation. Yet, worldly people generally speak of "cultivating the Way," not knowing by what means they cultivate it.
Why is it that the Brahma-faring takes non-abiding as its meaning, while the cultivation of the Way takes non-cultivation as its cultivation?

If there were something to be cultivated, there would necessarily be something not cultivated. This is what is meant: [the text here implies a paradoxical identity between cultivation and non-cultivation].
The contention between existence and non-existence is a sickness of the mind. To speak of "falling into" existence or non-existence refers to karma already established;

to speak of one who does not differentiate between existence and non-existence refers to thoughts yet to sprout. First, it speaks of the practice one is able to perform; next, it speaks of the Dharma upon which one relies.
One should not act based on what is seen, heard, sensed, or known; this is clearly intended to point toward [the ultimate].
There is no dharma upon which to rely. Since dharmas have no reliance, how could one speak of attainment or realization?

Why is this so? Because all dharmas are signless (*animitta*) and without signs; there is nothing to demonstrate. This absence of attainment, absence of realization, signlessness, and non-demonstration is called the cultivation of the path.
He asked again, "What is meant by a bodhisattva’s firm and powerful diligence?

He replied, "If a bodhisattva perceives neither a single characteristic nor a diverse characteristic among all phenomena, this is called the great adornment of a bodhisattva’s firm and powerful diligence. [Note:
Not dwelling internally within the mind that practices is "not seeing the one"; not becoming attached externally to the phenomena being practiced is "not seeing the other."
Seeing that the internal and external are distinct, and having already departed from the middle, one should sever all dependence; thus there is no adversary, no destruction, and no indolence.
When Prajñā illuminates delusion, there is no delusion that is not shattered—this is the meaning of "having no adversary. Therefore, it is called "strong.
Because the Dharmakāya is signless and has no decay or ruin, it is called "firm. Liberation is without action, yet there is nothing it does not perform; this is named... [the name follows].
Because one practices these three dharmas with perfect diligence, it is called "Great Adornment" (*mahā-vyūha*).
This is because one does not destroy the *dharmatā* (the true nature) of all phenomena. [Note: One does not perceive any difference.
To be without attachment to, without severance of, without increase to, and without decrease from all phenomena;

to see neither defilement nor purity, and to transcend the nature of phenomena—this is called the bodhisattva’s first firm and powerful diligence, namely, that the body does not arise and the mind does not arise.
[Note] To explain the meaning of this first firm and powerful diligence: the body does not initiate the activities of walking, standing, sitting, or reclining.
Because the mind, when seen, does not give rise to the conceptualizations of seeing, hearing, knowing, or perceiving, it is called "foremost.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the Devaputra Avivartin, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
Having praised him, he addressed the Brahmā Viśeṣacintī, saying, "As the Devaputra has said, that the body does not arise and the mind does not arise—this is the foremost."
Firm and vigorous diligence. [Note] The World-Honored One’s confirmation that the words of the Devaputra are correct ensures that future generations may certainly believe them.
An ancient said: "If one gives rise to a mind of diligence, this is delusion and not true diligence; if one can keep the mind free from delusion, diligence will be boundless.
Thus we know the words of the ancients are not false, and their manifestation of the Dharma is revealed herein.
Brahmā, I recall that in my past lives, I practiced all manner of deeds with firm and vigorous diligence; I maintained the precepts and the dhūta ascetic practices;
I made offerings and showed reverence to my teachers and elders; I dwelt in seclusion, applying myself single-mindedly to the Path, reciting and studying the teachings until I was widely learned;
I took pity on sentient beings and provided them with their necessities; and I persevered with earnest diligence in all difficult practices and austerities throughout the past.
The Buddha did not grant me the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
It is because I dwelt in the marks of exertion arising from body, speech, and mind. [Note] From upholding the precepts to showing respect is the cultivation of morality (*śīla*);

practicing the Way in empty and quietude is the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi*); reciting and reading with extensive learning is the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*); and providing for their necessities is...
Cultivating generosity is the practice; performing difficult austerities is the cultivation of patience; and diligent, energetic exertion is the cultivation of vigor.
Thus, these six perfections encompass all that can bring about supramundane merit; therefore, they are called "all-pervasive, firm, and powerful vigor.
Yet, when the World-Honored One cultivated these six perfections before the various Buddhas, he did so by relying upon the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because body and mind undergo arising, one cannot receive the prediction of enlightenment nor realize this unconditioned true reality;
because body and mind are fundamentally without arising, one does not reach this [state]. The following passage explains the meaning of "not turning back" to establish this point.
"Brahmā, because I later attained the firm and powerful diligence as described by the Son of Heaven, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me this prediction, saying:
'In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.
Therefore, Brahmā, if a bodhisattva wishes to quickly receive such a prediction, they should cultivate this kind of firm and powerful diligence regarding all dharmas."
One does not give rise to the sign of diligence. [Note: If one gives rise to the thought of practicing the six perfections, one cannot fulfill them in a single thought-moment;
if one cannot fulfill them in a single thought-moment, there is a sequence; because there is a sequence, there is engagement with conceptual discrimination;

because there is engagement with conceptual discrimination, one falls into conditioned proliferation (*saṃskṛta-prapañca*); therefore, one cannot receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). If, however, one does not give rise to such thoughts...
Because the six perfections are fully realized in a single thought-moment through non-arising, one does not even perceive "one," let alone "six.
This non-perception of "one" is called the foremost, steadfast, and powerful diligence.
The World-Honored One cited this as his own testimony so that those ten thousand generations hence might know where the fundamental aim resides and have a basis for reliance.

“World-Honored One, what is this diligence characterized by non-arising? The Buddha said: “Diligence that is equal to the emptiness of the three periods of time is called diligence characterized by non-arising.
[Note: When not a single thought arises, the past and future limits are severed; when the past and future limits are severed, there is also nothing in the middle because it lacks a name.
Therefore, it is said that the three periods of time are equal to emptiness.
The World-Honored One said: "What is the diligence that is equal to the emptiness of the three periods of time? The Buddha replied: "The past mind has already ceased;
the future mind has not yet arrived; the present mind does not abide. [Note] Herein, the empty nature of the three periods of time is directly demonstrated;
the subsequent text explains why the three periods of time are empty.

If a dharma ceases and does not arise again, if it has not yet arrived and thus lacks the characteristic of arising, and if it lacks abiding and thus abides in the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and furthermore, if the true mark itself has no arising—then if a dharma is without arising, there is no past, future, or present.
If there is no past, future, or present, then from the very beginning its nature is eternally non-arising; this is called the "vigor of the equality of the three times as empty."

This enables a bodhisattva to swiftly receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). [Note] A verse from the *Avataṃsaka* states: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable eons;
it is neither past, nor future, nor present. Thus understanding the matters of the three periods of time, one transcends all skillful means and accomplishes the ten powers (*daśabala*).

This meaning is identical to the present passage. It is like two tally-sticks meeting; if one wishes to give rise to the mind [of awakening], they accord with it. Furthermore, it is called "Awakening" (*bodhi*) because it is white.
Clouds extend ten thousand li.
A Bodhisattva of the Brahma-heaven who achieves such Dharma-patience (dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti) is able to thoroughly comprehend all dharmas without anything to be relinquished;
this is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). [Note] In the previous "Chapter on Bestowal of Prophecy," Jālinīprabha said: "Relinquish all afflictions."
It is called *dānapāramitā*. The World-Honored One said that being able to relinquish all marks is called *dānapāramitā*.
Here, it is said that realizing that dharmas have nothing to be relinquished is called *dānapāramitā*. Why do these preceding and following [statements] appear to be contradictory?

The former was taught in contrast to the *vastu-pāramitās* (provisional practices) of the Three Vehicles, where the Bodhisattva rejected them as non-expedient; the latter is established based on the single mind (*ekacitta*).
Since this is established based on the true doctrine of the One Vehicle, it is said that there is no "giving up" in the act of giving up.
If there were something to be given up, then there would be something not given up; how, then, could it be called the foremost, steadfast, and vigorous diligence?
To thoroughly comprehend that all phenomena are without outflows (*anāsrava*) is called the *śīlapāramitā*. [Note:

Although those of the Two Vehicles maintain the precepts of what is to be practiced and what is to be refrained from, they are constantly swayed by the dualistic notions of existence and non-existence; thus, even Arhats are said to have "broken precepts.
The Mahāyāna, however, thoroughly comprehends that within the single mind there is no falling into outflows; this is called the pure, outflow-free precept of the Mahāyāna.
To thoroughly comprehend that all phenomena are without injury is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). [Note:
What is meant by "without injury" is to be without any mental activity regarding all phenomena, remaining far removed from grasping and rejecting, and abiding in equanimity and mastery.
To thoroughly comprehend that all phenomena are without arising is called the *vīrya-pāramitā*. [Note:
This refers to firm and steadfast diligence.
To thoroughly comprehend the equality of all phenomena is called the *dhyāna-pāramitā*. [Note: Because one comprehends equality, the mind...]
When the mind does not arise and [thoughts] do not arise, then distraction is severed; this is called *dhyāna-samādhi*.

To thoroughly comprehend that all phenomena are without discrimination is called *prajñāpāramitā*. [Note: If one relies on the expression of words and letters, there appears to be a sequence of before and after;
yet if one realizes the mind and accords with the ultimate meaning, it is truly but a single thought-moment. Why is this? Because one has realized the One.

Since all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma, there is nothing to be abandoned; because there is nothing to be abandoned, the two extremes of existence and non-existence do not give rise to gain or loss.
Since there is no gain or loss, the outflows of gain and loss are extinguished; as taking and abandoning are forgotten, there is no injury.
Without taking or abandoning, the mind does not arise; when the mind does not arise, one realizes the equality of all phenomena. Thus it is realized.
Because all dharmas are equal, there is no discrimination; this is knowing that the essence of the six perfections is but a single thought-moment.
If a bodhisattva realizes and penetrates in this way, then regarding all dharmas, there is neither increase nor decrease, neither right nor wrong. [Note:
This is explained and established in the following text.]
Although this bodhisattva practices giving, he does not seek its karmic fruit. [Note] Internally, because he does not perceive a giver or an object given, there is no decrease;
externally, because he does not perceive the attainment of results or rewards, there is no increase.
Although one maintains the precepts, there is no attachment. [Note: If there were the "wrong" of violating them and the "right" of maintaining them, then attachment would arise.
However, because one realizes that all phenomena are equal and fundamentally lack wrongness or rightness, although one maintains the precepts, there is no attachment.
Although one practices patience, one knows that both the internal and external are empty. [Note] Internal emptiness means that the mind capable of enduring is not perceived;
external emptiness means that the object being endured is not perceived.
Although one exerts diligence, one knows there is no characteristic of arising; although one practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), there is nothing upon which to rely. [Note:
The meditative concentrations of the two vehicles are excluded because they rely on the emptiness of mind.
Although one practices wisdom, there is no grasping at signs. [Note] Wisdom possesses the capacity for clear reflection;
if one were to grasp at this capacity for clear reflection, it would not be the supreme wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Brahmā, having accomplished such dharmakṣānti (receptivity to the Dharma), manifests all modes of conduct yet remains undefiled by them.
[Note: This concludes the preceding section and initiates the subsequent one; previously, his attainment of the essence was clarified, while hereafter, his attainment of its function is elucidated.
This person attains the mark of equality in the world and is not shaken by gain or loss, defamation or praise, fame or insignificance, suffering or pleasure;
because they have transcended all worldly dharmas, they neither exalt themselves nor disparage others, neither rejoice nor grieve, neither move nor become indolent.
With a non-dual mind, free from all conditions, they attain the dharma of non-duality for the sake of the assembly of those who have fallen into the dharmas of dualistic views.
To give rise to the mind of great compassion and, for the sake of receiving a body [in saṃsāra], to teach and transform sentient beings—Brahmā, this is called the first firm and steadfast diligence.
[Note: Because the mind does not arise, a single thought-moment is fully endowed with the six pāramitās.
Because it is fully endowed with the six pāramitās, one is not turned by the eight winds; because one is not turned by the eight winds, then...
When praised, one does not exalt oneself; when reviled, one does not debase oneself. One is not moved by gain, nor is one led into indolence by pleasure.

There is no cause for joy in praise, nor cause for grief in suffering. Because there is no duality within and one is detached from external conditions, both internal and external are as they are, and all phenomena are equal.
Although one realizes this equality, one does not abandon sentient beings, but rather gives rise to the Great [Compassion].
Compassion is defined as this: although the mind is liberated and nothing arises, yet there is also nothing that does not arise.
It is what is called attaining the patience regarding the emptiness of non-self, while giving rise to great compassion for sentient beings and taking on a body for their sake.
[Note: Since it is said that because the mind does not arise, it is called "firm and powerful diligence," why then does one further give rise to great compassion?
The commentary explains: It is for the sake of attaining the patience regarding the dharma of non-self and emptiness, and for the realization of non-self.

Because there is nothing that is not self, and because sentient beings who fall into the two views are themselves like me falling into the two views, one mobilizes [compassion] through the realization of the identity of essence.
Out of compassion, he takes on this body with the intent to deliver beings from it; thus it is said: "The sage has no self, yet there is nothing he does not take as his own.
This is what that means.

When this teaching was explained, eight thousand bodhisattvas who possessed the marks of firm and vigorous diligence attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and the Buddha conferred upon them their prediction [of enlightenment].
The prophecy was given that they shall all attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and each achieve the Buddha-way in a different land, all bearing the same name:

Firm Diligence (*Dṛḍhavīrya*). [Note: Although they attain Buddhahood in different lands yet their names are the same, this means that while phenomena may differ in a thousand ways, the principle remains non-dual. Because phenomena differ in a thousand ways, those various bodhisattvas...
Because each attains realization according to the specific practice undertaken on their respective grounds, they are said to have "different lands.
Because there is no difference in principle, whatever they realize is equally non-arising; therefore, it is said that their "names are the same."
Chapter Twenty-one: The Simile of the Ocean [Note]:
Eight thousand bodhisattvas, upon hearing this Dharma-gate of firm and vigorous diligence, simultaneously realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having realized this patience regarding dharmas, they were like the myriad streams within the ocean, which receive all things without exception, even descending to the level of a chariot axle.
Because the rain neither diminishes nor increases [the ocean], Kāśyapa took it as a metaphor for the sea;
the Tathāgata’s confirmation of this may be called "beating the drum and playing the lute, two masters meeting."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, it is like a great dragon that, when wishing to rain, pours its rain upon the great ocean;
these bodhisattvas are also like this, raining the rain of the Great Dharma upon the minds of bodhisattvas. The Buddha said:
"Kāśyapa, as you have said, the reason the great dragon kings do not rain upon Jambudvīpa is not because they lack [the power to do so]."
It is because [the earth] is stingy, yet it is simply because its ground is incapable of receiving [such rain]. Why is this?

If the Great Dragon were to let fall rain as thick as the axle of a chariot, then Jambudvīpa, along with its cities, towns, villages, mountains, forests, ponds, and pools, would all be swept away like a jujube leaf carried off by a current.
Therefore, the Great Dragon does not pour down great rain upon Jambudvīpa.
Kāśyapa, the reason these bodhisattvas do not rain down the Dharma-rain upon other sentient beings is not because they harbor a mind of stinginess;
rather, it is because those beings' vessels are incapable of receiving such teachings as these.
Therefore, these bodhisattvas rain down such inconceivable [teachings] only into the hearts of bodhisattvas who are like a profound wisdom and immeasurable great ocean.

The unsurpassed rain of Dharma. [Note] These bodhisattvas refer to the non-retrogressive devaputra, the Brahmā Viśeṣacinti, and immeasurable great oceans of bodhisattvas such as the eight thousand bodhisattvas.
The metaphor of raining upon the great ocean signifies preaching the inconceivable Dharma of the Mahāyāna to those of the Mahāyāna; the metaphor of not raining upon Jambudvīpa signifies this.
The inconceivable Dharma of the Mahāyāna is not taught to those of the Two Vehicles;

it is not because of any stinginess, but because they are incapable of receiving and sustaining it, and thus it is not taught to them as a provisional means to entice them. Rather, it is to suppress their pride and advance them.

This is because those of the Two Vehicles are attached to the conditioned, to attainment, and to realization; if they were to hear that there is no cultivation and no realization, [they would fall into despair].
If one who has attained the state of being free from loss suddenly realizes they were originally immensely wealthy, they will become terrified and flee, no longer recognizing their own family estate.
Kāśyapa, it is also like the great ocean, which can receive heavy rains falling as thick as chariot axles without increasing or decreasing;
these bodhisattvas are likewise: whether for one kalpa or even a hundred kalpas, whether listening or speaking, their minds remain as such.

It is profoundly serene, neither increasing nor decreasing. [Note: In the preceding passage, those such as the non-retrogressive devaputras were likened to dragon kings because they did not rain down the Dharma-rain upon other sentient beings;
here, because they are capable of receiving the great rain, those such as the non-retrogressive devaputras are likened to the great ocean.
The one who is able to preach the Dharma is likened to the great ocean.
Since these are precisely those who can hear the Dharma, it is said: "If one speaks, it is heard by that Bodhisattva;
thus there is hearing without hearing, and speaking without speaking. Their minds are serene, neither increasing nor decreasing.

In the text, the speaker is illustrated first, followed by the listener; thus, speaking comes before listening. As for the concluding passage, whether it be "listening" or "speaking," listening comes first.
The subsequent statement regarding the semblance of perversion (*viparyāsa*) is intended to show that the meanings of the preceding and following passages are mutually complete.
Kāśyapa, it is also like the great ocean: when the hundreds of rivers flow into it, they all become of one salty taste;
in the same way, these bodhisattvas, upon hearing various teachings and various discourses, are all able to believe and understand them as such.
The single flavor of emptiness. [Note] All differentiated wisdoms are realized as being of one flavor within the true mind;
there is no other substance, because the self-characteristic of the true mind is beyond all relativity.
Kāśyapa, it is also like the great ocean, which is clear, pure, and free from defilement; when turbid waters flow into it, they all become clean.
These bodhisattvas are likewise: they purify the stains of all fetters, resentments, and the afflictions (*kleśa*). [Note:

Because fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is fundamentally free from afflictions and fetters, even if afflictions should enter fundamental wisdom, the delusions are naturally severed, just as [the ocean purifies incoming water].
The great ocean is originally still, pure, and free from turbid currents; even if turbid water should flow into it, it naturally becomes clear and clean.
Kāśyapa, it is also like this: the great ocean is exceedingly deep and bottomless, and these bodhisattvas are likewise able to contemplate in such a manner.
Because it consists of immeasurable dharmas, it is called "profound"; because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot fathom it, it is called "bottomless.
[Note: Because its great wisdom is deep as an abyss, it is called "profound"; because its great practice is difficult to fathom, it is called "bottomless."
Kāśyapa, it is also like the great ocean, which gathers immeasurable waters; these bodhisattvas are likewise, gathering immeasurable dharmas and immeasurable wisdom.
[Note: Because they integrate all differentiated dharma-gates through true wisdom, they are said to have "immeasurable dharmas.
Since the dharmas are immeasurable, their wisdom is also called "immeasurable. As for "immeasurable," it means...
This refers to what is called "vastness. It is not merely a matter of many things being immeasurable, but rather the immeasurability of the immeasurable.
It is like the nature of the ocean, which is one and integrates the hundred rivers; though it does not even maintain its oneness, the hundred rivers are fully gathered therein.

Therefore it is said that the minds of all bodhisattvas are like the great ocean. Kāśyapa, just as the great ocean accumulates various and immeasurable precious treasures, so too are these bodhisattvas:

they enter various gateways to the Dharma, gather the jewels of all dharmas, and through practicing various paths, they give rise to an immeasurable accumulation of the jewels of the Dharma. Kāśyapa, furthermore, the great ocean possesses...
There are three kinds of jewels: first, those of little value; second, those of value; and third, those of priceless value.

The Dharma taught by these Bodhisattvas is likewise so: according to whether the faculties of sentient beings are sharp or dull, they enable them to attain liberation—some attaining liberation through the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), some through the Middle Vehicle (Madhyayāna), and some through the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).

One attains liberation. [Note: What is called "entering various dharma-gates" refers to the gathering of the jewels of all dharmas, which possess the characteristics of both the mundane and supramundane five vehicles;
yet, when distinguished, they are seen to consist only of the three vehicles. For example, although jewels are immeasurable, only the priceless one is considered precious;

likewise, although vehicles are immeasurable, only the Mahāyāna is the reality. Although those two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha) are indeed provisional means to accommodate the capacities of sentient beings...
It is appropriate that they also be called "Jewel-Union," as can be known from the text.
Kāśyapa, just as the great ocean gradually becomes deeper, so too do these bodhisattvas gradually become deeper toward *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
[Note: Relying on the immeasurable Dharma-gates of the Mahāyāna, they are successively refined and transformed through progressive stages.
Because they advance toward and reach the stage of wondrous enlightenment,
it is said that they become increasingly profound. Kāśyapa, furthermore, just as the great ocean does not harbor a dead corpse,
so too these bodhisattvas do not harbor the minds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor do they harbor stinginess, greed, violation of precepts, anger, laziness, distracted thoughts, or folly.
The mind of delusion likewise does not harbor views of self, person, sentient beings, or life-span. [Note:
Because the Bodhisattva relies on the Great Vehicle to perfectly cultivate the wondrous path and does not rely on the Small Vehicle’s biased study of arising and ceasing;

because they constantly practice the six perfections and the Brahma-conduct, remaining unattached to minds of stinginess, greed, and delusion, and crossing over immeasurable conceptualizations—they likewise do not harbor views of self, person, and so forth. If one were to say...
If I were to cultivate the Mahāyāna up to the six perfections and the Brahma-conduct, I would then be attached to the views of self, person, and sentient beings.
Kāśyapa, it is also like this: when the kalpa comes to an end and is consumed by fire, all small ponds, rivers, streams, and springs dry up first, and only then does the great ocean finally vanish;
the extinction of the True Dharma is just like this—the various practices of the Lesser Vehicle [perish first].
The True Dharma first comes to an end, and only thereafter does the True Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s ocean-like mind perish. [Note:

When the kalpa ends and the oceans dry up, it is only natural that the conditioned phenomena of the world should thus cease; however, that the True Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s mind should likewise perish is unlikely.
If it were indeed to perish, one would fall into the view of annihilationism; how could this be called the Perfect and Eternal Way of the Mahāyāna?

There are three meanings to this: first, when the true Dharma of the world is about to perish, sentient beings with evil karma predominate and those with few roots of goodness lack the capacity to be transformed;
therefore, the Bodhisattva transforms other regions separately. This is called "extinction," but it does not mean total annihilation.
It is like a physician who, upon examining a patient, finds that even one part of them can still be saved, and thus does not immediately depart.
When one realizes that a certain patient cannot be saved and that remaining would be useless, one departs for another region;
this does not mean the physician abandons the patient and leaves, but rather that the patient has abandoned himself. This is like the worldly classics:
when people practice benevolence and righteousness, the Dharma endures; when they do not practice benevolence and righteousness, the Dharma perishes. Thus, in which age has there ever been no ruler?
If there were no such petty people in every generation, when would the Dharma abide and when would the Dharma perish?
That which causes the Dharma to perish lies in the person, not in the Dharma itself. The two preceding metaphors illustrate these phenomenal characteristics; the third is as follows:

the mind is like the Two Vehicles who destroy the view of existence, while the Pratyekabuddhas realize the emptiness of dharmas in their essence. Through the practice of the perfections (pāramitās), they destroy the "dust-sand" [afflictions] at the sixth stage.
The faculty of mind (*manas*) is extinguished in the eighth stage; the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is extinguished by the Vajra Path;

and from the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*) through the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣmabodhi*), all are completely extinguished. Therefore, it is said that the True Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle perishes first, followed by the extinction of the Bodhisattvas' True Dharma and their minds.

All stages prior to Subtle Enlightenment are likewise termed the "Lesser Vehicle" because they have not yet realized the ultimate perfection. Thus, according to the facts, their extinction occurs therein.
The person and the dharmas have never been extinguished; according to principle, extinction resides in ignorance, yet their nature has never been extinguished.
Kāśyapa, these bodhisattvas would rather lose their bodies and lives than abandon the true Dharma. Do you think that bodhisattvas lose the true Dharma?

Do not entertain such a view. [Note: Because it was stated above that the bodhisattva’s mind of the true Dharma might be extinguished, there is a fear that the view of annihilationism (ucchedadṛṣṭi) might arise.
Therefore, the World-Honored One raised a parable to clarify that one should not hold such a view:

"Kāśyapa, it is like a diamond jewel in that great ocean named 'Gatherer of All Treasures,' which remains unburnt and undestroyed even when the seven suns arise and the fire reaches as far as the Brahma-world; instead, it moves on to another great ocean."
It is impossible for this world-system to be consumed by fire while this precious jewel remains within it;
likewise, it is impossible for these bodhisattvas to perish when the True Dharma is extinguished and the seven false dharmas arise—even if they must go to other world-systems.
What are these seven? First, the treatises of non-Buddhist paths; second, evil associates; third, the erroneous application of the path and its teachings; fourth... [and so forth].
Fifth, they will mutually afflict and disturb one another; sixth, they will enter the thorny forest of false views;
seventh, they will not cultivate merit and virtue; eighth, there will be none who attain the Way. When these seven evils emerge, these bodhisattvas will know that sentient beings cannot be saved.

Consequently, they shall go to Buddha-lands in other directions, never being separated from seeing the Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and teaching and transforming sentient beings. Thus their merits increase.

"Long-cultivated roots of goodness. [Note] Herein, the metaphor clarifies that although the Bodhisattva has entered cessation (*nirodha*) and his capacity for response has been exhausted such that he should forget about converting others, he nevertheless departs to convert other lands.

How could the Bodhisattva originally bear to depart? Yet, when evil dharmas appear in the world and the conditions for conversion are no longer favorable, he must go—just as a physician cannot bear to abandon a patient, yet must depart when there is no way to save them.
It is likewise with these seven kinds of evils; how could there not have been Buddhas in the world? Why then do they only depart at the end of a kalpa?
It is because even while a Buddha is in the world, he must rely on the presence of evil dharmas to preach the Dharma for crossing over conditions and to enable the practice of the teachings.

If there were no evil dharmas, even if the True Dharma existed, what would there be to use it for? Therefore it is said: "The Bodhisattva penetrates that which is not the Way in order to practice the Way of the Buddha."
If one encounters the end of an eon when the world can no longer be established, where would a Bodhisattva wish to abide?
It is just as a physician reveals his wondrous skill through the presence of a patient; even if one possessed the talents of [Hua]tuo or Bian Que, what use would they have without a patient?
Thus we know that a skilled physician must rely upon a chronic illness; if the patient’s allotted lifespan were already exhausted, [the physician’s skill would be of no avail].
If that physician does not depart even after [the world has been consumed], he is deluded; this is a metaphor based on the world of *sabhāgatā* (homogeneous existence).
If one relies on the differentiation of individual karma, then virtuous people always rely upon the True Dharma, while evil people occasionally witness the end of the kalpa.
Therefore it is said: "The world sees it burned away to nothingness, yet my Pure Land is not destroyed. This is precisely what is meant.
Kāśyapa, it is also like the great ocean, which serves as the refuge for immeasurable sentient beings;
these bodhisattvas are likewise so, for sentient beings rely upon them to obtain three kinds of happiness: the happiness of humans, the happiness of devas, and the happiness of nirvāṇa. [Note:
These three kinds of happiness encompass both the mundane and the supramundane; the happiness of humans and devas is mundane happiness, while nirvāṇa is supramundane.
"Worldly pleasures, Kāśyapa, are like the great ocean: though it is salty and undrinkable, these bodhisattvas are likewise;
no Māras or non-Buddhists can swallow them up or extinguish them. Then Mahākāśyapa said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, although the great ocean is deep..."
It may still be possible to measure these [other things], but these bodhisattvas are immeasurable. The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"The atoms of the trichiliocosm may still have their number known, but the merit of these bodhisattvas is immeasurable and cannot be numbered."
[Note] Kāśyapa described and established that the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is so profound and vast it cannot be measured; even the great ocean is insufficient as a metaphor.
The Tathāgata further provided a metaphor: while the number of atoms in the world may still be known, the merit of a Bodhisattva cannot be known.
This is because where there is great wisdom, there is subsequently great virtue. Thus, the great ocean [is surpassed by it].
How could the nature of dust be known? Since that which is unknowable can still be known, the wisdom and merit of a Bodhisattva are ultimately unknowable.
This is because the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) belongs neither to knowledge nor to ignorance;
knowledge is deluded thought, while ignorance is indeterminate (avyākṛta). Not only are these unfathomable to the followers of the Two Vehicles, but even the Tathāgata does not know them as such.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this matter, spoke in verse:
"Just as the great ocean can receive all waters without ever reaching fullness, so too are these bodhisattvas: they constantly seek the benefit of the Dharma without weariness."
Sufficient. [Note] This verse describes how the Bodhisattvas possess a vast and magnificent presence, capable of receiving the Great Dharma and seeking it without satiety.

Furthermore, just as the great ocean receives all flowing streams, with everything returning to it without increase or decrease, so too do these Bodhisattvas listen to and receive the profound Dharma without increase or decrease.
[Note] These two preceding verses correspond to the passage in the prose section concerning "receiving the axle."
The meaning of "rain" is explained at length through a single verse, which opens into two parts: first, a verse praising the insatiability of receiving the Dharma;

second, a verse that further explains the meaning of this insatiability. Although a bodhisattva never reaches a time when their reception of the Dharma is complete, in reality, they receive it without the notion of receiving.
Regarding both receiving and non-receiving, there is neither increase nor decrease, because these two are not the same.
Because the followers of the Two Vehicles possess the notion of attainment, Zhuangzi says: "In the time of Yu, there was a great deluge for seven years, yet the sea did not overflow;
in the time of Tang, there was a great drought for nine years, yet the sea did not dry up.

This [sea] receives the rain of chariot axles without increasing or decreasing, which is identical in intent to that passage; however, it does not explicitly state the reason why it neither increases nor decreases.
The omission of the word "only" (唯) when stating that they receive [offerings] without ever reaching fullness seems to be a textual deficiency.

Furthermore, just as the great ocean does not accept turbidity—yet whatever turbid water flows into it becomes entirely pure—so too these bodhisattvas do not accept any defilement of afflictions (*kleśa*).
[Note: This is the third passage from the prose section.]
Furthermore, just as the great ocean has no shore or bottom, so too these bodhisattvas possess immeasurable merit and wisdom that cannot be fathomed by any sentient beings.
[Note: The prose version states that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot fathom them;
here, the text "sentient beings cannot fathom them" serves as a complementary expression for the former.

Furthermore, just as the great ocean has no distinctions such that the hundreds of rivers flowing into it all become of one taste, so too these bodhisattvas are such that the teachings they hear and receive are of a single characteristic.
[Note: This refers to the second passage in the prose section, where the preceding and following parts do not follow a sequential order.]

Furthermore, just as the reason the great ocean exists is not merely for the sake of a single sentient being, so too these bodhisattvas universally give rise to the mind of the Way for the sake of all beings.
[Note: Because the characteristics of the world are all produced by the collective deluded perceptions of sentient beings, it is said that it is "not for the sake of a single sentient being."

Just as the ocean treasure named "Gathering All Jewels" is the cause for the collection of all jewels, and because of this treasure there exist manifold jewels, so too is the treasury of Bodhisattvas:
from the jewel of the Bodhisattva, the Three Jewels emerge. [Note] In the Sanskrit language, *bodhisattva* means "one who awakens sentient beings";
because they are able to awaken the world, the Three Jewels flow forth from them.
Just as the great ocean produces three kinds of jewels, yet this great ocean itself is without discrimination, so too is the Bodhisattva’s preaching of the Dharma:

he delivers beings through the Three Vehicles without making distinctions between self and other. [Note: It was previously stated that the Three Jewels consist of the low-priced, the priced, and the priceless;
the prose version is detailed while the verse is concise.
Furthermore, just as the great ocean gradually deepens, so too do these bodhisattvas, for the sake of sentient beings, cultivate merit and dedicate it toward the profound *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
[Note: This verse describes the bodhisattva’s practice of benefiting others.
Furthermore, just as the great ocean does not harbor corpses, so too these bodhisattvas, having generated the pure mind and the vow for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*),
do not harbor the defiled minds of the śrāvakas. [Note] This verse indicates that the bodhisattva exclusively cultivates the Mahāyāna and does not dwell upon the Lesser Vehicle.
Just as the great ocean contains a firm and solid jewel called "Gatherer of All Jewels," which is never consumed even when the kalpa is destroyed by fire,
but is instead transported to other Buddha-fields; so too, when the True Dharma is extinguished, those who possess firm and resolute diligence can uphold the Dharma,
and knowing that sentient beings cannot be saved, they transport it to other Buddha-fields throughout the three thousandfold world system.

When the world is about to be destroyed and the fire-kalpa is about to arise to burn heaven and earth, the myriad streams and rivers will dry up first, and only then will the king of waters (the ocean) subsequently exhaust itself.
It is the same for those who practice minor paths: when the Dharma is about to perish, they are extinguished first;

the Bodhisattva, being courageous and valiant, does not spare his own body to protect and uphold the True Dharma, and only afterwards is he extinguished. [Note: The myriad streams and flows reach the sea.]
Because it is ultimate, it is called the "Water King" verse. There are two types of verses: first, the *gūqi* (isolated verses), and second, the *chóngshòng* (repeated verses).

Because they repeat the meaning found within the prose (*chángxíng*), they are called *chóngshòng*; the verses herein are precisely these repeated verses. Sometimes the prose is detailed and the verses are concise;
sometimes the prose is concise and the verses are detailed. Herein, the prose contains twelve similes, whereas the verses contain only eleven. This is because...

This means that while the prose is detailed, the verses are concise. Furthermore, as the sequence is not arranged in order, it will become clear if one reads the preceding and following sections together.
Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, this Dharma-jewel within the mind does not perish; it abides in the purity of the profound mind.
The Dharma uses these wholesome dharmas to cultivate the path. [Note: The preceding section used the great ocean as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva;
this section concludes by identifying the Bodhisattva with one's own mind. That is to say, both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are alternative designations for one's own mind.
If one does not bring them back to one's own mind, one will invariably push everything off onto the sages and saints, claiming "I have no share in this. Therefore, all sentient beings...
To willingly accept one's lot and voluntarily withdraw from worldly ambition is why such a withdrawal makes it difficult to abandon inferior aspirations;
yet, when these aspirations are brought into alignment, one becomes capable of proceeding toward the path of ultimate truth—this is the intended meaning here.

Just as hundreds of thousands of sentient beings rely upon the ocean, yet it does not become [smaller] for the sake of even a single sentient being, so too is the Bodhisattva’s generation of the mind (cittotpāda):
it is for the sake of liberating all sentient beings. [Note: In the preceding verse, the metaphor of the great ocean was already employed;
why then is this stated again? Is it not redundant? The previous passage used the Bodhisattva’s path-mind as a metaphor for the great ocean, whereas this verse...

The preceding passage converged upon one's own mind, and since one should universally gather all sentient beings through the profound cultivation of wholesome dharmas, one must resolve their minds accordingly.
While the preceding passage was focused entirely on analogies, this section is focused entirely on the Dharma; therefore, there is no redundancy.
The measure of all the great oceans throughout the worlds of the ten directions may still be fathomed;

yet the path traversed by these bodhisattvas cannot be fathomed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. [Note] The preceding metaphor used one great ocean to illustrate that the wisdom and merit of bodhisattvas are immeasurable;
here, it uses all the oceans existing within all the worlds of the ten directions.
There are still things that can be measured, yet the bodhisattva’s practice of the path is beyond measurement, thereby further manifesting its superiority.

Kāśyapa, you should know that among all those who are courageous and diligent, whose minds of dedication and vows desire to become Buddhas and deliver sentient beings, there is not even one who can equal them, let alone surpass them.
[Note] This was what the Tathāgata later told the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa regarding why [the bodhisattvas] are superior.
This is because he possesses great courage and vigor, skillfully confronting the armies of Māra;

he directly pursues the Buddha-vehicle without plotting minor paths, universally delivering sentient beings without seeking his own peace. Therefore, even all those of the Two Vehicles cannot rival him, let alone surpass him.
From this point on, each and every element is resolved back into one's own mind.
This is the attainment of a mass of jewels like the great ocean; this is a worthy field of merit to be honored;

this is the supreme Great King of Physicians, capable of curing the illnesses of all sentient beings. [Note: There are two kinds of illness among sentient beings: those of the body and those of the mind.
Worldly physicians can only treat the body and cannot treat the mind. The Bodhisattva, being skilled in understanding expedient means, treats both body and mind together.
It is said: "He is the Supreme King of Physicians.
He is the refuge of the world, the island of protection, the lamp of illumination, and the ultimate path. [Note: Sentient beings drift upon the ocean of existence;
the Bodhisattva manifests as an island to ensure they are free from peril and fear, acting as their protector.
Because there is a state of abiding that serves as a savior, causing sentient beings to surely reach the other shore without falling into delusion, it is called the ultimate path (*niṣṭhā-mārga*).

It enables those in the world who possess the eye of ignorance to obtain the eye; having obtained the eye, they are able to partake of the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*). [Note: Sentient beings are [afflicted] by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because those who are obscured are likened to those born blind, they are said to lack the eye of wisdom;

yet when Bodhisattvas preach the Great Dharma for them, it causes the Dharma-eye to become clear and bright, enabling them to partake of the nectar of immortality, for the Great Dharma is metaphorically compared to that nectar.
This is being the Dharma King of all worldly phenomena; this is Śakra’s wisdom of decisive judgment. [Note: All phenomena in the world take the true nature (*dharmatā*) as their sovereign.
Because the Bodhisattva has realized the true nature and skillfully expounds the essentials of the Dharma, being peerless in all respects, he is called the "Dharma King.
Formerly, Śakra, knowing his own life was ending and that he was destined to fall into the class of swine, sought...
None of the various non-Buddhist teachers were able to save him, and his doubts only increased further. A wise minister then advised him to take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Upon hearing this, Śakra immediately resolved to take refuge; he was released from his rebirth as a pig and his lifespan was doubled.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the realization of the Unborn.
This is the practice of the Brahma-king in the four dhyānas; this is the ability to turn the Brahma-wheel of Dharma;
this is the Great Wise Guide and Teacher who reveals the true and correct path amidst all false scriptures; this is the valorous one capable of destroying Māra;
this is the purity that eliminates afflictions and defilements; this is the cultivation of pure dharmas like the light of the full moon, lofty and manifest like the sun, with wisdom transcending all.
Like Mount Sumeru; like dense clouds raining down ambrosia; fearless like a lion;
with a mind as supple and gentle as an elephant king; like a mountain of diamond that no externalist can destroy;
pure like water; possessing fierce majesty like a great fire; and like the wind, unobstructed.
To be as immovable as the earth is to uproot the root of pride; to be without discrimination is to be like a medicinal tree;
to maintain pure precepts is to be like a lotus flower; to be unstained by worldly dharmas is to be like the udumbara flower, which appears but once in ten million billion kalpas;
this is to know how to repay the Buddha’s kindness; this is to ensure that the [Dharma] lineage is never interrupted.
The Buddha-seed is the practice of diligent effort; great compassion is the means by which one transcends through loving-kindness and sympathetic joy;
the mind that is able to renounce the five desires is the constant seeking of the jewel-treasure of the Buddha-dharma; practicing generosity is the most supreme;
maintaining pure precepts is to be without equal; patience is to be peerless and brave; and diligent application is to be free from weariness. This is the practice.

Possessing the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they are able to reach immeasurable Buddha-fields, constantly behold the Buddhas, and listen to and receive the Dharma.
As they have heard it, they explain it for others; they know the paths traversed by sentient beings and follow their inclinations, dispositions, and the sharpness or dullness of their faculties.

This is called skillfully knowing the power of expedient means (*upāya-bala*). They are those who kindle the lamp of wisdom and attain the state of salvation; they are those who skillfully know all things.
All phenomena arise from the causes and conditions of harmony and conjunction; this is the definitive understanding of the characteristics of causes and conditions.
To be free from the view of self and to delight in equanimity is the correct contemplation of all phenomena.

To thoroughly know that phenomena come from nowhere and go nowhere, and that the *dharmatā* is eternally abiding and immovable, is to see that all conditioned phenomena are empty, thereby increasing one's great [wisdom].
Compassionately rescuing sentient beings. [Note] The meanings of all the preceding phrases arise from the fact that the Dharma-treasure within this mind is indestructible.
If one knows that the Dharma-treasure of one’s own mind naturally possesses the aforementioned merits, then by tracing each phrase back to its source, they will become clearly intelligible;
thus, there is no need for further annotation. Through pure right contemplation, one realizes that nothing exists.
Coming and going, yet always unmoving; the reason for being unmoving is that all phenomena (*dharma*) possess the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Because one knows this emptiness, one feels compassion for those sentient beings who are attached to inversions (*viparyāsa*), and thus gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
These three sections herein represent the intention of concluding the preceding [discussion] and manifesting what follows. The subsequent text explains how sentient beings are attached to inversions.
This is the underlying meaning.
Sentient beings give rise to deluded thoughts, and because [the Bodhisattva] wishes to deliver them, he practices the Path. [Note: The Bodhisattva penetrates the root and understands the source;
what path could there be to practice? It is only because he wishes to deliver sentient beings that he manifests the practice of the Path to provide an exemplary model for others.
This does not mean that one practices such conduct oneself.
Ordinary beings, through the discrimination of "self" and "what belongs to self," travel upon various false paths.

[Note] This explains that the arising of all the various sufferings of sentient beings—who are deluded by the inversion of attachment—stems entirely from discrimination; thus, they travel upon various false paths. If one is free from delusion...
Where there is conceptualization, there is discrimination; where there is no discrimination, there is nothing. Where there is nothing, how could there be manifold sufferings?
One who is able to clearly understand the true reality (*dharmatā*) of phenomena preaches the Dharma for the purpose of severing all views.
[Note] This is why he preaches the Dharma for the sake of severing the inverted views of sentient beings.

Ordinary people, due to their inverted attachments—perceiving the impermanent as permanent, the impure as pure, the non-self as self, and suffering as pleasure—cannot know the prior limit of birth and death.
One who is able to know this [truth] understands that these arise from inversion: there is no self, no person, and no sentient being.
"I shall thus cultivate the right path regarding the impermanent, the non-pleasant, the non-self, and the impure. [Note: The reason for this is...]
Sentient beings who preach the Dharma do so because they have established four perversions (*viparyāsa*) regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

These four perversions are: to conceive of the mind, which is impermanent, as permanent; to conceive of the body, which is impure, as pure; to conceive of phenomena, which are selfless, as having a self;
and to conceive of sensation, which is suffering, as pleasure. Due to these inversions, [they wander] within the prior limit of birth and death (*pūrvakoṭi*).
The Bodhisattva whose future limit is unknowable teaches the True Dharma so that others may know how to cultivate and realize the four virtues of Nirvana—
permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Kāśyapa,
you should know that regarding the various merits praised by me for this Bodhisattva, they cannot be [exhausted] within his practice.

It is like taking up a single speck of dust from the entire earth; if one gives rise to the bodhicitta and does not regress, even if one were to provide offerings to the three thousand great thousandfold worlds, or if there were further offerings surpassing these, one should offer them all to such a person.

If a person resolves their mind on becoming a Buddha, they are then honoring and making offerings to me, as well as to all the Buddhas of the ten directions in the past, future, and present. They shall likewise be honored by all.
Having paid respectful offerings, [the commentary states]: The aforementioned merits praised thus far do not truly belong to others;

they are all one's own original family wealth. It is only feared that one cannot arouse the resolve to shoulder this burden fully, causing the legitimate heir within the deep palace to willingly become a beggar outside the gate.
If one can truly awaken and realize directly that this is the very reality manifest before one, [one will attain it].
How could accomplishment be attained through ordinary deeds? That which enables one to awaken the bodhicitta allows one to fully receive the offerings of the world.

Fearing that people do not understand that awakening the mind lies within oneself—rather than attributing it to others or seeking it in external, empty matters of reverence—the Tathāgata again explains this with a verse, saying: "If you wish to become a Buddha, do not look outward."

Seeking to be revered, one should respect oneself; fearing that others may not believe, one further cites the Buddhas of the ten directions as witnesses—there is none who did not attain this through respecting oneself.
Thus, one should know that once the bodhicitta has been awakened, one must protect and mind one's own heart;
this is called respect, and this is called making offerings. Therefore, in the Lotus Sūtra, King Bhaiṣajyarāja offered his body as an offering.
The Buddhas of the ten directions praise them with one voice, saying that this is true diligence and true offering;
for by thus burning away the body of ignorance, one is making an offering to one's own Dharma-body.
Chapter Twenty-Two: The Establishment of the Dharma [Note]:

Eight thousand bodhisattvas, having heard this teaching on the firm and vigorous practice of pure conduct, attained the realization of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Their merit is inconceivable, comparable to the great ocean which cannot be measured; this is now set forth in succession.
The twelve similes are employed as metaphors for the Bodhisattva’s great faculties and great practices;
only those who possess such great faculties and great practices are capable of upholding the Great Dharma and circulating this Way so that the lineage of the Buddhas shall not be severed.
Therefore, this chapter is titled "Establishing the Dharma," with the intention of ensuring its circulation.

At that time, the Brahma-son Viśeṣacintin addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying, "You should request the Tathāgata to protect and mind this sutra so that it may be widely disseminated during the final five-hundred-year period of the future degenerate age. Mañjuśrī asked, "What do you think?
Does the Buddha have anything to say or show in this sutra such that it requires protection and mindfulness? Viśeṣacintin replied, "No."
Brahmā, for this reason you should know that all dharmas are without speech, without demonstration, and without protective mindfulness;
these dharmas can ultimately never be extinguished nor can they be protected by mindfulness. If one wishes to protect these dharmas, it is as if one wishes to protect empty space. [Note:
All Mahāyāna sūtras invariably state in their *parīndanā* (circulation) sections that they are "protected by the Buddha's mindfulness," such as in the case of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.]
The sūtra cites the Buddhas of the six directions as witnesses and quotes the *Guangchangshe suohunian jing* (Sūtra on the Protection and Mindfulness of the Broad and Long Tongue).

How can it be that within this [text], Mañjuśrī answers that there is no protection and mindfulness? Is it not the case that the Tathāgata’s teachings throughout his entire life contradict themselves?

However, because all that is said regarding protection and mindfulness in the various sūtras does not transcend the "protection and mindfulness of non-protection and mindfulness," I fear that people might...
Mañjuśrī, in the Sudden Teaching, one directly reveals the single true Dharma-realm and sweeps away all names and words to wondrously penetrate one’s own mind.
Thus, in the preceding "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths," the Buddha told Brahmā:
"The Noble Truths are devoid of falsehood. That which is false is namely: attachment to a self, attachment to sentient beings, and attachment to a person."

To be attached to lifespan, to be attached to nourishment, to be attached to existence, to be attached to non-existence, to be attached to birth, to be attached to cessation, to be attached to saṃsāra, or to be attached to nirvāṇa, O Brahmā—if a practitioner says, "I know suffering," this is false; "I have abandoned the origin," this is false;
"I have realized cessation," this is false; "I have cultivated the path," this is false. Why is this? Because such a person has lost [the true nature].
To lose the Buddha’s protective mindfulness is why it is called false and vain. What is meant by the Buddha’s protective mindfulness?

It refers to not recollecting any dharmas; this is called the Buddha’s protective mindfulness. Previously, being attached to a self and to persons and so forth is the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*);
subsequently, saying "I have severed the accumulation [of suffering]" and so forth is the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). The Buddha does not protect one who clings to these two views.
When mindfulness does not recall anything, both the views of annihilationism and eternalism are simultaneously dispelled;
