thus, that which the Buddha protects through his mindful attention becomes clear and manifest, leaving no further room for doubt.
Herein, Mañjuśrī’s words in response to Brahmā are so intimate and direct that they are like a single stroke of a precious sword, severing the roots of doubt once and for all.
Brahmā Bodhisattva, if he wishes to receive any teaching, he speaks of it as being non-dharmic.
Why is this? Because he has transcended all speech; this is called the Bodhisattva’s delight in the absence of dispute. [Note:

Since sentient beings do not understand that the nature of words is empty within the Tathāgata’s Great Dharma of the Three Vehicles, they frequently give rise to contentious arguments. Therefore, after preaching any sutra, one must necessarily preach the *śūnyatā* (emptiness).
The *Dharani for the Protection of the Reciter of the Mañjuśrī Sūtra* states:

"If there is anything received that is spoken as non-Dharma, this refers to those who do not realize that the nature of words and letters is empty. If one realizes that the nature of words and letters is empty, then this speaking is non-speaking and this listening is non-listening.
Since there is neither speaking nor listening, one transcends all treatises; what room is there for contentious debate?"
Brahmā, if there is a bodhisattva among this assembly who thinks, "Now this Dharma is being taught," you should know that such a person is not one who hears the Dharma.
Why is this? Because it is precisely by not hearing the Dharma that one truly hears the Dharma.
[Note] The preceding passage, "transcending discourse," explained that the Tathāgata has nothing to teach; here, "not hearing" is explained as "hearing."
The Tathāgata has nothing to point out and nothing to preach; since there is nothing to point out, one knows that all phenomena are like empty space.
What, then, is there to protect through mindfulness? That which is called "not protecting through mindfulness" is in truth the fulfillment of protection—namely, protecting one's own mind.
It is here that the meaning is clarified and established.
Brahmā asked, "For what reason do you say that one who does not listen to the Dharma is truly listening to the Dharma?
Mañjuśrī replied, "Not leaking through the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—this is listening to the Dharma. Why is this?

If, within the six internal sense bases, one does not leak [into] forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, then that is listening to the Dharma. [Note: Sentient beings are afflicted by ignorance.]
Covered within, it relies upon the body of the sense organs; externally, it clings to the objects of conditions; in between, it grasps at the consciousness-mind.
Thus, one revolves through the three realms of existence and wanders to and fro among the six paths. To shatter this, the Tathāgata proclaimed the profound essence, which is called the Dharma-wheel.

It causes all sentient beings to internally relinquish the body of the sense organs and externally detach from the objects of conditions. When both the internal and external are empty, where can consciousness find a place to lodge?
When consciousness has nowhere to rest, this is called Bodhi. One who can understand it in this way knows that the Buddha has nothing to speak and I have nothing to hear;
that which cannot be heard, word by word, dissolves back into one's own self.

That which cannot be spoken, dharma by dharma, exists for the benefit of others. Therefore, the Sixth Patriarch said: "Simply believe that the Buddha is wordless, and the lotus flower will [emerge] from [the mud]."
"His mouth has uttered the truth.

At that time, thirty-two thousand devaputras, five hundred bhikṣus, three hundred bhikṣuṇīs, and eight hundred upāsakas in the assembly, having heard what Mañjuśrī had spoken, all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Having attained this patience, they [were established therein].
Having spoken these words: "So it is, so it is, Mañjuśrī! Just as you have said, one who does not listen to the Dharma is indeed listening to the Dharma.
[Note: This Dharma that has been taught must necessarily have those capable of realizing it;

for if there were no such persons capable of realization, it would be difficult to inspire confidence. Therefore, the thirty-two thousand devaputras and others are the persons capable of realizing it.
After this single realization, the responses to challenges are inexhaustible, serving to manifest the inconceivable tenet of this sutra and to perfect this eloquence of joyful speech.
At that time, Brahmā Viśeṣacintin addressed the bodhisattvas who had attained forbearance, saying: "Have you not heard this sutra?"

The various bodhisattvas said: "As we have heard, that which is not hearing is itself hearing. [Note: Those who have not yet attained the mind of awakening are merely called *devaputra* (sons of heaven) or *bhikṣu* (monks);
only after attaining *kṣānti* (patience/endurance) are they named bodhisattvas—those who, it may be said, do not pass through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* (incalculable eons) but protect the *dharmakāya*.
Yet, when it is said that "not hearing is hearing," is this not because one has attained it by hearing this sutra?
Is "not listening" itself a form of listening? Or is it that through listening one awakens to the state of no-listening—this too would be listening.
How can you say it is not listening? Is this not deception? It is not deception. For one who awakens to their own mind awakens to the fact that the Buddha has nothing to preach.
Because one listens to what is unspeakable, there is nothing for me to hear. To awaken to this state of no-listening is to enter [the Way].
Regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is said that "not hearing is hearing.
Again, he asked: "How do you know this Dharma? They replied: "We know it by means of not knowing. [Note:
If one says that not hearing is hearing, then there would be no knowing; since there is no knowing, how can one know this Dharma? He replied:
In this context, to claim knowledge while being ignorant is to transcend all verbal discourse; thus it is called "ignorance. Because the self-nature is clearly manifest, it is called "knowledge.
It is because one knows the self-nature that it is so designated.
He asked again, "By attaining what do you say that you have attained 'patience' (kṣānti)? They replied, "Because all dharmas are unattainable, we say that we have attained patience.
[Note: If there is no hearing, there is nothing obtained externally; if there is no knowing, there is nothing realized internally.
Since there is neither attainment nor realization, what does it mean to say one has "attained patience"? To attain patience means to attain...
The nature of these myriad dharmas is emptiness; because it is solely the emptiness of nature, one attains non-attainment, which is true attainment.
In the *Suyāma-sūtra*, it is asked: "How does one practice in accordance with this Dharma? The answer is: "By not practicing in accordance [with anything], one practices in accordance. [Note:

That which is without attainment and without realization is called the attainment of patience (*kṣānti*). One should likewise practice that which is without practice, practicing that which is without anything to be practiced. How so?
Is it by following that which has no course that one courses? If there were something to follow, it would not be called "following that which has no course.
Only by having no course does one constantly follow the true mark (*dharmatā*) in coursing.
He asked again, "Have you clearly understood and thoroughly penetrated this Dharma?
They replied, "We have clearly understood and thoroughly penetrated all dharmas, because there is neither 'other' nor 'self. [Note: This "Dharma" refers to one's own mind.

Because there is no hearing, no knowing, and no attainment, yet one attains the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) of dharmas—this may be called thorough penetration. Brahmā feared that they might fall into partiality.

Because of this attachment, he specifically asks about the fault within the answer; it is not merely that one clearly understands and penetrates this single dharma, but rather that all dharmas are equally understood and penetrated.
This is because the one is the all and the all is the one, such that there is no distinction between "this" and "that.

If one were only to penetrate this single dharma and fail to understand that all dharmas are equal—where existence and non-existence mutually negate each other to form a pair—one would fall into partiality.

To establish "is" and "is not" simultaneously is not called attaining patience (*kṣānti*). To directly realize one's own mind such that neither a single dharma nor all dharmas are attained—this is called thorough penetration (*prativedha*).
At that time, there was a devaputra in the assembly named Viśuddhalakṣaṇa who addressed the Brahmā Sahantīputra, saying: "If there were..."
If one hears this sutra but the Buddha does not bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), I shall bestow upon them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because this sutra does not subvert cause and effect, and it can give rise to all wholesome dharmas.
[Note]: The Devaputra named Pure Appearance (Viśuddhalakṣaṇa) has no Dharma to hear externally, no mind capable of realization internally, and no patience (*kṣānti*) to be attained within the mind.
His true mind is devoid of all traces; it is a single path, empty and profound, and is therefore called "Pure Appearance. As the ancients said:
"The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the faculties and their objects; simply by being free from delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness (*tathatā*)."
That which is called the "pure mark" is the departure from deluded conditions. Because it is the departure from deluded conditions, it is named *tathatā* (Suchness).

Since the Buddha is solely *tathatā* and his self-nature is primordial, when it is said that "the Buddha does not grant the prediction [of enlightenment], but I do," this refers to what one’s own mind acknowledges for itself.
Therefore it is said: "Only when a person personally consents will they truly encounter [it]. Another commentary explains: "This does not negate cause and effect."

This refers to the inevitable principle that the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit reaches back to the source of the cause; thus it is said that [the nature of hearing] is not destroyed.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If one takes a mind of birth and extinction as the fundamental cause for cultivation, yet seeks the Tathāgata’s fruit of non-birth and non-extinction, such a thing is impossible.
This speaks to the fact that the cause and effect would otherwise be incompatible. This sutra [establishes its teaching] by means of non-hearing.
Without reception, without discourse, without demonstration, without cognition, and without attainment—being fundamentally detached from arising and ceasing—one takes this as the cause;
because the movement toward the fruit is thus inevitable, it is said that "cause and effect are not destroyed."
One is able to destroy the enmity of Māra and depart from all attachment and aversion. [Note: Attachment invites Māra, while aversion brings about enmity;
when this sutra simultaneously dispels both aversion and attachment, the enmity of Māra is thereby shattered.
It enables the minds of sentient beings to attain purity and causes those with faith to all find joy, eliminating all anger and resentment.
[Note: Because there is neither hearing nor knowing, the mind attains purity; because there is no attainment yet it is treated as attainment, anger and resentment are eliminated.
This sutra is that which all virtuous persons cultivate and practice. [Note: "All virtuous persons" refers to the Bodhisattvas;
this distinguishes them from those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), because the followers of the Two Vehicles do not give rise to faith or inclination toward this sutra.
This sutra is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas; this sutra is guarded together by all the devas, humans, and asuras of the world.
[Note: While other sutras mention all eight classes of beings, why does this sutra specifically mention only devas, humans, and asuras, and not the remaining groups?
It is because the faculties of devas and humans are sharp, and their capacities are fit to receive [this teaching].

The Dharma-Asura’s anger is so heavy that it is extremely difficult to arouse the resolve for enlightenment; this is to reveal that there is a specific reason why these true dharmas are both difficult and easy to manifest.
This sutra is definitive and leads to the stage of non-retrogression. [Note: All phenomena reach their ultimate limit in the mind; since they have reached it...
Why would one’s own mind ever regress? This is because this sutra points directly to one’s own mind.
This sutra is not deceptive, for it leads to the site of enlightenment; this sutra is true and real, capable of enabling sentient beings to attain all Buddha-dharmas.

[Note] Because he directly abandons expedient means, it is said that [the teaching] is "true and real. Because he teaches only the unsurpassed path, it is said that he "attains all Buddha-dharmas," which is different from the three vehicles' dharmas.
This sutra is able to turn the wheel of Dharma. [Note: If one realizes one's own mind—that which is called the bodhi of all Buddhas—all issues forth from one's own mind.
This sutra can eliminate doubt and regret. [Note: Because one has not yet realized that all phenomena are but mind, one falsely gives rise to doubt and regret;
once one understands that all phenomena originally stem from one's own mind, then doubt and regret are eliminated.
This sutra can open the way to the holy path. [Note] It is said that one's own mind is the Buddha, that one's own mind makes the Buddha, and that outside the mind there is no Buddha;
since it reveals that the Buddha is precisely one's own mind, it is said to "be able to open" it.
Those who seek liberation should listen well to this sutra. [Note: Although various sutras expound upon liberation, they discuss both the provisional and the ultimate;
however, this sutra points directly to one's own mind without relying on expedient means, and therefore it must be listened to with great care.
Those who wish to attain dhāraṇīs from this sutra should maintain it well. [Note: This sutra takes the absolute, non-contingent single mind as its central tenet;
if one awakens to this mind, then all distinctions will be thoroughly understood. Therefore, one should maintain it well.

This sutra should be skillfully expounded by those who seek merit. [Note: Those who wish to seek merit practice two kinds of giving: the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣa-dāna*) and the gift of the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*).
Between these two gifts, the gift of the Dharma is supreme; therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"For example, suppose one were to bestow all the enjoyments upon all sentient beings of the six realms throughout worlds as numerous as six hundred million *asaṃkhyeya*s."

Even if one were to provide all the requisites for pleasure to those who have reached eighty years of age and further teach them the Dharma so that they attain the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*,
up to *arhat* or *pratyekabuddha*, it would not equal the merit of a fiftieth person who successively rejoices in even a single four-line verse of this sutra;
the former merit does not approach a hundredth part, nor a hundred-thousand-millionth part of the latter.
When compared to even a single instance [of such merit], it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy;
since even the merit of one who merely rejoices lacks any portion of wisdom, how much more so for one who, despite being capable of upholding this sutra, fails to obtain superior merit?
This sutra should be well-contemplated by those who delight in the Dharma. [Note: Now, one who delights in the Dharma may delight in the teachings of the Three Vehicles;
yet if they do not understand their own mind, they will merely possess the name of "delighting in the Dharma" without attaining its reality. This sutra exclusively conveys the single mind.
If one can awaken to this essential principle, then every phenomenon is the mind; by stripping away the empty to preserve the real, one should therefore contemplate it well.
This sutra can bestow happiness leading all the way to nirvana. [Note: Nirvana is described as "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
they are dharmas of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss.

While other sutras employ skillful means to guide beings by referring to what is termed "arising and ceasing" rather than true bliss, this sutra points exclusively to the nature of quiescent extinction, which differs from arising.
Because it is extinguished, it is said to be able to bestow happiness.
If this sutra cannot be severed by Māras, non-Buddhists, or those who cling to acquisitions, then this sutra should receive offerings, and people can follow its meaning.
[Note: The two phrases here are poorly translated; they should read: "Regarding this sutra, people..."
That which has been attained cannot be severed by celestial Māras or followers of external paths, and because it accords with the true meaning, one should receive the offerings of others.
It is not known who among those various realized ones [is supreme]. The first phrase is deficient in meaning;
the intent of this sutra is that for one whose realization is true and firm, celestial Māras cannot sever their roots of goodness, nor can followers of external paths destroy them.
Because his philosophical discourse cannot be refuted by non-Buddhists, he is able to follow that discourse;
because the celestial Māra cannot sever his roots of goodness, he should receive the offerings of others, for it is known that his realization of the meaning is true.
This sutra can cause those of sharp faculties to rejoice; this sutra can cause those of wisdom to be filled with joy.
[Note] "Sharp faculties" distinguishes them from the followers of the Two Vehicles; "wisdom" distinguishes them from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Because non-Buddhists do not believe in this sutra, it is said that although they are clever, they lack wisdom. Because the followers of the Two Vehicles do not fully comprehend this sutra, they are called the Two Vehicles.
Diligence is not the way for those whose minds lack faith or who do not understand the power that exceeds their reach or the truth that surpasses their comprehension;
therefore, one knows that this sutra is cherished only by those of keen faculties and wisdom.

Mañjuśrī, if a Dharma-master can abide in this practice, recite it, and maintain the incantations (*dhāraṇī*), they shall attain these ten powers (*daśabala*) in the present life.

[Note: This conclusion clarifies that the Sudden Teaching (*tun-zong*) is fundamentally different from the Gradual Vehicle (*jian-sheng*); its cultivation and realization over three great eons (*tri-kalpa-asamkhyeya*) are bypassed in a single stroke.
If, when mindfulness is present, one is willing to have confidence that [this] is fundamentally co-existent from the beginning, the Buddha spoke of the power of this mantra-ritual.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings were struck with awe and their hair stood on end;

surrounded by immeasurable hosts of spirits and deities, they approached the Buddha’s presence, prostrated themselves at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, we are the Four Heavenly Kings.”
"O King, those of us who have attained the stage of *srotāpanna* and follow the Buddha’s teaching shall each lead our respective kinsmen,
retinues, and subjects to protect the Dharma Master. If any good man or good woman cherishes the Dharma and is able to uphold,
recite, and explain such sutras as these, we, the Four Heavenly Kings, will constantly go to protect that person wherever they may be."

Whether at a city or a village, in a secluded and quiet place, or whether we are householders or renunciants, we and our retinues shall always attend upon and provide for you, ensuring your mind remains peaceful and free from weariness, and that no one is able to cause you any disturbance. [Note:
In Sanskrit, *srotāpanna* means "one who has entered the stream"; here it refers to the fruit of Stream-entry, having entered the flow of the Noble Path.]
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Not entering into form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas is called a Srotāpanna.

Because the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) do not enter, the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) cease their pairing; because the six sense organs cease their pairing, the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*) become tranquil.
When the organs and objects are completely merged and extinguished, this is called "protecting the Sūtra. The Sūtra is one's own mind; the demons are external objects. [The internal mind...]
If one maintains protection, external objects will cease to cause disturbance;

therefore, the Four Heavenly Kings first declared that because I had attained the stage of Srotāpanna and was able to follow the Buddha’s teachings, they would lead their kinsmen to protect and uphold this sutra.

To say "I have attained the fruit of the sages" is known as a manifestation of the mind of protection. Since one has not yet attained the Path of the Sages, the six sense-objects leak many impurities, and Māra gains an opportunity.
If one suddenly awakens to the fact that the dust of demons cannot enter one's own mind, then what form can external objects take?
If the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*) is correct, then all mental factors (*caitasika*) are protected; hence it is said, "leading all one's kinsmen. Urban centers and the like are places of movement;
empty, secluded places and the like are places of stillness. Remaining at home is to engage with the mundane world; leaving home is to transcend the dust of the world.
Furthermore, for anyone who is willing to protect this mind, whether in motion or stillness, whether engaged with desire or seeking transcendence from the dust of the world,
none of these shall pose any hindrance. Moreover, Blessed One, within a radius of fifty *li* wherever this sutra is located, neither devas nor sons of devas, neither nāgas nor sons of nāgas,
neither yakṣas nor sons of yakṣas, nor kumbhāṇḍas or sons of kumbhāṇḍas, shall be able to find an opportunity to cause harm.
At that time, Virūḍhaka, the World-Protecting Heavenly King, spoke these verses:
"All my retinues, kinsmen, and subjects shall together protect and make offerings to this Dharma-preacher."
At that time, the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa spoke these verses: “I am a prince of the Dharma, born through transformation from the Dharma.
I shall provide for all those sons of the Buddha who seek Bodhi. [Note:
The Heavenly King calls himself a "prince of the Dharma" because he has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and follows the Buddha’s teaching. Furthermore, there are two types of *srotāpannas*.
If one follows the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) to cultivate and realize mere emptiness, this is the Srotāpanna of the Hīnayāna;

if one relies on the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) to cultivate and realize wondrous existence, this is the Srotāpanna of the Mahāyāna. Since the Heavenly King today should be of the first fruit of the Mahāyāna, he is called a "Dharma Prince" (dharmaputra).
That the Son of Heaven has realized the fruit thus clarifies the sign of the wondrous existence that illuminates the ultimate truth within the conventional.
At that time, the celestial king Gandharatha spoke these verses:

“If there are any Dharma masters who can uphold such a sutra as this, I shall constantly provide protection for them throughout the ten directions. [Note: “Such a sutra” refers to that which is without speaking, without showing, without hearing, and without attaining;
therefore, it is said to be free from the marks of words and free from the marks of mental objects—just so.

An ancient said: "If one's exhalation does not involve external conditions and one's inhalation does not dwell within the realm of emptiness, then one constantly turns hundreds of thousands of myriads of scrolls of such a sutra—how could it be limited to only one or two scrolls?"

At that time, the Heavenly King Viśvabhū spoke in verse: "Regarding this person who has resolved their mind upon the Way (bodhicitta), there is no sentient being among all beings capable of providing them with the offerings they deserve.
[Note: The previous passage speaks of "upholding such a sutra," while this one speaks of "resolving the mind upon the Way";
though the expressions differ, the meaning is the same. This is because no sentient being is able to provide the offerings.
Among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is supreme. The offerings prepared by sentient beings do not exceed the four worldly requisites;
however, when a practitioner upholds this sutra, that is the offering of the Dharma, for it is an offering to the Buddhas.

Sentient beings do not participate in this. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "This is true diligence; this is true offering. It continues: "Even kingdoms, cities, wives, and children [are not comparable]."
This is beyond their reach.
At that time, the prince of the Vaiśravaṇa devas, named Subhadra, took a parasol made of the seven treasures and offered it to the Tathāgata, then spoke this verse:
"World-Honored One, I shall now receive and uphold such a sutra as this, and I shall also explain it for the sake of others."
"I possess such a mind. [Note] "Such a mind" refers to the mind that upholds the sutra for oneself and also explains it to others.
The meaning of the verses previously spoken by the Heavenly King merely stated protecting others and did not mention upholding one's own goodness;
thus, it was not yet comprehensive. This son of heaven, however, upholds the sutra for himself and also speaks it for others; this excellence of benefiting both self and others is unsurpassed.
Because it was possible to increase [the merit], the World-Honored One accepted the prediction that he would become a Buddha; this is the broad explanation of his intention.
The World-Honored One knows my mind and my practices in past lives—from the initial resolution to sincerely seek the Buddha-way until now.

Since the World-Honored One possesses the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdha*), I now offer this wondrous parasol, wishing that I may likewise attain such a mark of the invisible crown of the head.

[Note] Not only do I now uphold this sutra and preach the Dharma for others, but I also sincerely dedicate all the merits I have accumulated since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta) in the past, praying only for the Buddha-way and not for any other vehicle.
What is called the "Buddha-way" is precisely the mark of the invisible crown (uṣṇīṣa). Even the Tathāgata himself cannot see the mark of the protuberance upon his own head.
Because it is free from self-view, it is covered by the *uṣṇīṣa* and unseen by others;

because it is free from other-view, it is a ground beyond the reach of both self and other—this is the destination of the Buddha-way. The destination of the Buddha-way is the return to one’s own mind.

Since the mind does not know the mind and the mind does not see the mind, and because the mind does not see the mind, one is free from the views of self and other; this is the metaphor for its attainment.
This is the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa.
With a heart of love and reverence, I gaze up at the World-Honored One, wishing to achieve the pure eye and behold Maitreya Buddha. [Note:
Previously, one offered the canopy to the Buddha and vowed to attain the Buddha-way; here, one relies on the causal conditions of gazing with love and reverence.
"I pray that I may obtain pure eyes to behold Maitreya Buddha. "Pure eyes" refers to the purification of the Dharma-eye.
The World-Honored One, whose wisdom is supreme, immediately replied in verse: "Upon the end of your life here, you shall be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven;
descending from Tuṣita, you shall be born [here again] and behold Maitreya Buddha. [Note: Having been born in that heaven, why do you not see him immediately?
As for why those born in the lower realms can still see [the Buddha], there are two reasons. First, that celestial realm consists of both inner and outer precincts.
The inner precinct is like a royal palace where the sovereign and his immediate retinue reside; the outer precinct is like a provincial town where the common people reside.
If one is born in the outer precinct, one cannot face the Buddha directly, just as commoners cannot have an audience with the sovereign.
Second, while Maitreya is in the heavens, he is merely called a Mahāsattva; as long as he has not yet sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he is not called a Buddha.
After making offerings for twenty thousand years, he will then go forth from home. Having gone forth, he will purely cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya).
During this Fortunate Aeon (Bhadrakalpa), he will see all the Buddhas and make offerings to them all, while cultivating the holy life there.
After sixty billion kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood, named Ratnacchattra (Jewel Canopy).
Your land will be exceedingly majestic and pure, inhabited solely by a community of bodhisattvas to whom you shall preach the sublime Dharma. Your lifespan shall last for one entire kalpa;

after your parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for half a kalpa, benefiting all sentient beings. [Note: At the time Maitreya Buddha appears in the world, the human lifespan is eight thousand years.]
Ten thousand years hence, after twenty thousand years, one shall practice the path while living at home and making offerings, and subsequently go forth as a renunciant.
There are three types of "homes": first, the worldly home; second, the home of the triple world; and third, the home of ignorance.
Now, those who go forth after twenty thousand years leave the worldly home. Those who purely cultivate the Brahma-conduct and make offerings to the Buddhas leave the [other] two.
To receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood is to emerge from the house of ignorance.

The Buddha’s name is Ratnacchattra (Jewel Canopy) because he gives birth to the Dharma-jewel to shelter and nourish all sentient beings; since the celestial son offered the canopy to the Buddha, cause and effect are perfectly aligned from beginning to end.
By upholding this sūtra of the true mark, one leaves behind the defilements of all frivolous conceptualizations.
Therefore, the land is adorned and pure; as they directly inherit the Mahāyāna and do not scheme for the Lesser Vehicle, there are only Bodhisattva-saṃghas and no followers of the Two Vehicles.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra, surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of devas, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
I shall now likewise protect those Dharma-preachers who are able to uphold such a sutra as this; I shall provide offerings and support to wherever this sutra may be located.
When it is being read, recited, or explained, I shall go to that place for the sake of hearing and receiving the Dharma.
Furthermore, I shall augment the strength of the Dharma-preacher and ensure that the sequence of the Dharma-words is not lost or omitted. At that time, Śakra—
The son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, named Gopaka, took a pearl canopy adorned with the seven precious gems and offered it to the Tathāgata, then spoke this verse:
“I always clearly understand the conduct of the World-Honored One;
I shall likewise practice in this way, seeking the all-encompassing wisdom of a Buddha. [Note: To practice in this manner is to practice without practicing. To practice without practicing is...
The Buddha’s practice is to know that those who seek the wisdom of a Buddha should practice that which is non-practice.
World-Honored One, in previous lives, there was no Buddha to whom I did not give; I shall follow this practice and relinquish all that I possess.

[Note]: This commentary explains that when a practitioner relinquishes all external possessions, such as supreme wealth and treasures, as well as internal things, including even their own body and life, and further abandons everything conditioned and unconditioned, mundane and supramundane—this is called the "gift of non-practice.
Therefore, it is said: "there is nothing that is not given."
"Now, before the Dharma King, I shall uphold this sutra and preach it extensively for others to repay the kindness of the Tathāgata. [Note:

A verse from the *Avataṃsaka* says: "Even if one were to carry it on the crown of one's head for kalpas as numerous as dust motes, or offer one's body as a seat throughout the three thousandfold world-system, if one does not transmit the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, there is ultimately no way to repay his kindness; this is because the Tathāgata appeared in the world for this very purpose."
It is said that because it was his original intention to propagate the Dharma, he was naturally able to uphold the sutras himself and also taught them to others, encouraging them to do the same;
this is how one repays kindness. All else is not within his concern.
If one loves and cherishes this sutra, that person is identical to me; I shall provide offerings for them so that they may attain Bodhi.
[Note: What concern is it of mine if others uphold this sutra, such that I would offer worship and protection?
It is because those who uphold the sutra are destined to attain Bodhi and will become the protectors and saviors of all sentient beings. Therefore, for the sake of all...
Since all bodhi flows forth from this mind of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), whoever can maintain this mind will certainly attain bodhi.
Therefore, World-Honored One, while the śrāvakas are unable to protect the Dharma in the future age of terror, I shall protect this sutra.

[Note]: Śrāvakas, being unable to protect [the teaching], are driven by the intensity of their fear and suffering and possess a mind so intent on attaining realization that they cannot follow along within saṃsāra to uphold this sūtra.
Bodhisattvas, however, view saṃsāra as a pleasure grove; only thereafter are they capable [of such protection].
The World-Honored One comforted me and severed the doubts of the devas, saying: "How long will it be before you attain Buddhahood as I have?
Your wisdom is already fully realized; I shall now bestow upon you a prediction: 'In the future, you shall become a Buddha no different from me.
After ten million kalpas have passed, and after another hundred kalpas have elapsed, you shall then attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be King of Wisdom."

[Note]: The Buddha constantly teaches the Dharma to lead people to quickly transcend birth and death; yet this Devaputra does not weary of birth and death, but constantly remains in the final age to protect the sutra.
Because of what these devas doubt, he requests a resolution: "If I thus protect the sutra now, how long until I attain Buddhahood?
That the Buddha immediately grants him a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) is both to comfort the Devaputra and to sever [his doubts].
The doubts of the various devas likewise serve to shatter the attachments of the followers of the Two Vehicles who are deluded regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Previously, the Devaputra Subhūṣa, relying on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as he was directed toward the Path, offered a canopy of the seven jewels; here, because one enters the conventional from the ultimate (*paramārtha*), it is called a "canopy of pearls.
Yet, it is adorned with the seven jewels, signifying that the ultimate does not obstruct the conventional. Thus, it transcends the Three Vehicles and stands as the sovereign among all wisdoms.
Therefore, the Buddha is titled the King of Wisdom.
At that time, Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I shall abandon the bliss of meditative concentration to go to where this Dharma-preacher is.
If there be good men or good women who are able to preach this Dharma, why is this so?"
"From such sūtras as these, Śakra, Brahmā, and all the noble lords have emerged.
World-Honored One, I shall provide offerings to these sons and daughters of good family; they should receive the offerings of all the world’s devas, humans, and asuras.
[Note] Previously it was said that upholding the sūtra leads to the attainment of bodhi; here it is said that upholding the sūtra gives rise to nobility.
Thus one knows that there are no worldly or world-transcending dharmas that do not flow forth from this mind.
At that time, the Devaputra Sublime Brahmā spoke these verses:

"Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, laymen and laywomen of pure faith, whoever is able to receive this sutra is a place of offerings for the world; even if there is but a single person who can practice this sutra..."
I shall preach such a sutra for the sake of others, spreading a seat of manifold exquisite flowers reaching as high as the Brahma-heaven;

seated upon this throne, I shall preach such a sutra. [Note: At any place in the world that is worthy of offerings, wherever this sutra is received and practiced, I shall spread the seat and exhort the preaching of the Dharma so that the life of wisdom may never be severed.
If, in an evil age, one hears this sutra from another, one should give rise to a sense of rare wonder, leap for joy, and exclaim, "Excellent! [Note:
When even during the time of the Buddha’s presence in the world there were many who doubted and slandered this sutra, how much more so will those who hear it in the subsequent evil ages?
If immeasurable worlds were entirely filled with great fires, one must pass through them to hear such a sutra as this. [Note:
Having given rise to a sense of wonder, one should conceive the thought that it is difficult to hear;

then, even if weapons and soldiers are before one, tigers and wolves are behind, and great fires fill the way, one proceeds directly without the slightest fear or hesitation to hear the sutra. Formerly, at Fenyang...
Zhao Gong entered the world and formed a bond of friendship with six individuals—Ciming Yuan, Fahua Ju, Zengye Jue, Dayu Kuan, and others.
Because of obstacles caused by the Five Gō [period of turmoil], they feigned being part of a military company and traveled among them, lodging in the grass and sleeping under the open sky.
They then went to attend upon [their masters], whereupon all obtained the benefits of the Dharma; their fragrance has spread for a thousand ages, serving as an excellent mirror for future students.

Furthermore, one who can open the sutras of the Buddha-way—if there are those who wish to hear them—they should heap up treasures like Mount Sumeru and provide offerings to such a person until they are exhausted.
[Note] This distinguishes the superior; those who wish to hear the sutras and have not yet reached their turn to sit in the assembly should receive offerings even while listening in advance.
In this way, it can be known that the merits of being able to hear, uphold, practice, and explain [this teaching] become increasingly superior.
Of these three sons of gods, the former two rely upon the interval between the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—protecting and upholding the sutra;
since both the ultimate and the conventional are established as skillful means, they receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. The latter one relies upon the Middle Way.
Because the ultimate truth of the Way consists in hearing the sutras and being protected by mindfulness, one does not hear of such matters as receiving the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
Since within the ultimate truth there is neither the attainment of Buddhahood nor the non-attainment of Buddhahood, neither the receiving of a prediction nor the non-receiving of a prediction,
it is called "Wondrous Purity" (Miaofan).
Chapter Twenty-Four:
Entrustment [Note] "Entrust" (*shuku*) means to hand over or to commission; "to trouble" (*ru*) means to weary.

Because the Buddha considers that sentient beings in the final age will lack hearing of this teaching, he entrusts and commissions this unsurpassed Great Dharma to the various great Bodhisattvas and great [Śrāvakas], thereby troubling them with this responsibility.
In future ages, may my disciples not reject birth and death nor loathe saṃsāra as they propagate this sutra,

causing others to resolve their minds for awakening and ensuring that the life-force of wisdom remains uninterrupted. Should anyone receive, uphold, read, or recite it, I shall certainly employ my spiritual power to protect them,
enabling them to achieve success and remain far removed from demonic obstacles.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested his supernormal powers, causing Māra Pāpīyān and his host to come before the Buddha and speak these words:
"World-Honored One, I and my followers now stand before the Buddha and make this vow:
wherever this sutra is circulated, whether it be those who preach the Dharma or those who listen to it, as well as in those lands, no demonic activities shall arise."
"You should protect this sutra. [Note: In Sanskrit, *māra* means "obstruction," for with an evil mind he obstructs the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, at the beginning of the entrustment (*parindanā*), the Tathāgata first manifested supernatural power to subdue Māra, causing him to vow to protect the sutra;
thus, others will not be able to create obstacles. However, there are many kinds of Māras; to speak briefly, they are as follows:...

There are five kinds [of māras]: the māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*), the māra of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-māra*), the celestial māra (*deva-māra*), the māra of desire (*kāma-māra*), and the māra of sleep (*svapna-māra*).
Among these, the māras of desire, sleep, and so forth are all subsumed under the five aggregates and afflictions, and belong to the internal realm;

the ghost-māras (*bhūta-māra*) and environmental māras (*viṣaya-māra*) and so forth are subsumed under the celestial māra and belong to the external realm. According to the facts, when the Māras and their armies behold the Buddha’s spiritual power, [they are subdued].
To resolve with vigor to protect the Dharma is what corresponds to the celestial Māra; yet according to principle, both Māra and his armies are actually the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The Tathāgata is one’s own mind, and spiritual power is its wondrous function. When the mind unfolds its wondrous function, the five aggregates and all afflictions are none other than bodhi;
therefore it is said: "If the mind is deviant, all phenomena are deviant; if the mind is correct, [all phenomena are correct]."
This sutra directly reveals that these various phenomena are precisely one's own mind, differing from other sutras which remain mired in mundane matters;
thus, it is known that they are indeed one's own mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted golden light that illuminated this world and addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "The Tathāgata..."
Now, because he protects and maintains this sutra for the benefit of all Dharma masters, this sutra shall remain in Jambudvīpa for as many years as there are until the Buddha-dharma does not perish.
[Note] "Golden light" refers to the light of true wisdom; "illuminating this world" means that this defiled land is thereby transformed into a Dharma-nature land.
His addressing Mañjuśrī indicates that this alone is the fundamental source.

The practitioner is able to realize this land of the light of dharma-nature; thus, it is revealed that this very body and land are pure despite being defiled, for there is no separate purity elsewhere.
Because there is no separate purity elsewhere, one need not loathe this world or long for another;
rather, by remaining in this land, one is protected and mindful as they uphold this sutra. This is how the intent of the entrustment is fulfilled.
At that time, the sentient beings in the assembly scattered all kinds of flowers, all kinds of incense, and all kinds of powdered incense upon the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we pray that this sutra may long abide in Jambudvīpa and be widely proclaimed and disseminated.
[Note] Flowers symbolize causal practice; incense symbolizes faith; powdered incense represents subtle faith. This is because there is no [fixed] practice.
Because they practice, they extensively gather all forms of conduct; thus it is said "all flowers.
Because they take faithless states as the essence of faith, thereby perfectly exhausting all modes of faith; thus it is said "all incense.

Because through this true faith and by conforming to that signless holy life (*brahmacarya*), they are capable of proceeding toward the fruit of Buddhahood; thus it is said "they scatter them upon the Buddha," [indicating] the cause.
This is the sign of proceeding toward the fruit.
Thereupon the Buddha asked Ānanda, "Will you receive and uphold this sutra? Ānanda replied, "Yes, indeed; I shall receive and uphold it.
"Ānanda, I now entrust this sutra to you; receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it extensively for others. [Note] As...
Regarding the passage where [the Buddha] comes before the Bodhisattvas and addresses Mañjuśrī within the Vaipulya assembly:

because Mañjuśrī is the eldest son capable of inheriting the family legacy, Master Li (Li Tongxuan) correlates Mañjuśrī with the trigram Gen. Gen represents the feet, which possess the capacity for guidance;
thus, he was entrusted to protect the sutra in the末世 (final age) and to lead and uplift future students. As for the Śrāvakas...
The reason for the specific entrustment to Ānanda in the middle [of the sutra] is that Ānanda was the disciple entrusted with dhāraṇī who compiled the Dharma-treasury so that it might be circulated.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if a person receives, maintains, reads, recites, and explains this sutra, how much merit will they obtain?"

The Buddha Guṇarāja said to Ānanda: "If one were to provide all manner of requisites for pleasure throughout one's entire life to as many Buddhas and their Saṅghas as there are letters, phrases, and syllables in this sutra, and if another person were to offer reverence, respect, and praise to this sutra—even to the point of making offerings to it—the latter’s merit would be superior.
[Note: This passage describes the merit of upholding the sutra as set forth in the *Cangjing* (Sutra of Constant Recitation).]
The sands of the Ganges, the atoms of the seven treasures, the lands, the two vehicles, and even the offerings made to all Buddhas can all be counted and known;
how could this [sūtra] not surpass other sūtras? It is not so. Why is it that the excellence and inferiority of their merits are as they are?
It is because all the words, letters, and phrases herein are themselves the mark of Suchness (*tathatā*); since Suchness is inexhaustible, the merit is likewise inexhaustible.
Even if one were to exhaustively compare it to the sands of those rivers, seven precious jewels would not suffice as an analogy for even a ten-thousandth part;
for this sutra is a teaching of sudden enlightenment that does not establish numerical quantities, but merely follows the literal words.
This person shall, in the present life, attain ten treasuries of virtue. What are these ten? They are: seeing the treasury of the Buddha, because they obtain the divine eye;
hearing the treasury of the Dharma, because they obtain the divine ear; and seeing the treasury of the Sangha, because they attain the stage of non-retrogression within the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
[Note: The name "Sangha" means harmony. Because one realizes that the fundamental nature of all dharmas is originally without harmony, one attains non-retrogression. If...
To fail to penetrate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) while clinging to the existence of composite conjunctions is the view of ordinary beings, not that of a Bodhisattva.
This is because they possess an inexhaustible treasury of wealth and the "jewel-hand" (*ratnapāṇi*). [Note:

The "jewel-hand" refers to the Bodhisattva who, having ascended to the first stage (*bhūmi*), possesses millions of *asaṃkhyeya* offerings, including incense, flowers, pavilions, banners, streamers, jeweled canopies, and even the seven treasures of gold and silver.
Because all articles of sustenance emerge from his palms, and because he increases [virtues] stage by stage (bhūmi) up to the final ground, he is called "Jewel-Handed" (*Ratnapāṇi*).
Because his treasury of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is endowed with the thirty-two marks, he is the "Treasury of Retinue," having obtained an indestructible retinue.
[Note: Worldly retinues have both unions and separations, whereas the supramundane retinue always assembles together. As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* says:
All afflictions are my retinue.

Because I have attained the *dhāraṇī* of the Dharma-treasury of that which has not yet been heard, I possess the treasury of mindfulness; because I have attained the treasury of eloquence, I am free from fear;
because I have destroyed all the treatises of external paths, I possess the treasury of merit; and because I benefit sentient beings, I possess the treasury of wisdom.

Because it preserves all the Buddha-dharmas, when the Buddha preached this sutra, seventy-two nayutas of sentient beings attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
and countless sentient beings, no longer clinging to any dharmas, exhausted their outflows (*āsrava*) and attained liberation of mind. At that time, Ānanda immediately rose from his seat...
Rising from his seat, baring his right shoulder, and bowing his head at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, what shall this sutra be named? How should it be upheld? The Buddha told Ānanda: “This sutra is named ‘The Compendium of All Dharmas’; it is also named ‘The Adornment of the Buddhas’;
it is also called ‘The Questions of Brahmā Viśeṣacintin’; and it is also called ‘The Discourse of Mañjuśrī. It should be so titled.
Uphold this. [Note] Herein, four names are listed in succession: the first two pertain to the Dharma, and the latter two pertain to persons.

Regarding the two aspects of the Dharma, the former subsumes the immeasurable into the single Way of True Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), while the latter reveals the one as the Way of the wondrously existent (*prabhāsvara*) in its immeasurable manifestations.
Both of these are inherently possessed within our own single mind and must not be treated in a partial manner.
The term "both" (*jien*) is used because they are presented together. Regarding these two [aspects] within human beings: first, their names are established based on *upāya-jñāna* (expedient wisdom);
second, their names are established based on *mūla-jñāna* (fundamental wisdom). These two are mutually constitutive from beginning to end and serve as reciprocal conditions for one another;
since neither can be dispensed with, they are presented together.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince, the Brahma-son Siṅhaghoṣa,
the Elder Mahākāśyapa who practices as a bodhisattva, the Venerable Ānanda, the assembly of devas, and all the people of the world received and upheld the Buddha’s words,
and they were all greatly filled with joy.
A Brief Commentary on the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Fascicle Four (End)
